title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in Dallas
summary: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
story: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
DALLAS -- Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.

Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of an escalating feud between Conway and Noble that had lasted years. Both men lived in Dallas.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.

Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.

During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued prosecutors hadn’t proven their case. “This is capital murder and the state has brought you a lot of speculation," defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody,” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.

title: After 8 nominations without a win, Glenn Close is 'overwhelmed' by honorary Oscar
summary: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
story: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
When Glenn Close got the call that she’d been chosen to receive an honorary Oscar, the 79-year-old actor had two somewhat unconventional thoughts.
“My first reaction was I don’t need a consolation prize,” Close told The Associated Press in a recent interview. “And my second reaction was, I don’t know … do I want to end my loss record?”

Close does indeed have an Oscars record going: Over the course of her career, she’s been nominated for acting prizes eight times and never won. It’s a distinction she has worn with grace and humor over the years, and she’s in good company: Peter O’Toole was similarly nominated eight times without a win.

The honorary Oscar, also known as the Academy Honorary Award, is indeed different from a competitive Oscar. Although the golden statuettes are the same, the award is not given for a specific film, but for a body of work and contributions to the motion picture industry. The voters, or rather selection committee, is also much smaller: The film academy’s Board of Governors as opposed to the entire Academy membership. There are no “losers.” And, since 2009, the prizes have been presented not during the Academy Awards but in a separate event in Los Angeles known as the Governors Awards.

Perhaps most importantly, however, with no broadcast television cameras, the Governors Awards have the luxury of time, for touching montages and thoughtful speeches by friends and collaborators, and the honorees themselves. There is space to reflect without the pressure of a ticking clock, or an orchestra ready to play you off.

“I’m still processing it and it means it means a lot, you know, at this point in my life,” Close said. “I’ve been a working actor for over 50 years, I got my first Oscar nomination 43 years ago. So it’s been a life, you know? And it’s overwhelming.”

The occasion has Close thinking about her own history with the Oscars, and how much things have changed over the years. Her first nomination came for her first film role, in George Roy Hill’s “The World According to Garp.” She remembers receiving the news while shooting “The Big Chill,” where her performance as Sarah Cooper, the woman hosting the gathering after the death of their friend, would earn her a second nomination.
“It was the furthest thing from my mind,” Close said. “I never even thought about the possibility of being nominated for an Oscar. I still can remember my absolute astonishment.”

The thing that she remembers most about that first ceremony, held at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in 1983, was what she wore: “The most beautiful little velvet dress,” she said, designed by her friend, costumer Ann Roth.

Some of her memories are about what other people wore, like the one time she sat behind Madonna and marveled at her “fabulous” white fur. Then there was the year she was nominated for “Fatal Attraction,” when there was a whole section of the crowd outside that had styled their hair in tight curls like her character, Alex Forrest.
“That was fabulous,” she said.

What was a little confusing, however, was when she walked out to present an award with her co-star Michael Douglas and the audience laughed. She was eight months pregnant at the time and had to fly to Los Angeles on a private plane, with her OB-GYN as chaperone, because she wasn’t allowed to fly commercial.

“At first, I thought, why are they laughing?” Close said. “And we realized it was because in the movie, I say I’m pregnant with this child and he doesn’t want to have anything to do with it, denies it, and there was always a question whether she really was telling the truth or not. And there I was, hugely pregnant, walking out with Michael. So it was very funny.”

Douglas recently made headlines for saying on The Graham Norton Show that Close deserved to win that year. When asked if she was surprised that he’d said that, Close paused and said: “Publicly, yeah.”
While the phrase “it’s an honor to be nominated” has become a bit of a cliché, it’s also a kind of mantra for Close, who has never done a role thinking that it would lead to awards.

“I have the DNA of an outsider,” Close said. “So because of that, I’ve always felt the greatest honor was to actually be in the room … the winner loser thing — especially in the temperature of our country now — for me, does not apply. The fact that you are in the room with some of the most creative people on the planet is what counts.”

She hasn’t decided where she might put her statuette in her home, but she is already thinking about how she can share it with the people of Bozeman, Montana. Close has been grateful to be able to continue working as much as she does (just this year she’s appeared in the Spanish language epic and presumed Oscar nominee“La Bola Negra,” the latest season of “All's Fair” and a new Hunger Games movie ). But her ability to leave, to go home to a place away from Hollywood, is the thing that allows her to recharge between performances.

“In some ways, I want to share it with the community here,” she said. She wants to find a place where, “for a day, people can go and see what a real Oscar looks like.” And she has an idea for where: A “fantastic bakery called the Wild Crumb.” But, she added, she hasn’t talked to them about it yet.
At the Governors Awards on Sunday, Close will be accompanied by her daughter and son-in-law, and wearing a custom Armani gown, which she’s very excited about.

The honorary Oscar doesn’t negate Close’s competitive Oscars record either. O’Toole also received one, in 2003, after all. Now, she’s just feeling grateful and putting the finishing touches on her speech.
“It’s incredibly special and it’s a huge honor,” Close said. “I don’t know how I’m going to get through it because it’s very emotional for me. But I will somehow.”

title: Irma P. Hall, 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers' actor, dies at 91
summary: Irma P
story: Irma P

Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.

Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.

She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”

Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.

“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”

Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.

Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.

Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.

In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”

In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Movie Review: James Gray delivers a milestone crime drama in ‘Paper Tiger’
summary: Miles Teller and Adam Driver play brothers trying to work on a deal in 1986 New York in James Gray's “Paper Tiger.”
story: Miles Teller and Adam Driver play brothers trying to work on a deal in 1986 New York in James Gray's “Paper Tiger.”

The American Dream has seldom looked so bleak as in “Paper Tiger,” James Gray’s beautifully punishing tragedy about a middle class family in Queens. With operatic grace and 35 mm grit, “Paper Tiger” shrewdly and authentically explores ideas about wealth, worth, the cost of family and the price of wanting more.

In 1986 New York, Wall Street might be booming in its “greed is good” era, but across the East River — where the grass still grows tall and the twin towers look small and distant on the skyline — Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) is up early making storm windows for the winter. This is being done very much against the wishes of one of his teenage sons, who is trying to sleep in. Winter is three months away anyway, he complains.

Irwin is an ordinary dad, kind and a little goofy, resplendent in a constant stream of neatly but not stylishly tucked-in plaid shirts and windbreakers. He seems older than his years, though he’s probably barely 40. Part of that might be due to the choices Teller has made for his voice and accent, sounding a little like Peter Falk in “The Princess Bride,” but it’s also spiritually true that every generation gets to believe that all the ones prior were always “old.”

Irwin is married to Hester ( Scarlett Johansson ), a practical but spirited woman who has started to fantasize about life in the suburbs. They live in a modest house where you can practically feel the texture of real life. It's a home of laughter, love and schoolwork — both parents dream of their boys going to Ivy League schools and doing better than they did. The boys also have their eyes on a fancier life, whining, “Why do we always have to buy crappy stuff and live crappy?”

They wouldn’t be the first ungrateful teens who fail to recognize just how good they have it. But they get glimpses of the rich life in their uncle Gary (Adam Driver), a former police officer who now does quite well as a security consultant. He has the suit and car, and the grand gestures he makes seem casual. When we meet him, he’s dropped by Irwin and Hester’s with a steak dinner for five from “Luger's.”

Gary proposes an idea to his brother, an engineer with a specialty in risk assessment: There’s a project in the works to clean up the Gowanus Canal, and they might be able to help. The businesses, once controlled by the mafia, are being taken over by Russian immigrants. Gary has spotted an opportunity to help them navigate the ins and outs of regulations.

The offer of a windfall comes as a relief for Irwin, stressed by the looming cost of college for two kids. Gary, too, is going through an expensive divorce. Irwin wonders if there is something shady beneath it all, but Gary reminds him that “we’ve never played in the dirt.” Still, there’s a foreboding feeling that this is not going to be as simple, clean and easy as Gary is promising. The movie, after all, began with a quote from Aeschylus: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.”

It’s only a matter of time before things start going very wrong: One night, Irwin takes his boys out for a “nighttime risk assessment,” and they soon find themselves swarmed by paranoid Russian goons with guns.

Gray, who finds new notes in a genre he’s already put his mark on with films like “Little Odessa,” “The Yards” and “We Own the Night,” is masterful at slowly, methodically building tension and dread to an almost unbearable crescendo. The decisions these brothers make, first together, then separately, take on the grandeur and weight of a classic tragedy.

Hester, meanwhile, becomes a physical manifestation of the polluted canal as she endures her own secret health crisis. Like many mothers before and after her, she feels it is her duty to bear the weight of a death sentence in private. There are louder, uglier, bigger things happening all around and she doesn’t want to worry anyone. It’s a beautiful performance from an actor who often gets lost in franchise and spectacle.

But it’s Driver who really steals the show as a man doomed by the responsibility he feels for his brother. Beneath Gary's easy smile, charm and flash festers a different kind of heartbreak and loneliness. He can also be shockingly violent. And, when it comes down to it, the brotherly loyalty and desire to protect at any cost might only go one way.

It builds to one of the more thrilling and inventive showdowns in recent film history — a rare movie that embraces, rather than tries to disguise, the omnipresent sound of planes taking off and landing at a nearby airport.

The whole grimy affair is agonizing, as everyone tries in vain to do the right thing. The morbid joke is that it was rigged from the beginning — not just the job, but the entire system, the false promises of capitalism, the ways in which corruption is enabled, and the paradox of honest wealth.
“Paper Tiger” may be set 40 years ago, but in the most fundamental way, it’s not a movie about our past.

“Paper Tiger,” a Neon release in select theaters Friday and nationwide on Nov. 20, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “language and some violence.” Running time: 115 minutes. Three and a half stars out of four.

title: Jordan Firstman has been a lot of things, but 'Club Kid' confirms he's a filmmaker
summary: It’s taken some time but Jordan Firstman, with “Club Kid,” feels like he’s finally made it
story: It’s taken some time but Jordan Firstman, with “Club Kid,” feels like he’s finally made it
NEW YORK -- When Jordan Firstman arrives for lunch at a Manhattan bar, he sees a burger on one side of the table, and a salad on his.
“What are you guys trying to tell me?” he asks with mock offense.

Firstman isn’t on a diet but he is trying to keep himself in line. His directorial debut, “Club Kid,” is one of the year’s biggest breakthroughs. In it, Firstman stars as a gay New York party promoter named Peter who’s blindsided by a hard-to-fathom revelation: He has a 10-year-old son (Reggie Absolom).

Since its debut at the Cannes Film Festival, “Club Kid” — vivid with downtown nightlife that Firstman knows firsthand — has been a sensation. After a bidding war, A24 picked it up for $17 million and is releasing the film in the heart of awards season. Minutes before sitting down for a recent interview, “Club Kid” was nominated for best feature and Firstman for breakthrough director by the Gotham Awards.

Beginning with the Cannes premiere — where Firstman reveled in puns of the theater’s name, Debussy — it’s been a surreal ride for the Los Angeles-based viral comic turned filmmaker. His movie dreams have come true, but there are perils in being famous for “Club Kid.”

“When you make a movie like this and have a culture surrounding it, people are shoveling drugs in your face. It’s a big exercise in saying no,” Firstman says. “I messed up once and I didn’t again. You could see it in my eyes in press the next day. But I want to be on my game.”

Firstman, 35, has been a viral video star (you might remember his pandemic bit as the publicist for banana bread), a consultant on “Big Mouth” and a writer for HBO’s “Search Party.” He’s released a comedy-music album (based on secrets shared by Instagram followers) and been an increasingly accomplished actor, on the series “I Love LA” and the 2023 film “Rotting in the Sun.”

But with “Club Kid,” Firstman has finally arrived at the role he always most wanted: filmmaker. Eleven years ago, Firstman made the short “Sold.” about a needy screenwriter celebrating a breakthrough that may be imagined. Now that he has arrived, he intends to stay.

“This is the first time of my career I’ve actually had the mind to be like: There’s something more important than what I’m saying. I’ve said the wrong thing in the past and I’ve gotten punished for it,” says Firstman, who last year was slammed online for criticizing the authenticity of gay sex on “Heated Rivalry.” “My movie is so important to me that if I have an opinion, I’m telling my friends or I’m keeping it to myself. You could ask me about my least favorite movie right now, and I’d be like: ‘I really liked it, actually.’”

“Club Kid” stands out for its unique duality. It’s a crowd-pleaser with a plot not unlike Adam Sandler’s “Big Daddy,” but it’s also a moving and faithful depiction of gay life. It’s an edgy, ketamine-covered movie about club life, but it’s also a tender movie about growing up.
Those dichotomies — sweet and childlike, provocative and satirical — Firstman believes are his superpower.

“I’ve gone so back and forth on the subject of: Am I mainstream?” Firstman says. “There’s something maybe about my look that feels familiar to people. I think I feel like people’s cousin, or something. But then my insides are very specific and broken and transgressive and subversive. I have perversions. I have issues that are unsavory. My gift, and this is going to sound sexual, is making hard things soft.”
Firstman smiles. “And I’ve done it before. I’ve made a lot of hard things soft.”

The story of “Club Kid” may sound contrived, but it comes from a more personal place than its narrative twist suggests. Even that has some truth. Firstman, just after finishing the script, was a sperm donor for his older sister's wife.

Firstman's screenplay attracted Alex Coco, producer of Sean Baker's best picture-winning “Anora.” “Club Kid,” shot on 35 mm, similarly became an authentic portrait of New York, shooting in real, underground parties. The colorful ensemble includes Miss Benny, Alaska Riley and Saturn Risin9 as Peter’s hard-partying friends.

“A lot of it was similar to how we approach Sean’s movies: casting people from the community, whether they’re first-time actors or seasoned actors,” Coco says. “Shooting in real locations, embracing the chaos of shooting in a living, breathing world.”
For Coco, Firstman may have played around with different personas, but “Club Kid” represents his true self.

“He’s becoming who he always was. He started off with shorts early in his career wanting to tell meaningful, personal stories about the queer experience,” Coco says. “He’s so talented that he’s able to succeed creatively in almost everything he does. But I think the most natural state of who he is is this version, which is a more serious, big-hearted filmmaker.”

In one memorable scene in “Club Kid,” Peter and a love interest played by Diego Calva exchange sincere reflections on their earliest sexual encounters. Firstman, the son of journalists for Newsday, grew up in Northport, Long Island, making weekend trips into Manhattan as a teen. For Firstman, that scene reflects his own coming of age.

“It’s a very New York gay thing to not take your own trauma seriously, or think it’s not worth it,” he says. “I had that happen to me when I was a kid by a couple people — some consensual, some less so. I think throughout my whole 20s, I was just like, ‘Haha!’ Then I got into my 30s and started going to therapy and taking it more seriously.”
Firstman shrugs and smiles. “Damaged goods,” he says.
Yet Firstman usually projects uber-confidence, which he acknowledges has shaped perceptions of him.

“I have my moments, for sure,” he says. “I do think to be gay is to be broken. But I think there’s something very beautiful about brokenness. I think that’s why all my characters have that shield around them or a harder edge. Deep down, they’re very sensitive and sad. Peter is the first time I got to really just show my heart. I think there’s been this perception of me that I’m, like, a b----”
“I have some unsavory qualities like anyone else,” adds Firstman. “But I did just want to show the world a little bit who I am.”

Meanwhile, Firstman is getting used to his new life as an acclaimed, Cannes-approved auteur and — maybe more surprisingly — a monogamist. He's now “in some form of a relationship,” he says. Acting on an instinct, Firstman invited someone he had met only once to Cannes. Just as his movie launched, he was falling in love. “A lot,” he sighs, “was happening at once.”

The arrival of so much maturity, Firstman grants, has been head-spinning. Yet his mischievousness is far from gone. When it comes time for Firstman to leave for a photo shoot uptown, he stands and makes one request: “Give me a good headline,” he says. “All people read is the headline.”
Any suggestions?
Firstman hardly pauses. “Jordan Firstman is a talented, childlike genius,” he says, grinning. “And hot.”

title: At Sing Sing prison, incarcerated men get preview of new PBS documentary on nation's justice system
summary: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system
story: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system

OSSINING, New York -- As the lights dimmed inside the chapel at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility in New York, around 30 incarcerated men sat scattered across the pews, waiting to preview a new docuseries on the history of the nation’s criminal justice system.
Our Lady of Hope chapel was soon abuzz with discussion, as some learned new things about an American institution with which they already have a great deal of personal experience.

The four-part series, “Crime and Punishment in America,” is set to premiere Monday on PBS. It spends eight hours tracing how the justice system evolved, from the colonial period to present day, and viewers get to hear from legal scholars, formerly incarcerated people, victims’ families and corrections officers.

The U.S. maintains the world's largest incarcerated population, with nearly two million people behind bars in prisons and jails. In 2024, each state incarcerated more people per capita than most countries, according to the Prison Policy Initiative.

“What are we hoping to accomplish with this?” film director Lynn Novick said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Digging into the history and revealing it will help us to have a different conversation about what justice means in this country.”

Novick developed the series with frequent collaborator Ken Burns, an acclaimed filmmaker with numerous PBS documentaries to his name. In 2019, the two partnered on “College Behind Bars,” which followed a Bard College program to provide a liberal arts education to incarcerated people.

Sing Sing was Novick’s sixth screening for prison populations in correctional facilities: Maine, Connecticut, California and Washington state prisons, as well as New York City’s Rikers’ jail, have hosted previews of “Crime and Punishment in America.”
Sing Sing prisoners were shown a 47-minute reel from the full series.

“I hope that as people see this documentary, that they are challenged to think about what we have to do differently,” said Michael Shane Hale, 54 and from Kentucky, who has served 32 years of a 50-to-life prison sentence.

Hale said the viewing public should no longer question whether it's possible for prisoners to turn their lives around. The question, he added, should instead be “what do we do with transformed people?”

The conversation at Sing Sing was more animated than Novick had anticipated. Some of the prisoners gathered in the chapel were invigorated by news of California Gov. Gavin Newsom saying he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.

Several prisoners inundated a panel of speakers with concerns about what rehabilitation through incarceration looks like for their families and for victims. Others drew connections between their crimes, mental illness and economic circumstances.

“Nobody is the sum of their worst mistake, right?” said José Colon, 44 and from the Bronx, who entered prison at age 17 and has been incarcerated for nearly 28 years. “No matter where you are in life, there’s always room for growth.”
John Rizzo, another Sing Sing prisoner, asked the panel what “rehabilitation” means to society.
“When we come in here, we’re tainted,” Rizzo said later in an interview with the AP. “When we go back out into society, when is the incarcerated individual going to be acceptable again?”

Rizzo has served 16 years so far on a conviction for conspiracy and attempted murder. He said he spends his time helping peers apply for prison jobs and studying for a bachelor’s degree in behavioral science that he intends to earn while incarcerated.

Reginald Dwayne Betts, a panelist and poet who served eight years for a carjacking at 16, agreed with Rizzo. He said people seemed to focus on his past when he returned to life after prison. “It was always, ‘Can you tell me more about your crime?’” he said.
Betts has created a documentary following his life and became known for his work installing libraries in the nation’s prisons.

Daniel F. Martuscello III, the first former correction officer appointed commissioner of the New York State Department of Correction, said he agreed to screen Novick's film because he sees it as an extension of the prison’s Rehabilitation Through the Arts workshops.

“It’s our obligation, not only as commissioners, but as people running the system, lawmakers, to make sure that we’re telling that story,” Martuscello said. “Because to not do so, it takes away from that transformation, and really, it degrades public safety.”

John J. Lennon is an incarcerated Sing Sing prison journalist and a recipient of a 2026 Guggenheim Fellowship, a prestigious and competitive grant to support scholars, artists and scientists for work “under the freest possible conditions.” In-prison programs, he says, are what allowed him to build a writing career after entering prison with a ninth-grade education.
He said New York, and the nation as a whole, has much more reform work to do.
“If you want accountability in America, then there has to be forgiveness on the table,” Lennon said. “There has to be mercy on the table.”

title: US visa restrictions force some African contestants out of Miss Universe competition
summary: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration
story: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico because of visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration, while two others are struggling to obtain visas.

Representatives from Zambia and the Republic of Congo have withdrawn from the pageant, which takes place this month in the U.S. territory, after failing to secure visas. Contestants from South Sudan and Zimbabwe are still awaiting theirs.
The United States has imposed sweeping travel restrictions affecting dozens of countries, many of them in Africa, under proclamations issued during Trump’s second administration.

Last December, the administration expanded restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while maintaining a full suspension of entry for nationals of the Republic of Congo and South Sudan.

“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement this week announcing the withdrawal of their representative, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka.

In the Republic of Congo, Georgina Kambongo made history when she was crowned the Central African country’s first Miss Universe representative. National organizers say her inability to travel to Puerto Rico is linked solely to Trump’s travel restrictions.

“American visa challenges have delayed that journey, but the fight is not over,” Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, said in a social media post. “After months of preparation, I am not giving up. I remain confident that God who began a good work in me will bring it to completion.”
In South Sudan, organizers said contestant Adut Deng’s participation remained uncertain despite months of efforts to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals.
“South Sudan deserves to be seen, heard, and represented. Our queen carries the hopes, dreams, beauty, and resilience of a nation,” organizers said in a statement.
The competition’s 75th edition is expected to attract up to 120 contestants. Delegates began arriving in Puerto Rico on Sunday for rehearsals and other preliminary activities.
A national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, followed by swimsuit and evening gown segments the following day. The winner will be crowned on Nov. 24.

title: British women to receive automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
story: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
LONDON -- British women convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will be automatically pardoned Monday, the government said.
The action follows Parliament's passage last year of a landmark vote to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section from the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons and some will be issued posthumously.

“For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police had investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once “dragged from hospital beds to police cells” and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

“This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they’ve always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for “compassion, not punishment.”

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant more than 10 weeks.

title: Doctors are raising concerns about US babies born with measles
summary: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles
story: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles
For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.

From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday.
“This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.

The condition's emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it's had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases.

“We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn't happen.

The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn't get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert.

Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania's health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation.

People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles.

“What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.”

Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth.

MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications.

If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says.

Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal.

Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That's something that sadly we're learning more about,” he said.

Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots.

This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas.

“We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York.

title: Huge crowds, low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as pope visits South America
summary: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
story: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles.
Cases are already surging in the region this year and mass gatherings provide an opportunity for one of the world's most contagious viruses to spread further.

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, and officials in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru have been preparing for potential problems to different degrees for months, including mounting vaccination campaigns and increasing surveillance to try to limit spread.

Uruguay, where thousands of people attended a prayer vigil and a Mass celebrated by Leo, implemented a nationwide intensified surveillance monitoring period until Nov. 29, three weeks after Leo’s departure from the country, according to Nataly Rodriguez, director of epidemiology at Uruguay’s health ministry. Uruguay has also taken steps to boost its vaccination rate to among the highest in the region.
“As a preventive strategy, the ministry has been emphasizing the importance of keeping vaccination schedules up to date,” Rodriguez said.

The Nov. 6-17 trip to the continent where around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics live marks a return home for Leo, who spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop.

Ahead of the visit, PAHO assessed the public health risk of measles in the context of the religious mass gatherings in South America as “very high.” That's in part because there has been a nearly five-fold increase in cases between January and October compared with the same period last year.
“We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized,” said Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO. “It’s a very complex situation.”

Measles spreads easily through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. A person can be contagious even before they show symptoms. The virus first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes and a rash. It most commonly affects children and while it usually isn’t fatal, it can be.

The vaccine for measles is extremely effective, but the first of two doses is not usually recommended for babies until their first birthday. In order to stop the disease from spreading in a community, to protect infants and others who can't get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated with two doses.

As of 2025, only Uruguay had achieved that number, according to data from the World Health Organization. Peru has reached 90% with one dose and 82% with two doses while Argentina has reached only 84% with one dose and 55% with both doses.

PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and the end of October, nearly five times the number recorded during the same period in 2025. At least 81 people have died so far this year due to the disease.
With nearly 3,000 cases, Peru has seen the fourth highest number of cases in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.
In the five Peruvian cities Leo will be visiting including Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa, a total of 170 measles cases have been identified so far in 2026.

Ahead of the Pope’s visit, Salas Peraza said PAHO had supported efforts to encourage vaccination in Peru, including initiatives targeting adolescents, deploying equipment to strengthen vaccine storage and delivery capacity, and intensifying vaccination along the border with Brazil.

In late October, authorities carried out measles vaccination campaigns in areas with the highest rates of transmission. These included a dose for babies aged six to eleven months, as well as vaccination for people up to 29 years old.
By the end of September, 1.2 million vaccine doses had been administered since April in Peru, with more than two million additional doses available.
Still, with vaccination rates so far below the threshold needed for community protection in parts of the region, experts say conditions are ripe for further spread.

In Argentina, authorities issued a warning in late October about the high risk associated with the pope’s visit, after estimating that they expected up to 4 million people in the province of Buenos Aires.

But Argentina President Javier Milei has slashed Argentina’s healthcare budget, eviscerating agencies tasked with planning, financing and tracking immunization campaigns. The cuts coincided with a measles outbreak that in April 2025 led to Argentina’s first measles death in two decades and some are concerned that efforts are falling short.

Marcela Lopez Yunes, a doctor and pediatric infectious disease specialist, said she hadn’t seen what she considered sufficient public communication to encourage vaccination. “We need to do a little more to give diseases such as measles the attention and importance they deserve,” she said.

A spokesperson for Argentina's health ministry said that while the federal government is in charge of purchasing and distributing vaccines, provinces are in charge of administering them to their populations. They also said that there is an ongoing public service announcement speaking to the importance of vaccination in general.
Leo took aim at Milei’s austerity measures as he arrived in Argentina Sunday, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first.
Associated Press journalists Ramiro Barreiro in Montevideo, Uruguay, and Franklin Briceño in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
summary: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head
story: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head

WASHINGTON -- Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer’s, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn’t have Alzheimer’s but advanced CTE instead.
The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn’t involved with the research.

Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed.
The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan.

title: Trump administration will fund new research on controversial psychedelic drug ibogaine
summary: Federal officials say there's new funding to study the medical potential of a powerful psychedelic
story: Federal officials say there's new funding to study the medical potential of a powerful psychedelic

WASHINGTON -- Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.
The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug.

Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs.

Veterans organizations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.

Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.
“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”
Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.
Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and “best-in-class research.”
“For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce,” Collins said.

Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.

Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.

Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.
Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.

The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.

Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: “Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it.”

title: US, Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
summary: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
story: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
NEW YORK -- International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.
“It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.
Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.
“It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have “eliminated” measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.
A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and lauded Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.
As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.
Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City.

title: Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
summary: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, highlighting the severity of the situation
story: Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, highlighting the severity of the situation

BUNIA, Congo -- Congo’s Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the spread of the disease.

According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.

The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces.

The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
While Ituri accounts for nearly 70% of total cases, North Kivu has emerged as the main site of new transmission, according to Congolese Health Minister Roger Kamba.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.

The outbreak has affected some schools in Ituri, with more teachers contracting the disease. Two head teachers in Bunia, the provincial capital of Ituri, told The Associated Press they are worried about their teachers and students after losing members of staff.

"Our students and the entire staff have been left traumatized. At this stage, we need psychologists to support us, as the situation is extremely difficult,” Isaac Singoma, one of the headteachers, said.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the outbreak in Congo. The disease has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

title: Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
summary: An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world
story: An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the world

MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.

The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.

“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.

Haines' family asked well-wishers to make donations to the international charity Save the Children instead of sending flowers. The appeal has raised more than 1.4 million Australian dollars ($950,000), Save the Children Australia said Monday.
Haines was “overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians” through their donations and looked forward to working with Save the Children to use the money to “improve the lives of children,” she said.

Her shocking injuries renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers. However, public incitement against officials is growing.
Security at several lawmakers’ electorate offices has been enhanced in response to the alleged attack.
Within hours of Haines being struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser Troop Carrier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a news conference her catastrophic injuries were not an accident.
“All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery,” Albanese said in a statement Monday in response to her hospital discharge.

“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family. We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese added.

Police have yet to disclose a motive for the alleged attack. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man who lived in the Wangaratta area, has been charged with offenses including intentionally causing serious injury.
Nugent has been in custody since bystanders dragged him from his SUV and rendered first-aid to Haines at the scene.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement a day after Haines was hospitalized describing the lawmaker as a “friend for more than 20 years” and the circumstances of her injuries “unfathomable.”

title: Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
summary: Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of Peru
story: Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of Peru

LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.

During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.

The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.

For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

“I have felt at home, and you have reminded me that the Church truly is a family. It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” he said at the end of Mass.

Mogrovejo, who lived from 1538-1606, is revered for having denounced abuses against Indigenous and enslaved people by Spanish colonizers. He is also remembered for having crisscrossed his vast diocese on foot and horseback to minister to his flock, learning Quechua and Aymara to better preach to its Indigenous members and overseeing the translation of church teachings so they could understand.

Following his example, Leo traveled across Peru to where the Catholic hierarchy rarely goes to minister to his flock, going high up in the Andes mountains and deep into the Amazon rainforest and points in between. On his final full day in Peru on Sunday, Leo went from his former diocese of Chiclayo on the north Pacific coast to the southeastern Andean city of Cusco, to the northeastern Amazonian city of Pucallpa and back to Lima on the coast.

The climatic and altitude changes alone were exhausting — from hot, humid Chiclayo to chilly and rainy Cusco (at an oxygen-challenging altitude of 3,400 meters or about 11,150 feet) to the steaming heat of the Pucallpa rainforest and back to the gray humidity of Lima.

It was a daylong lesson in what it means to be a shepherd. But it also served to say “So there!” to the nay-sayers, including some in the Vatican who had questioned whether Leo would have to change the course of his pontificate given his lung cancer diagnosis.
On Monday, Leo proceeded with his program as planned and made clear he wasn't saying “adiós” or goodbye forever to Peru.
Speaking to the crowd outside the Vatican residence, Leo thanked Peruvians for having accompanied him on his trip. “Have a good day, thank you very much, and until later!” he said.
At the home for the elderly in Callao, where Leo visited with residents, Leo bid farewell again saying “hasta pronto, hasta luego,” another way of saying “see you soon.”

Callao Mayor César Pérez told The Associated Press that Father Roberto, as he is known to the Peruvian people, would drive approximately 12 hours from Chiclayo in northern Peru to Callao during the pandemic because he wanted to ensure the well-being of older residents.
Leo delivered food and other supplies to the home but didn't enter the facility in order to protect the residents from the virus, Pérez said.
The Peru stop capped a visit that began on Nov. 6 in Uruguay and proceeded on to Argentina, the homeland of Leo’s predecessor Pope Francis, who never returned during his pontificate.
The trip itself was in doubt after Leo underwent lung cancer surgery Oct. 13 in Rome. But Leo said as the visit began that he had “no doubt” that he would make it.
Rosa María Flores, who was attending Leo's final Mass, was glad he did. She said the most important thing about the pope’s visit was that he brought faith to the people of his homeland of Peru.
“We have so much crime, so many deaths; we’re in great need of peace, reconciliation and faith,” she said. “I know that he’s pouring blessings on Peru and that things will get better for all of us.”

One of the most meaningful visits for Leo was to the sanctuary of Mogrovejo in the city of Zaña in the diocese of Chiclayo. Leo revealed that he had come there the night before he was ordained a bishop to pray, so important to him was the saint who died there after falling ill during one of his own missionary visits.

“This is a kneeling place for Robert Prevost,” the Rev. David Farfan, the parish pastor, told AP. Many of the pope’s actions, he said, “helping people in the world, as a peacemaker, he did them while also kneeling in this sacred place because a saint passed away here.”
