title: A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
summary: A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 people
story: A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 people
BANGKOK -- A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.

The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.
There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.

Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.

Phuket Gov. Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tires. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.
He said the victims appeared to try to escape the fire to the higher floors. One body was found on the third floor and 10 others were found on the fifth floor.
Phuket is on an island in southern Thailand and a popular tourist destination.

title: Macron leaves summit of French-speaking nations with leadership dispute on hold
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization’s leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo
story: French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization’s leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo

SIEM REAP, Cambodia -- French President Emmanuel Macron left a summit of French-speaking nations on Monday with uncertainty still hanging over the organization's leadership after a dispute between Rwanda and Congo roiled the proceedings.

After days of intense negotiations in the capital of Cambodia, member states decided that the incumbent secretary-general, Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, will stay for another year before making way for a new leader of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
Mushikiwabo was seeking a third term at the summit, which Congo had opposed, going as far as threatening to leave the OIF if she was reelected.
Congo has more than 110 million people — far exceeding France’s population of 70 million — and its withdrawal would be a significant blow to the organization.

Congo, the United States and U.N. experts accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.
The French president’s office welcomed the one-year postponement and said it would allow the organization "to overcome divisions and preserve the consensus in the francophone family.”
Congo’s Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner said on X that “a wise compromise” would preserve unity in the Francophonie.

Macron held bilateral talks, including with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet and Vietnamese leader To Lam, and attended the summit of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers — all French-speaking places.

On Sunday, the French president’s office said Macron met with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and called for the three African countries presenting candidates for the OIF leadership role — Mauritania is the third — to hold talks and agree on a “consensus solution.” France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of 71.7 million euros ($79 million).
The leadership dispute comes after the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.

Rights groups and U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews also called on world leaders attending the meetings to press Cambodia for the release of rights activists and to allow greater democratic freedoms in the de facto one-party state.

Hun Manet, who chaired the summit, criticized Thailand in his opening remarks Sunday and reiterated that Cambodia had not started the fighting that erupted between the Southeast Asian neighbors in 2025 over competing claims to border territory. Several dozen civilians and soldiers on both sides were killed and hundreds of thousands of people displaced.
Macron praised the Cambodian leader for choosing peace as the theme for the summit, and said France encourages a return to dialogue to find a peaceful, negotiated solution to border disputes.

In a Facebook post Sunday, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul wrote that Thailand has “always respected all agreements with Cambodia and will always adhere to international law." He also restated Thailand’s position that bilateral disputes should be resolved without third-party involvement. Thailand’s aversion to outside involvement is partly rooted in two rulings by the International Court of Justice awarding Cambodia ownership of a centuries-old temple on disputed land along the border.

Macron on Monday visited Siem Reap, home to Cambodia's Angkor Wat complex and UNESCO World Heritage site, to join King Norodom Sihamoni in marking the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.

Cambodia's Apsara National Authority told The Associated Press that restoring the West Mebon temple, built in the 11th century during the Angkor era, cost $12 million over 14 years. The joint France-Cambodia project involved transporting replacement stones and heavy machinery by boat to the island temple while managing water levels to prevent flooding during seasonal rains.
The site had been damaged by natural elements, human activity and war.
Macron arrived in Malaysia later Monday and was scheduled to meet Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim for talks expected to focus on defense partnership and the supply of critical minerals.

Macron's trip to Southeast Asia comes at a time of widespread protests in France, with more than 600,000 people taking to the streets earlier this month to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement. The protests have seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.
Sopheng Cheang reported from Phnom Penh and Peck from Bangkok.

title: Army airstrike kills at least 13 in West Kordofan, says rights group
summary: A rights group says an army airstrike killed at least 13 people
story: A rights group says an army airstrike killed at least 13 people

CAIRO -- A Sudanese army airstrike killed at least 13 people and destroyed several homes in western Sudan in a country ravaged by more than three years of fighting between the army and its rival paramilitary, a local rights group said Monday.

Women and children were among those killed in the strike in the Abu Qalb area of Abu Zabad locality in West Kordofan, according to the Emergency Lawyers, a group that tracks violence throughout the war in Sudan. The AP couldn’t independently verify the toll.

The war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises since it broke out in April 2023, killing at least 59,000 people, displacing around 13 million and pushing parts of the country into famine, according to aid organizations.
The Emergency Lawyers blamed the army for the airstrike in West Kordofan.

“The continued use of indiscriminate airstrikes on residential areas poses a direct threat to civilian lives and constitutes a grave violation of the rules of international humanitarian law," the group's statement said.

Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces fighting with the army, wrote on Facebook on Monday that his troops went through Abu Zabad locality and “eliminated” RSF positions in West Kordofan.

Much of the fight in Sudan concentrated in Darfur and Kordofan and recently shifted towards Blue Nile province. Drone warfare has also surged during the war, becoming the deadliest threat to civilians. Both sides are being supplied with drones by countries in the Middle East and beyond, experts have said.

title: Cape Verde’s president is reelected for a second 5-year term, provisional results show
summary: Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidate
story: Cape Verde’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second term, defeating five challengers, including the country’s first female presidential candidate

PRAIA, Cape Verde -- PRAIA, Cape Verde (AP) — Cape Verde ’s president, José Maria Neves, has been reelected for a second five-year term, beating five challengers, including the first woman presidential candidate in the country’s history, provisional results show.

Neves called his reelection as president of the Atlantic island nation off West Africa “a great victory.” The election was dominated by high unemployment and the high cost of living, which has fueled emigration.
Provisional results showed Neves comfortably edged out his opponents, garnering 64% of the vote while Joana Rosa, the main opposition candidate, won 31.4%.
Rosa called Neves to concede defeat.
The small country has a history of smooth transfers of power and is one of the most stable in a region fraught with tense elections.
“The president of the republic does not have a majority; the president of the republic belongs to everyone,” Neves said in his victory speech.
Turnout was low, with only 31.7% of the 418,000 registered voters casting a ballot.
Neves said the low turnout could be explained by high emigration, population movements within the country and outdated voter records. He promised a study to examine the issue.

Under Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs policy and holds most executive power. The directly elected president’s role is largely ceremonial, although the president can veto legislation.

title: Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
summary: Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit
story: Prince William and Princess Catherine have arrived in India for a three-day visit

MUMBAI, India -- MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the annual environmental prize awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.

The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, which will make its debut performance in India.
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.

Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.

The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they were scheduled to meet with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India a decade ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the U.K. throne.

The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
She traveled to Italy without William in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

title: EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
summary: The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks, financial institutions.
story: The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks, financial institutions.

BRUSSELS -- European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.

The bloc also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, and targeted several businesspeople with links to the energy sector, the trade in oil and petroleum products. It slapped asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of others accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation.

At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must now be the one to make concessions, and they rejected any fresh demands.
"We actually don’t have a ceasefire and they continue to weaken Ukraine and kill people every single day,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters after chairing the meeting.

After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.

But the Europeans have likened it to the “treaty” that Russia offered NATO before launching its full-scale war in 2022. They see it as an attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to how they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.

“In 2021, Russia's demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are a pretext for keeping the war going,” Kallas said. “Ministers were very clear today. We don’t need a new security architecture. We need to restore the one we have. Russia has broken all the treaties that underpin it.”

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: “Europe has a security architecture – we don’t need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture.” He said that is “the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view.”
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys also insisted that Europe does not need another security framework, saying that Russia cannot be trusted and has already broken past agreements.

“It’s very clear that we don’t need another one. We already have one. Secure Ukraine, strong Europe, strong trans-Atlantic bond,” he told reporters. “It’s not about the rules. Rules are working. The problem is that Russia is breaking them.”

U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have positioned themselves as mediators and have been talking to Russia and Ukraine for just over a year. In that time, no lasting ceasefire has been agreed, and little obvious progress has been made toward peace.
Major differences remain over the control of territory and future security arrangements.

European leaders and officials, including Kallas, have expressed skepticism about the talks. The only tangible progress has been exchanges of prisoners, which are often used by warring parties as a trust-building measure during peace talks.

At a summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders agreed that Europe should be represented in future talks by a team of security advisers from France, Germany, the U.K., Italy and Poland as well as senior officials from the EU’s main institutions.

The Europeans concede that as Ukraine’s biggest backers they cannot also act as mediators. Their role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction and Ukraine’s future. Only Ukraine itself can decide on matters involving its sovereignty, they said.

As the EU's top diplomat, Kallas believes that she should have been involved in the talks, in line with the bloc's treaties. But she still expressed hope that the Europeans can “now move away from the discussion of who” will represent them and focus uniquely on their demands of Russia and how best to support Ukraine.
Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody
summary: Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is being moved to a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of Ueno Bank
story: Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is being moved to a military prison as he awaits trial over the collapse of Ueno Bank

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay -- A Paraguayan judge on Monday ordered former President Santiago Peña moved to a military prison after reports that he had been held in a suite with a private gym, as he awaits trial over the implosion of a major digital lender, which toppled his government earlier this month.

Judge Osmar Legal ordered Peña transferred from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital, Asunción, where local media reported that his quarters also included a private bathroom and a spacious dining room.
Under the court order, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, Peña will now be held at the Viñas Cué military prison, apart from other detainees.

President Pedro Alliana opened a news conference Monday by announcing that he had ordered the dismissal of the regiment’s commander, Col. José David Daiub, following allegations that Peña had received special treatment there.
Alliana, who served as Peña’s vice president, pledged to give prosecutors whatever resources they need to investigate the bank’s collapse.
“Paraguayans deserve to know the truth,” he said.

Peña is in pretrial detention on charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Prosecutors allege that he used his influence to steer public money to Ueno Bank, a lender used by more than half Paraguay’s adults, as its executives made large insider loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. He denies wrongdoing.

Paraguay’s central bank seized Ueno on Nov. 3 after declaring it insolvent, freezing the accounts of nearly 3 million customers and more than $850 million in public funds, and disrupting payments for households and small businesses. Three days later, the Senate removed Peña from office, and Alliana took over. A judge ordered Peña jailed the next day.

Ueno’s dizzying growth had become a symbol of Peña’s effort to sell landlocked Paraguay to foreign investors as a low-tax, business-friendly hub. A former International Monetary Fund official and one of the Trump administration’s closest allies in the region, Peña won access in Washington and on Wall Street. That was unusual for a country of Paraguay’s size and economic weight.
The bank launched its digital brand in 2022 and by June had 2.9 million customers in a country of about 6 million. It even sponsored the national soccer team.

But Ueno was also intertwined with Peña’s government. He held a stake in Ueno’s parent company until last year and appointed the bank’s former chairman, Carlos Carvallo, to lead the central bank. Carvallo also faces charges in the case.
Since Peña’s arrest, authorities have searched two of his four homes, one in Asunción and a mansion in the resort town of San Bernardino, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) away.

Prosecutors say the mansion was built partly with about $577,000 in loans that Ueno granted Peña while he was president, and investigators found a vault hidden behind a false wall there. They have also asked the United States, Luxembourg and Argentina for help tracing money that may have been diverted from the bank.
Alliana acknowledged that the crisis had shaken Paraguayans’ faith in their banks. “The closure of Ueno Bank has deeply affected numerous Paraguayan families,” he said.

More than 1.8 million depositors have so far received about $640 million, Alliana said, from a deposit guarantee fund that Paraguay created in 2003 after a series of financial crises wiped out dozens of banks and finance companies.

Most small savers have been repaid in full. The fund has paid out up to about $19,600 per person, out of a guarantee of about $36,700, and authorities haven't said when the rest will be paid. Investors in Ueno’s mutual funds aren’t covered and must wait for the bank to be liquidated.
Still, more than 75% of the roughly $2.8 billion deposited at Ueno, much of it belonging to larger savers and public institutions, has yet to be returned.

For pension funds that had money at Ueno, Alliana said that authorities have preliminarily identified about $600 million in viable assets at the bank, such as loans expected to be repaid, that they plan to use to reimburse the funds. It remains unclear how much of the pension money and other public deposits will be returned.

Teachers walked off the job and blocked roads across the country last week to demand the return of their retirement savings, and retirees’ groups have pressed Alliana and Congress to pass an emergency law to guarantee it. That followed days of unrest in Asunción after Ueno’s collapse, when thousands of people took to the streets demanding their money back and Peña’s ouster, at times clashing with police.
Isabel DeBre reported from Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Nayara Batschke from Santiago, Chile.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: Pakistan's imprisoned ex-leader Imran Khan appeals for urgent medical care
summary: Imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife
story: Imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad.

In an open letter and conveyed to the judges through his lawyer, Khan said his blood pressure had risen sharply and that doctors had warned him he was at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

According to the letter released to the media by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar, the former premier said that his wife, Bushra Bibi, also needed further eye surgery and could permanently lose her sight without it.

Khan has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in a graft case. He was removed from office in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Despite his legal troubles, Khan remains a central and popular figure in Pakistan, and the PTI wants his release.
Khan's wife is also serving a prison term on graft charges.

Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, a Cabinet minister, disputed Khan’s account, saying he was receiving regular medical care and accusing him of seeking political advantage. In a post on X, Chaudhry said Khan has been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, where his health and blood pressure were found to be satisfactory.

He said Khan received meals of his choice and had access to books and television. The government was responsible for ensuring Khan’s medical care and protecting his legal rights, as it was for every prisoner, Chaudry said.
The latest development comes days after authorities allowed Khan's lawyers to see him at the prison.
“Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” he said according to the letter. “I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive.”
The letter was addressed to the chief justices of Pakistan’s Supreme Court and other courts.
“I appeal to Your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” Khan said.

Earlier this year, Safdar, Khan's lawyer, told the Supreme Court that the former premier had lost roughly 85% of vision in his right eye. The government at the time denied the claim, and one of Khan’s sisters said his eyesight had significantly improved following medical treatment, which authorities say is ongoing.

The government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has said that Khan isn’t being held under a government order, but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by the courts following judicial proceedings.

The government has rejected allegations that Khan was being held in solitary confinement or denied contact with his family, saying Khan had received more than 900 visits since his imprisonment in 2023.

title: Mexican drug kingpin Félix Gallardo, founder of Guadalajara cartel, dies at 80
summary: Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died of multiple organ failure.
story: Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died of multiple organ failure.

MEXICO CITY -- Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a former drug lord considered one of the godfathers of Mexico’s drug trafficking industry and a founder of the notorious Guadalajara cartel, died at a hospital in the western city of the same name. He was 80.
Félix Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died Sunday at 2 p.m. of multiple organ failure, the Jalisco state security department said in a statement.

The notorious drug kingpin had been hospitalized since Friday after being rushed from the Puente Grande prison, where he had been held since 1989. He was serving a combined 77-year prison sentence for drug trafficking offenses and the 1985 killing of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena.

Along with Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, Félix Gallardo founded the Guadalajara cartel, which dominated drug trafficking in Mexico during the 1980s and eventually splintered into several criminal organizations in the country’s north, including the Sinaloa cartel.

Caro Quintero was released on procedural grounds in 2013 but recaptured in July 2022. He was extradited to the United States in February 2025 along with 28 other prisoners wanted by U.S. authorities on drug-related charges.
All three cartel founders were convicted in Mexico in connection with Camarena’s killing. The DEA agent was kidnapped and tortured before his body was found in 1985.
Félix Gallardo had sought house arrest since 2019, citing his advanced age and deteriorating health, but courts initially rejected his requests.
In September 2022, a judge granted him house arrest, but the order was never carried out because of legal challenges by Mexico’s federal attorney general’s office.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Lula to govern Brazil for fourth term but faces challenges. Here’s what to know
summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges
story: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a surprise reelection victory but faces significant challenges

RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a surprise reelection victory in late October, but he faces a multitude of challenges on issues ranging from the economy and public security to relations with the United States.

While Lula ultimately bested challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by 4.4 million votes after trailing him in the first round, the country remains deeply divided and many voters expressed dissatisfaction with the leftist president's most recent term, which began in 2023.

Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result of the election, declared himself the victim of electoral fraud without providing evidence and fled to Miami. He has vowed to lead a fortified opposition from the U.S.
As Lula prepares to begin his next term, here is a look at challenges ahead.

Lula is facing pressure from investors who had counted on Bolsonaro winning the election after the far-right candidate received more votes than Lula on Oct. 4. Markets did not react well to his loss. Brazil’s currency, the real, dropped by 12% against the dollar the day after the election, while the stock market tumbled nearly 14% and has not rebounded since.
Investors believed a Bolsonaro victory would rein in government spending and are concerned about Lula’s future fiscal policy, said Sergio Vale, chief economist at consultancy firm MB Associados.
“Lula and the government have vowed not to touch spending while keeping all the promises made these last few years,” said Vale. “Unfortunately, they’re not compatible with fiscal responsibility.”

Lula’s government recently unveiled plans to save up to 60 billion reais ($10.6 billion) in public funds through curbs on tax breaks and spending caps — a proposal that is currently moving through Congress.

During Lula’s third term, Brazil’s public debt grew from around 7.2 trillion reais ($1.3 trillion) in 2022 to 11.1 trillion reais ($2 trillion) this year, which analysts say spurred inflation and contributed to high interest rates ultimately remaining unchanged from 13.75% despite variations over the course of the term.
The high cost of living also left many Brazilians unhappy with the state of the economy despite record-low unemployment.

Lula will face a Congress that shifted further to the right in October's legislative elections. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party secured the largest blocs in both houses, gaining an extra 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubling its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties.
Despite Bolsonaro’s departure for Miami, his party will remain a force to be reckoned with, retaining instruments to block governmental proposals and even challenge judicial authorities.

Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that led to President Jair Bolsonaro serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.

Their efforts would be helped if Rogério Marinho, Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator, becomes Senate president. He announced his candidacy last week, promising not to focus solely on impeachment. But, he said, “we will not turn a blind eye, because no one is above the law.”
Brazilians cited crime as a top concern ahead of the election and insecurity featured prominently in the election cycle.

While Brazil's homicide rate last year fell to its lowest level since 2012, the country continues to face the expansion of criminal activities that use digital technology and online platforms, violence against vulnerable groups — including people of color, women and children — and the need to modernize security and justice institutions, according to this year’s annual report from the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

Drug-trafficking gangs have expanded their reach in recent years and are now present in large swathes of the country, including parts of the Amazon rainforest, while paramilitary-type militias have entrenched their power in Rio and other states.
Brazil’s Senate recently approved legislation that strengthens the government’s power to fight criminal gangs. Lula has touted the changes as key to tackling one of his nation’s biggest problems.
Navigating the rivalry between the U.S. and China will be key in Lula’s fourth term, said Ana Garcia, an international relations professor at the Rural Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.

Relations between Brazil and the U.S. fell to an all-time low during Lula’s third term, after the Trump administration imposed several rounds of tariffs. Meanwhile, ties with China deepened, displeasing the U.S., analysts say.

But Democrats' sweeping gains in the midterm election also reflected a repudiation of Trump’s tariffs, and pressure to reduce them — including those targeting Brazil — is likely to increase, Garcia said.

Garcia expects Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo, who lives in Texas, to continue lobbying Trump administration allies against Lula’s government. But Democrats may increase scrutiny of Trump's policies abroad. In September, 31 Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing the Trump administration of “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s election.
“The midterms were a rude awakening for the Bolsonaros,” Garcia said.
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Russia fends off swarms of Ukrainian drones a day across its vast territory. But some get through
summary: The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours
story: The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours
The skies from the Black Sea to Moscow buzzed overnight with hundreds of Ukrainian drones, keeping Russia’s air defenses busy for hours.
By daybreak Monday, the military said it shot down 1,336 drones. That marked the largest number of them brought down since the start of the full-fledged invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The Russian military, in turn, ramped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to disrupt electricity and heat as winter sets in.
The surge in aerial attacks follows a week that saw little progress in the first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months.
Here's a look at Russia’s air defenses as it fends off challenges posed by Ukraine’s attacks:
Russia has more land than any other country in the world, and protecting that vast space is a major challenge despite its massive arsenal of defensive systems.

“Russia’s air defense system, like many air defense systems around the world, is not necessarily designed to protect the entirety of Russia’s territory and the air approaches to the country,” said Thomas Withington, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute.
While Ukrainian drones cruise at about 150 kph (about 95 mph), they fly very low, making it harder for radar to spot them.

Their range allows them to strike deep inside Russia. In one recent attack, they hit an oil refinery in Omsk in eastern Siberia, about 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) from the border. While their payload of about 50 kilograms (110 pounds) is relatively small, their precision allows them to inflict massive damage to such facilities and other infrastructure.
Ukraine also has used long-range Flamingo cruise missiles, capable of reaching up to 950 kph (590 mph), carrying a much heavier payload. Kyiv has fewer of these missiles than drones.

Like in previous attacks, the number of Ukrainian drones reported downed by Russia early Monday couldn’t be independently verified, and official reports haven’t said how many actually got through air defenses to hit their targets.
Withington noted that as a general rule of thumb, 10% get through and hit their targets.
“It’s a game of averages," he said, so launching more drones means that more get through.

He said Russia's air defenses, like most integrated air-defense systems around the world, are designed to shoot down aircraft, air launched weapons and ballistic missiles, and thus could struggle to engage drones.

“Drones are a very different calculus, and because of it, the performance of those systems is never going to be as optimal as it would be against a conventional threat," he said, adding that while air defenses shoot down or jam most of them, some will always get through.
While Russian air defenses around key facilities such as refineries have been bolstered, Ukrainian drones have continued to set them ablaze.

The large size of the targets makes them more vulnerable, Withington said, adding that Ukraine has learned a lot about the operation of Russia's air defense systems, enabling the military to polish its tactics and find loopholes.

“All of Russia’s air defenses, all of the systems they deployed, by and large have given up their secrets” after years of fighting, he said. “The more of that information and data you are armed with, the easier it becomes to defeat Russian air defenses."

In June, a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and also hit a nearby naval base, casting a cloud over President Vladimir Putin’s showcase economic forum in his hometown. Putin acknowledged the damage from the attacks, saying Russia would strengthen its air defenses.

On Monday, a Ukrainian drone damaged the well-protected Kerch Bridge linking the mainland and the Crimean Peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed in 2014, temporarily disrupting car traffic. The bridge has been attacked repeatedly over the years.

“Our air defense systems keep operating very effectively,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. “The system is working, but, unfortunately, no system in the world can provide 100% protection for various facilities against such massive strikes.”
From the early stages of the conflict, Russian authorities have prioritized protecting Moscow.

Media reports said additional air defense systems have been put on the outskirts of the capital, and some could be seen on top of some of the Moscow buildings, including the Defense Ministry’s headquarters facing the Gorky Park across the Moskva River.
While Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin repeatedly claimed that the bulk of the drones were downed, it's impossible to independently verify his claims.

Despite the dense protection around the capital, Ukrainian drones have managed to pierce the shield. Russia scaled down the annual May 9 Victory Day parade, fearing Ukrainian drone strikes. Days later, a massive drone attack on Moscow’s suburbs killed three people. Successive attacks repeatedly struck the oil refinery on the outskirts of the capital, disrupting its operation.

Another top priority has been to protect Putin’s residence in Valdai in northwestern Russia. In December 2025, Russian authorities reported a massive Ukrainian attack on the residence but claimed that none of the 91 drones hit the target.
Since Soviet times, Russia has developed a broad array of air defense systems, from portable ones to long-range weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
The S-400 Triumph is the main long-range air defense system capable of spotting and engaging aircraft and ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 400 kilometers (about 250 miles).

The even more potent S-500 Prometheus system that reaches as far as 600 kilometers (about 370 miles) also is available in small numbers. Russia also uses various models of S-300 air defense missile systems, an older but still very advanced and powerful long-range weapon.
For shorter ranges, the military has relied on the Pantsyr, the Tor and the Buk air defense systems.
While Buk and Tor use missiles to shoot down aerial targets, Pantsyr can use a combination of guns and missiles. A Pantsyr system sits atop the Defense Ministry building in Moscow.
Russia also has deployed teams armed with shoulder-fired Igla and Verba air defense missiles and machine guns for protection of key facilities. Helicopter gunships also are involved.
Withington said Ukraine and Russia could be expected to further ramp up the number of attacking drones to overwhelm air defenses.
“The long-term direction of travel, both for Ukraine and Russia, will be a continued exponential increase in the number of drones that can be launched at any given time," he said.

title: Mozambique's Mondlane is the latest opposition leader to go on trial in Africa
summary: Mozambique’s opposition leader will go on trial charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election
story: Mozambique’s opposition leader will go on trial charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election

MAPUTO, Mozambique -- Mozambique's opposition leader will go on trial Tuesday charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election that kept the country's long-ruling party in power.

Venancio Mondlane, who was the runner-up in that presidential election, is the latest opposition figure in Africa to face what some analysts say are politically motivated charges meant to silence or remove criticism.

Mondlane's trial follows the four-year prison sentence given to Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu this month for inciting people to disrupt a 2025 election. Lissu, who said he was prosecuted for calling for electoral reform, was acquitted of treason in that case.
One of Uganda's veteran opposition figures, Kizza Besigye, is on trial for treason and faces a potential death penalty if convicted.

Zambia's leading opposition figure and several supporters also face treason charges in their southern African country following another troubled election this year that rights groups say was characterized by a campaign of harassment against the opposition.

In Mozambique in eastern Africa, Mondlane lost to President Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party in the 2024 election. Frelimo has now governed Mozambique for 51 years since independence from Portugal in 1975 and has been accused of rigging elections and suppressing opposition, which it denies.

Mondlane rejected the 2024 results as fraudulent and called for protests and people to stay away from work after the vote. Postelection protests by thousands of people lasted months in the largest popular uprising against Frelimo. They were exacerbated by the killing of Mondlane's lawyer and another official with their opposition Podemos party, who were fatally shot in a car in what Mondlane called political assassinations.
Mondlane left Mozambique for a period following the killings claiming his life was in danger.

Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed in the protests and criticized the Mozambican authorities for what it called a brutal crackdown on protesters. Human Rights Watch alleged that security forces used live ammunition against protesters.
Election observers including a team from the European Union questioned the validity of the elections and said there were irregularities in counting and the alteration of some results.

Mondlane, who has since formed a new party, has denied the charges against him and said he was advocating for "electoral truth" with his messages on social media calling on people to protest and boycott work.

The charges against him include inciting terrorism and instigating terrorism and he faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted on the most serious charge of instigating terrorism, according to Mozambican legal expert Vítor da Fonseca.
Some legal analysts say the trial, which will be held in Mozambique's Supreme Court, will be a test of the judiciary's impartiality under Frelimo.
Alberto Manhique, a spokesperson for Mondlane's new party, said it is a target of oppression by the government and “there is no shadow of a doubt that Mondlane's trial is purely political.”
The president of the Supreme Court has denied any political influence and said it will rule according to the law.
Mondlane has not been placed under arrest and recently traveled to a democracy and human rights conference in Berlin. He has said he will attend the trial.

title: Guatemala ramps up security operations following declaration of state of siege
summary: Guatemala's interior and defense ministers have inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras
story: Guatemala's interior and defense ministers have inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras

GUATEMALA CITY -- GUATEMALA CITY (AP) — Guatemala’s interior and defense ministers on Monday inspected security operations in two departments bordering Honduras, days after President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency to curb drug-related violence in the Central American country.

The decree, announced on Saturday, suspends for 30 days several constitutional rights, including freedom of movement and assembly, and allows security forces to disperse groups by force, make arrests and enter homes without warrants.

Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda said Monday that the emergency measure also targets groups allegedly linked to drug trafficking that are involved in illegal jade and gold mining in the region.
“We are carrying out a series of coordinated and planned actions with the Defense Ministry and the public prosecutor’s office. We have a plan that we will execute over 30 days,” Villeda said.
Defense Minister Henry Sáenz said authorities are “establishing territorial control through checkpoints on routes and patrols along roads bordering Honduras."
This area in the eastern part of Guatemala has been the scene of a wave of violence over the past three months.
On Sept. 27, an armed attack left eight people dead in the municipality of Huité, in the department of Zacapa.

Initially, the army claimed the attack involved clashes between organized crime groups; however, days later, it announced that 107 military personnel had been placed at the disposal of the authorities to determine their potential involvement in the massacre, which claimed the lives of three women, including a young girl.
The prosecutor’s office is investigating whether the army’s actions were linked to the detention of suspected drug traffickers.

Separately, on Nov. 7, Congressman Julio César Portillo Paz and three members of the National Civil Police — who were part of his security detail — were gunned down by armed men in broad daylight in the municipality of Río Hondo, also in Zacapa.

Early on Friday morning, five people were killed in the same department. According to preliminary investigations, armed men arrived in several vehicles at a small village and abducted a man, whose whereabouts remain unknown. They then killed his mother, two brothers and two friends at the scene.

Also on Friday, the U.S. State Department designated three local drug-trafficking groups as terrorist organizations for financing violence and crime in the region. Among those designated are two family clans — Los Lorenzanas and Los Mendoza — which, according to authorities, maintain deep ties to Mexican drug cartels and operate within the area.

title: Haiti revs up for elections as enrollment closes for candidates
summary: For the first time in Haiti’s history, three women have registered as presidential candidates
story: For the first time in Haiti’s history, three women have registered as presidential candidates

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- For the first time in Haiti’s history, three women have registered as presidential candidates, joining 30 men vying to become the next leader of the troubled Caribbean country.

Next year’s general election is the first in more than a decade. The candidates include the widow of slain former President Jovenel Moïse, a respected economist, a well-known prosecutor accused of multiple summary executions and a former president accused of drug trafficking and sponsoring gangs.

Haiti hasn’t had a president since Moïse was gunned down at his private residence in July 2021 as part of a failed coup. Since then, Haiti has been led by various appointed prime ministers and a transitional presidential council that was dissolved in February.

Presidential and parliamentary candidates had until Sunday to register online. Haiti’s provisional electoral council is reviewing them and in January expects to publish a final list of names of those approved to run.

Haiti hopes to hold the first round of elections on July 18 next year and the second round on Oct. 4. Some experts question whether the country, which remains mired in gang violence, will be prepared by then.
Wolf Pamphile, founder and CEO of Haiti Policy House, a U.S.-based think tank, said nearly a million voters have been registered in the country of nearly 12 million people.
He noted that the government has set a benchmark of between 3 million and 6 million voters to hold what would be considered a legitimate election.
“That number is getting harder and harder to reach,” he said.
When the electoral process first began, officials were registering roughly 9,000 people a day. That has dropped to about 3,000 a day, Pamphile said.

As registration continues, gangs continue to fight Haitian police and soldiers, as well as a U.N.-backed international gang suppression force; Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince, and about 2,500 troops from El Salvador who were deployed after four aviation technicians from the Central American country were attacked in late October and remain missing.

The number of clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46% compared with the 21 days prior to the deployment of Salvadoran forces, said María Fernanda Arocha, an analyst with the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project.

She said that estimated fatalities during those operations have surpassed 100, with more than two dozen identified as civilians. Despite the ongoing fighting, more than 100 political parties have registered, political campaigns are heating up, and Haiti is pushing forward with its elections.

Martine Moïse: She's the widow of Haiti's former president and was injured in the attack at their private residence in July 2021. She was investigated in connection to his death and indicted in Haiti, but the charge was later annulled. She recently testified in a U.S. federal courtroom against several suspects accused of killing Jovenel Moïse.

Michel Martelly: A well-known musician known as “Sweet Micky,” he served as Haiti’s president from 2011 to 2016 under the Tèt Kale Party, which translates to the Bald-Headed Party. In mid-July, he returned to Haiti, marking a rare visit to his homeland. Martelly has been accused of facilitating drug trafficking and sponsoring multiple gangs. Canada sanctioned him in November 2022 and the U.S. in August 2024.

Claude Joseph: He’s a former foreign affairs minister who briefly served as interim prime minister after Moïse was killed. A Haitian judge indicted him and Moïse’s widow in the killing of Moïse, accusations they have denied. The indictment was later dismissed. After stepping down as interim prime minister, Joseph formed his own party: Engaged for Development.

Jean Ernest Muscadin: The Moïse administration appointed him as a public prosecutor representing the southern coastal city of Miragoane. He recently stepped down to file his candidacy for president. The United Nations has accused him of killing dozens of people suspected of being gang members or committing minor crimes. But Muscadin remains popular with many in Miragoane, with supporters calling him the “people’s prosecutor.”

Dominique Dupuy: She briefly served as Haiti’s foreign affairs minister in 2024 after Moïse nominated her to serve as Haiti’s permanent representative to UNESCO in 2020. In a recent and brief speech posted online, Dupuy said she recently traveled across Haiti and found love, strength and determination as she pledged to “start building the nation that our ancestors dreamt for us." She also promised not to take orders from anyone who's not from Haiti, and to reject “dirty money” as she campaigns. She and Savary Marie-Anne Savannah Hadid, a businesswoman and philanthropist who comes from a wealthy family, made history this year by becoming the first women to register as presidential candidates.

Etzer Emile: The respected economist and university professor recently announced his candidacy. He is running under the political platform Soley, which means “Sun.” He has said that employment, security and social justice are among his priorities.

Jocelerme Privert: The political veteran has served as senator, finance minister, interior minister and interim president of Haiti. In 2004, he was arrested and accused of organizing a massacre that targeted political opponents in the central coastal city of Saint-Marc. He served time in prison and rejoined the political scene after his release. He served as interim president from 2016 to 2017 following a delay in an election run-off between Moïse and Jude Célestin, a mechanical engineer who once again is seeking to become president.

Hans Joseph: The former director of Haiti's Anti-Corruption Unit, he was known for aggressively pursuing corruption cases against high-profile figures in a country where impunity reigns. Local media reported that several political parties sought him as a potential candidate, but he decided to join a newly formed party.

Jerry Tardieu: He's a well-known businessman and former parliamentarian who represented the upscale community of Petion-Ville and has been outspoken about gangs. He has served as CEO of companies in sectors including the shoe industry and real estate, and he was co-founder of the Royal Oasis Hotel. He runs a free library for children in Petion-Ville and has a master’s degree in public administration with a concentration in economics from Harvard University. He has pledged to create jobs and make Haiti safer: “I will refuse to preside over the fate of a country whose population lives in fear.”
Associated Press reporter Evens Sanon in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: British women to receive automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
story: The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnancies
LONDON -- British women convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will be automatically pardoned Monday, the government said.
The action follows Parliament's passage last year of a landmark vote to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section from the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons and some will be issued posthumously.

“For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police had investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once “dragged from hospital beds to police cells” and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

“This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they’ve always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for “compassion, not punishment.”

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant more than 10 weeks.

title: Kenyan farmers adopt new techniques to curb erosion during heavy rains
summary: Farmers in parts of Kenya are turning to simple soil conservation techniques to protect their crops and farmland ahead of the October-December rainy season that is projected to be heavier than usual
story: Farmers in parts of Kenya are turning to simple soil conservation techniques to protect their crops and farmland ahead of the October-December rainy season that is projected to be heavier than usual

LIMURU, Kenya -- After losing much of her farm’s topsoil to heavy rains two years ago, Elizabeth Itotia is taking no chances as Kenya faces the October–December rainy season, which is expected to bring heavier-than-usual downpours.

Itotia’s 5-acre (2-hectare) farm in Limuru, Kiambu County, in central Kenya, lies on a slope that makes it vulnerable to soil erosion. Catastrophic rains in 2024 washed away much of the nutrient-rich topsoil and destroyed several crops, including kale, spinach, cabbage, potatoes and native vegetables, leaving her with estimated losses of 200,000 Kenyan shillings ($1,500). More than 230 people were killed in the floods.
To restore the damaged land, Itotia and her family had to bring in topsoil from other farms, an effort that required additional labor and money to make the land productive again.

Her experience highlights the challenges farmers in Kenya face when extreme weather events cause losses. In a country where most farmers depend on the rainy seasons, recovering from such losses can take months or even years.

The Kenya Meteorological Department forecast El Niño conditions during the short-rains season, which runs from mid-October to December. The El Niño phenomenon is associated with warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. In East Africa, it can bring heavier-than-usual rains.

The rainy season coincides with the corn harvest in Kenya. Corn, the country’s staple crop, is planted during the long-rains season and harvested as the short rains begin. Heavy rainfall during this period could force farmers to harvest early or leave corn insufficiently dried, increasing the risk of aflatoxin contamination.
After learning about soil conservation techniques on social media, Itotia adopted a method that involves filling sacks with sand and placing them in trenches to slow runoff and reduce soil erosion.
Itotia has also planted Napier grass and bamboo, whose roots help hold earth together, in areas vulnerable to erosion. The Napier grass also provides fodder for her livestock.
Her neighbor, Esther Njoki, has adopted a similar approach, filling sacks with soil to slow runoff and limit erosion.
“We have never applied this technique before, even though the soil in this area is very light and easily swept away,” Njoki said.
She said that the loss of topsoil leaves the land muddy, making cultivation and moving around the farm difficult.

Samuel Munyiri, an agronomist at Osho Chemical Industries, said working the soil during the rainy season makes it more susceptible to being washed away. He said the sandbags being used by farmers were effective at reducing soil loss through runoff, especially in places where small channels have begun to form.

He advises farmers to adopt soil conservation practices such as terracing, constructing gabions — mesh boxes filled with soil or rocks to stop erosion — planting crops across slopes as opposed to along the slope and using cover crops that protect the soil from erosion.
He also urges farmers to consider crop that can tolerate high rainfall, such as corn, wheat and barley, and to adjust planting schedules, particularly during periods of prolonged heavy rainfall.
"Crops such as beans, potatoes and cabbages may be damaged by prolonged heavy rains and should be planted when the intensity of the rains is expected to subside,” he said.
Munyiri said cereals generally fare better than pulses during prolonged rains.
In Karatina, Nyeri County, in central Kenya, coffee farmer Moses Muhoro is also preparing for the rains after years of losses caused by heavy downpours.

In 2024, floods swept away the fertile topsoil on his farm, leaving behind less productive subsoil, the layer beneath the topsoil. The damage significantly reduced his coffee production the following year. Because coffee is an export crop, lower harvests can affect both farmers' incomes and Kenya's economy.
When The Associated Press visited Muhoro, he was digging trenches and filling sacks with soil to control runoff and prevent erosion.

“I learned this when I visited a friend who is also a farmer. His farm was steeper than mine, yet he had managed to minimize losses caused by heavy rains. I decided to try the same approach on my farm,” Muhoro said.
He said farmers in the area have suffered the effects of heavy rainfall largely because they lack timely information on how to prepare for and mitigate its impacts.

David Koros, assistant director of forecasting at the Kenya Meteorological Department, said the agency provides daily, weekly, monthly and seasonal forecasts to help the public and various sectors prepare for changing weather conditions.
He said rainfall was expected to spread across the country by the end of October, with November projected to be the peak of the season.

Areas that could receive above-average rainfall include the coastal region, the northeastern and southeastern lowlands, and the eastern region, including the capital, Nairobi. Parts of western Kenya and the Rift Valley were also set for above-average rainfall, although the effects might be less severe, Koros said.
Western Kenya and the Rift Valley are among the country’s key food-producing regions, and losses there could have implications for national food security.
Experts stress the importance of building long-term resilience to safeguard food security.
Tom Fletcher, the U. N. undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, said preparing early for climate shocks could help avert a humanitarian crisis.
Farmers also should be protected through insurance, said Alice Ruhweza, head of the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, an agricultural nonprofit.
