title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal and accepts sexual assault conviction
summary: French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set
story: French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set

PARIS -- French actor Gérard Depardieu said Monday he was dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set and will accept the 18-month suspended sentence. He also issued an apology.
“I was found guilty," Depardieu said in a written statement, as his appeal trial was scheduled to open Monday in Paris. He added that he “hears it” and accepts the sentence.
“I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered,” he said.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a 54-year-old set decorator and a 34-year-old assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” (“The Green Shutters”) in 2021. He received an 18-month suspended prison sentence in a case that was widely seen as a post-#MeToo test for the country’s film industry.

The court also ordered the 77-year-old Depardieu, one of the most prominent figures in French cinema for decades, to pay both accusers a total of 29,040 euros ($32,350) in fines, and that his name be listed in the national sex offender database.

“On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu wrote.
“I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that no longer exists,” he added. “I have therefore decided to withdraw my appeal.”

The comments contrast with the actors’ statements during the trial last year, when he had strongly denied the accusations. He acknowledged using vulgar and sexual language on the film set and grabbing the set dresser's hips during an argument, but denied that his behavior was sexual.
Depardieu is expected to face other legal proceedings soon.

In 2018, actor Charlotte Arnould accused him of raping her at his home. An investigating judge in August 2025 requested that the case go to trial and a Paris appeals court is to decide next week whether it will proceed.

For more than a half-century, Depardieu was a towering figure in French cinema, known for his commanding physical presence and versatility. In recent years, his behavior toward women has come under renewed scrutiny, including after a documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

title: At least 17 people were killed in separate shootings in South Africa
summary: Police in South Africa say at least 17 people were killed in two mass shootings on the same day
story: Police in South Africa say at least 17 people were killed in two mass shootings on the same day

JOHANNESBURG -- At least 17 people were killed in two mass shootings on the same day in South Africa. Motives have not been immediately established for the crimes some 530 kilometers (330 miles) apart, police said Monday.

Eight people were found dead inside a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, according to police, who said they had not immediately identified the victims or any suspects in the shooting Sunday.

Nine people were found dead with gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria. The shooting reportedly took place Sunday night and no arrests have been made.
The Jeffsville case is being investigated by the serious and violent crimes, murder and robbery unit in Gauteng province.
The incident is reported to have occurred between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m., police said.

“Police were alerted at approximately 07:30 this morning, 16 November 2026. On arrival, members found the bodies of nine people, six males and three females, inside the four-roomed shack with gunshot wounds,” said police spokesperson Brenda Muridili.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said the killings could be related to a previous shooting at a nearby informal settlement in Saulsville last year where 12 people were killed and 13 injured.
He said one of the people who was killed during the shooting was a “person of interest” in the shooting that happened in Saulsville last year.
“We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack,” Mthombeni said.
In the Saulsville case from last year, Mthombeni said police had made a breakthrough and arrested one suspect who is believed to be one of the mass shooters.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi, who visited the crime scene with the police on Monday, said the provincial government was coordinating with other provincial departments to support the police in their investigations of similar crimes happening in the province, which includes the city of Johannesburg.
In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help with identifying the victims but it was yet to be confirmed.
“It's still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” said Netshiunda.
Several mass shootings linked to criminal gangs have occurred in the past year.

In September, three gunmen barged into a small house in an impoverished neighborhood near the coastal city of Durban and opened fire on people attending a party, killing at least 11, including a pregnant woman.

In the same month, 17 people were killed and several others wounded when gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles stormed a tavern and opened fire at patrons outside the bar before moving inside and continuing to shoot.
In June, multiple shooters killed 12 people in a poor neighborhood in Johannesburg in an attack that police linked to criminal gangs.
Also in June this year, an armed gang opened fire in a poor neighborhood in Johannesburg, killing 12 people and wounding at least nine, before fleeing in a minibus.
Mthombeni said police had arrested three people in that shooting. They believe that it was linked to territorial battles between rival illegal mining gangs.
Two mass shootings two weeks apart in December last year killed 21 people. They also were carried out by multiple gunmen.

title: Ethiopia and Sudan accusations of backing armed fighters as fears of conflict grow
summary: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each country accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders
story: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each country accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders

CAIRO -- Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries.
Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.

In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the U.N. Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed.
Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement.

Each country denies the other's accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict.

Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.”
Here’s a closer look at what's behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region:
Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting.

So far, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or ACLED, a conflict monitor, though aid groups warn that the real number is likely much higher. Some 13 million people have been displaced.

The war, now in its fourth year, has left the Sudanese military in control of the north, east and central regions, including Sudan’s Red Sea ports and its oil refineries and pipelines. The RSF and its allies control western Darfur and parts of Kordofan along the border with South Sudan — both regions rich in oil fields and gold mines.
The latest flashpoint in the war is in Sudan's Blue Nile province, which borders Ethiopia.

In late August, the Humanitarian Research Lab, a Yale University research group that uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, found an increase in military vehicles and equipment at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, a city near the Sudanese border.
Based on satellite imagery, the Yale group confirmed the buildup was linked to the RSF.
“The RSF is engaged out of Ethiopia ... to try to open a second front,” said Nathaniel Raymond, head of the research group.

Fighting resumed in September in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, and Ethiopian federal troops fought between 2020 and 2022, when a peace deal was signed.

Later that month, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, suggested that Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt were supporting rebel troops who at the time had captured several strategic towns. The allegations drew sharp denials from the three neighbors.
In early November, Ethiopia expelled the six staff members of Sudan’s mission in Asosa and closed the consulate.

Naidoo, from Oxford Economics Africa, warned that continued fighting in Tigray could divert Ethiopia’s attention from its myriad other issues and increase the risk of weapons and fighters flowing across the border with Sudan.

“All the ingredients are present for an intensifying proxy war between Ethiopia and Sudan that further destabilizes both countries,” said Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa project director at the International Crisis Group.
Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated since late last year, when the RSF established camps on Ethiopian territory, according to Ladd Serwat, senior Africa analyst at ACLED.
In October, a drone strike blamed on the RSF hit a gathering of displaced people on Sudan's border with Ethiopia and killed 41, said the Emergency Lawyers rights group, which tracks the war in Sudan.

“Sudan and Ethiopia don’t operate in a vacuum; their relations amid these current domestic conflicts are shaped by external backers,” said Serwat, adding that Ethiopia is allied with the United Arab Emirates while Sudan is part of an Egypt-Eritrea regional alliance.
Turkey has been balancing, backing both Khartoum and Addis Ababa, he said.

Serwat added that Ethiopia’s support for the RSF is primarily logistical, while the UAE remains its main backer, funding camps and supplying weapons. The UAE has repeatedly denied any involvement in Sudan’s war.

Other issues have also marred relations, including Ethiopia's construction of a huge dam — Africa’s largest dam — on the Blue Nile, the main Nile River tributary. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the Ethiopia-Sudan border cost about $5 billion and was completed in 2025, aiming to boost Ethiopia's power production and economy.
But it has triggered a dispute with Egypt and Sudan, which have called for a legally binding agreement on the dam’s filling and operation to protect their own water resources.

Another issue is the disputed border region of Al-Fashaga, where Ethiopian farmers have long cultivated the area's fertile soil, according to the International Crisis Group. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved in to reassert control over the area as Ethiopian troops were distracted fighting with the Tigray rebels.
The Sudan-Ethiopia tensions may not have gained much attention, but if ignored, they could escalate further and lead to mass displacements of people, Raymond's Yale group said.
Associated Press writer Khaled Kazziha in Nairobi, Kenya, contributed to this report.

title: Cargo ship sinks off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast
summary: A Somali-flagged cargo ship has sunk in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, according to the transport ministry
story: A Somali-flagged cargo ship has sunk in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, according to the transport ministry
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A Somali-flagged cargo ship has sunk on Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on Monday, the transport ministry said.

All 12 crew members on board — eight Turkish citizens and four Azerbaijani nationals — were saved in the rescue operation that involved four ships, two from Bulgaria, one from Romania and one from Turkey.

The vessel’s crew sent a distress call at 9:15 a.m. that the ship was sinking approximately 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra. The BETUL 8 was sailing from the Romanian port of Tulcea to Egypt, carrying three tons of bulk wheat, according to the ministry.

There was no immediate information whether the cause of the incident was the result of a drone strike, like the several deadly drone attacks against merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania in recent weeks, that were widely blamed by analysts and political leaders on Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Last week, drones struck four additional vessels near the Romanian port of Sulina. Two of the ships caught fire, although no injuries were reported.

title: Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
summary: Southeast Asian leaders will gather in the Philippine capital this weekend for the annual ASEAN summit that will focus on global conflicts
story: Southeast Asian leaders will gather in the Philippine capital this weekend for the annual ASEAN summit that will focus on global conflicts

MANILA, Philippines -- Some of the world’s most intractable conflicts will be high on the agenda when Southeast Asian leaders gather in the Philippine capital for annual summit meetings this weekend. U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to join them for the final talks.
The three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts starts Sunday in a heavily guarded convention center in Manila Bay.

According to drafts of prepared post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press, no breakthroughs are expected in the discussions that will focus on calling for the peaceful resolution of the South China Sea disputes, the civil strife in Myanmar and the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

This year, the Philippines holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, a conservative regional bloc of 11 democratic and authoritarian states, including police states. The bloc has managed to keep together such a diverse grouping since its founding in 1967 largely because of its bedrock policy of non-interference in the members' domestic affairs.

In Manila, key rivals will again be face-to-face but no shake-ups are anticipated. ASEAN is known more for its photo-ops that project unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including the civil war in Myanmar.

Trump will land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and the Philippines has turned over the regional bloc’s annual leadership to Singapore.

He will, however, be joining three key meetings on Tuesday night, including a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails and a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, according to Philippine officials.
China will be represented by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday, but will leave before Trump arrives, the officials said.

The prepared communiques say ASEAN leaders and their major Asian and Western counterparts will exchange “views on regional and international issues of concern," before listing the conflicts that will be discussed.

“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the prepared statement says. It also underlines the "importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
On Saturday, ASEAN foreign ministers met for pre-summit talks, linking hands and posing for a joint photo on stage, their national flags lined up behind them.

The talks, hosted by Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, will include her report on a recent trip to Myanmar, where she pressed longstanding calls for the civil strife-plagued country to do more to comply with a five-point peace plan crafted by ASEAN leaders five years ago.

The leader and foreign minister of Myanmar, an ASEAN member, have been banned from attending the bloc’s annual meetings because of their government's failure to fully comply with the peace plan that calls for an immediate end to the deadly fighting that has gripped the country.

The prepared communiques also urged "all parties to commit to an immediate cessation of violence, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, inclusive dialogue with all stakeholders and the unconditional release of all those unjustly detained” in Myanmar.

On the South China Sea disputes that involve China, Taiwan and four ASEAN members — Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam — substantial progress has been made in negotiations for a non-aggression pact called the “ code of conduct ” between Beijing and the regional bloc, according to three Southeast Asian diplomats who spoke to the AP earlier.

They said, however, that the pact — which has seen more than two decades of consultations and negotiations between China and ASEAN — will not be finalized this year. Negotiations about it will resume next year.
The pact aims to prevent on-and-off confrontation in the disputed waters from degenerating into a full-blown conflict that can endanger Asia’s economies.

title: Bomb rips through Damascus suburb killing 2 including a child
summary: The device placed inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital.
story: The device placed inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital.

DAMASCUS, Syria -- An explosive device placed inside a car in a suburb of Syria's capital exploded Saturday evening, killing two people and wounding at least one, state TV and the Interior Ministry said.

The explosion took place in the southern Damascus suburb of Jaramana near a factory where batteries are produced, state TV said. It said two people were killed and two were wounded, without giving further details.
The Interior Ministry said the dead included a child, adding that one person was wounded. It said security forces cordoned off the area and started an investigation.

Several explosions have taken place in Damascus and its suburbs in recent months as the country’s security remains fragile nearly two years after five decades of Assad family rule ended in December 2024. Militants stormed the capital and removed then-President Bashar Assad from power.

Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority. The suburb has faced tensions between some members of the community and Sunni Muslim Syrians supportive of the country’s current Islamist-led government.

title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
story: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune.

The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts.

The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.”

In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.”
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share.

The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally.

The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation.

The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation, the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
story: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.

The S&P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss. The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time.

Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership. Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow.

Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities.

It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers.

“The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.”

Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%.

The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation.

Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer.

Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier.

The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.

It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates.
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates.

Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks. A report also showed that Japan’s economy contracted in the latest quarter.
AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: A top Puerto Rico government official resigns as corruption allegations swirl
summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
story: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her.

Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González, which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years.
Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General.

In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana.
Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed.
Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000.
Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her.
Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down.
Puerto Rico Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz, also a member of the governor’s New Progressive Party, has said that ongoing legislative investigations would continue even if Roig resigned.
As Roig faced increasing scrutiny, she alleged in recent months that she was being stalked and persecuted as she denied all accusations.
In a statement Monday, Roig said that nobody asked her to resign as she thanked the governor for “the time and space that allowed me to defend my reputation against attacks full of falsehoods.”
Her decision to step down on Dec. 31 angered many.

“The resignation should have been immediate,” said Puerto Rico Sen. Juan Oscar Morales, majority whip and a member of the governor’s party. “The Department of the Family needs leadership focused on addressing the agency’s problems and ensuring services for those who depend on it.”

Roig’s announcement came nearly four months after the governor’s chief of staff and deputy chief of staff announced their resignations as they, too, denied corruption allegations. The governor stood by them as she has by Roig.

title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement
story: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement

NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement.

The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers.

In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.”

But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union.
Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already.

Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said.
“We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post.

Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal.
Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely.

Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration.

“We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said.

In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later.
But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court.

title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035
story: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035

BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers.

The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey.

India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States.
Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy.

The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure. The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced.

“If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.”
The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan.
Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products.
“So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said.

The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source.

India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas.
Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses.

However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember.

India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035.
Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining.

Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power.

Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets.
Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers.

India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits. Although clean power accounted for 55% of installed power capacity by September, it generated about a third of the country’s electricity in the preceding three months, according to government data.
Over the past 16 months, India curtailed enough solar generation to power about 10 million homes because the grid could not accommodate it, according to government data and Ember.

The Green Energy Corridor plan aims to help states accommodate up to 135 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2033 by adding thousands of kilometers (miles) of transmission lines. The plan also includes additional battery storage.
But analysts question whether that's enough. The Berkeley researchers estimate that India needs as much as 250 gigawatts of energy storage to integrate renewable electricity over the next decade.
“You either have more transmission to get the power out and transfer it. Or if you cannot get the power out, you store it and then transfer it during some other hours,” Ember's Rodrigues said.

Shah, the economist, said two types of government policy could discourage investment in renewable energy: requirements that businesses pay higher rates to subsidize other consumers, and restrictions on electricity producers selling directly to private buyers.

He said India needs to allow electricity prices to rise and fall based on supply and demand, and make it easier for foreign investors to fund power projects. Domestic financing alone would not be enough to meet the country’s growing energy needs, he said.
“Currently, the government is a man in the middle, trying to interfere in a transaction between a private generator and a private buyer,” which creates a “choke point,” Shah said.

Battery supply chains pose another challenge, particularly India’s dependence on imported battery cells, mainly from China. Abhyankar said expanding domestic battery manufacturing could help India capture more economic benefits from the transition.

Despite those challenges, Abhyankar said India has already overtaken the United States in annual renewable energy growth, and its experience in expanding clean energy could be a model for other developing countries.
“What India is doing can be replicated in many countries in the Global South and can help these countries make the energy transition in an economically affordable manner," he said.

title: Tens of thousands march in Portuguese cities against surging home prices
summary: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices
story: Tens of thousands of people have marched in Portugal in the biggest protest yet against surging housing prices

LISBON, Portugal -- Tens of thousands of people marched through more than 30 cities and towns across Portugal on Saturday in the largest protest yet against soaring housing costs that many say have put buying or renting a home beyond their reach.

The housing crisis has fueled weeks of demonstrations. Some activists have camped in central squares in Lisbon and Porto, the country’s two largest cities. Riot police with dogs have dispersed some protests, drawing accusations of heavy-handed tactics.
The demonstrations took inspiration from protests that began in neighboring Spain last month over similar housing concerns. They come amid widespread social unrest across Europe this autumn.

Marching under the slogan “We won’t let them steal our right to housing,” participants ranged from teenagers to retirees. Drums, music and chants accompanied the Lisbon march as protesters carried large banners and flags.

Susana Pacheco, a 35-year-old data analyst who works part-time as an astrologer to help pay her mortgage, said she worried about whether her younger sister could afford to move out of their parents’ home.
“I’m really worried about young people,” Pacheco said. “I don’t know how they’re going to be able to pay” for their own home.
“Things have become intolerable,” said Ana Encarnação, 42, citing rising living costs and the widening gap between rich and poor.
Activists want ceilings placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing.
House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes, statistics show.

Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61%, followed by the Netherlands with 34%, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.

There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, housing prices rose by almost 20%, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.
Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68% increase since 2020, according to the government.

Foreign buyers and investment funds have fueled price rises by buying Portuguese real estate. The country’s mild climate and long coastline have helped it grow popular with digital nomads and other remote workers, as well as retirees. Tourism has also surged, with many city center apartments switched to short-term rentals.

The government has responded with measures such as lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals and promising to build 145,000 new homes. But it acknowledges that the effects won’t be immediate.

Portuguese President António José Seguro, whose role is mostly ceremonial but who wields political influence, convened a Council of State, an advisory body, to discuss the protests earlier this month and met Friday with some of the protesters.
AP reporter Helena Alves in Lisbon contributed to this story.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters
story: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters

PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.
“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”
Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.
Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: Trump heads to Asia with hopes of shifting the momentum after midterm setbacks hurt him at home
summary: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections
story: President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week and he's aiming to shift the momentum after Republican losses in the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump heads to Asia this week, hoping to make some big attention-grabbing moves on the world stage after his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections, diminishing his standing at home.

The Republican president is using the international trip to try to shift momentum, and he is poised to make a splash with a historic three-way meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia to talk about their nuclear stockpiles. Trump has long boasted about leveraging his relationships with the leaders of two of America’s biggest global adversaries, though he has failed so far to achieve major breakthroughs with them.

He first heads to the Philippines to meet on Tuesday with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing's aggression in the region. Trump will then go to China on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. There, he will have his third face-to-face meeting this year with Xi and see Putin, too.

A year ago, Trump used a similar Asia trip to agree on a trade truce with China and secure investment pledges from Japan and South Korea. This time, Trump is going with his party no longer in control of Congress as of January and with attention beginning to turn to a crop of presidential hopefuls who aim to replace him in 2028.

“I think he, like other presidents, has figured out that in a moment where things are really hard domestically: Get on an airplane and go international,” said Kurt Campbell, a former deputy secretary of state in Democratic President Joe Biden's administration and chairman of The Asia Group, a consultancy.
It's a pattern followed by some of Trump's predecessors.

Democratic President Barack Obama flew to Beijing days after his party lost the Senate in 2014 to negotiate carbon emission targets with Xi. Republican President George W. Bush went to APEC in Vietnam after the GOP lost control of Congress in 2006, though the Iraq War hung over his travels.

The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila as well as a host of commercial deals and will be the “guest of honor” at a leaders' dinner. In Shenzhen, he will focus on trade issues before the meeting with Xi and Putin.

Trump is leaving as airlines struggled to get passengers onto flights after a nationwide ground stop on Friday led to thousands of flight cancellations. Trump and his officials have blamed their predecessors, a contractor and Congress for the problems.
Trump is about to be bogged down at home in ways that may curb what he can do overseas.

His tariffs and war with Iran proved to be poisonous with voters. Going forward, Trump's ability to threaten import taxes or military assaults — two of his major foreign policy tools — will be limited by Democratic majorities on Capitol Hill in the new year.

Just last week, in a newfound vulnerability, his push to boost artificial intelligence was complicated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.
Huang had traveled with Trump on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September.

Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on AI and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition. But Trump does not plan to confront Xi on the issue, said administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president’s plans on a call with reporters.

The officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip. Even though the administration is discussing ways to close loopholes and further prevent Chinese businesses from using advanced chips made by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, the officials said they do not expect the restrictions to cause retaliation by Beijing.

Trump will be accompanied by Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is the world's wealthiest man and a frequent adviser to the president. Musk spent at least $445 million to try to help Republicans keep control of Congress, and Democrats are keen to investigate his ties to the administration.

Trump may find it easier to be in the company of foreign leaders than his own crumbling coalition at home. But his words and actions at the summits are now more likely to draw scrutiny in committee hearings when he returns to Washington.
“We’re going to have a very close eye on it," said Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Meeks and other leading Democrats on the committee have already called on the administration to provide more information about its approval of advanced AI chip exports after the Nvidia disclosures.
Democrats also will be pushing for a much tougher approach to Putin and Xi, leaders they view as authoritarian strongmen.
“It seems as though when Xi or Putin comes to America, he rolls out the red carpet for them — but other American allies come, he has not rolled out the red carpet for them,” Meeks said.

Democrats want the administration to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine and have called for the administration to fulfill an arms agreement with Taiwan, which China has sought to block.

Trump has suggested he wants to talk to Xi and Putin about nuclear weapons, an area that China has been reluctant to engage on in the past. China has a much smaller stockpile than the U.S. and Russia, giving it less incentive to agree to restraints.

The visit comes as Trump is at a crossroads over the war with Iran, which is widely blamed for his political support cratering at home. It's also a source of economic instability in Asia as jet fuel and diesel costs have soared. Trump has tried to play down the chances he will order major strikes against Iran to be resumed, though he also has said he does not see the need for talks.
Democrats are likely to scrutinize whether the president confronts Xi and Putin over r eports that China and Russia have aided Tehran, something Trump has previously dismissed.

Trump recently has played up chances for a settlement to Russia’s war in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not been invited to the talks in China, drawing outrage from Democrats and some Russia hawks in his own party. Administration officials said Trump is not expected to talk about Ukraine with Putin at the meeting.

The sheer number of issues hanging over Trump threatens to overshadow some important issues for the other regional leaders he'll talk to — namely the strength of U.S. support for countering China's influence in the Asia Pacific. In Manila, Trump is expected to participate in talks with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations including the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan. It will be the first meeting of the Quad leaders since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report.

title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport
story: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport

MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.

The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.
Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle.

On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.

The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days.
The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.
In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.

“We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.”
The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

title: New Orleans port sues to get control of tanker that crashed into cruise ship on Mississippi River
summary: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River
story: New Orleans port officials have sued the owner of a tanker that slammed into a cruise ship on the Mississippi River

Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city’s port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker.

Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.
The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker’s voyage data recorder has been recovered. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident.
NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months.

The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.
The first step is to make sure the 16,000 gallons (60,500 liters) of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said.
Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.
The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.
The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told WDSU-TV.

The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 66 degrees Fahrenheit (19 degrees Celsius).
Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

“It’s fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn’t taste very good,” Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.
Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him.
“They taught us not to drown,” Knab said.

Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday’s nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.

Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.

“Whether it’s 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success,” Montroll said.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 520-foot-long (160-meter-long) vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.

The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.
Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history
story: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history

MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.”

The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff.
“The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli, Prada Group's chief group marketing officer.

Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed.

Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces.

“We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli.

Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway.
And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo.

Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988.

The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport.

“Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.”

He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition.

Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission, targeted for 2028.
Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution.

Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment.
Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises.
The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.”

“It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. That was lovely.”

title: UK appoints climate security envoy as Thunberg criticizes COP31 leaders
summary: The United Kingdom has appointed a special envoy to address climate change security threats
story: The United Kingdom has appointed a special envoy to address climate change security threats

ANTALYA, Turkey -- The United Kingdom on Thursday announced the appointment of a special envoy to tackle security threats from climate change while small island leaders called for urgent action, describing planet heating as a life-or-death issue for their people at the climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya.
Alix Sebastien Pillay, the vice president of Seychelles, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, said his country's very survival is at stake.
“It is time to move past the talking,” Pillay said. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.”

Pillay was speaking on the second day of the leaders' summit at the U.N. climate talks, where government leaders addressed the state of a warming world and what they plan to do about it. While the entire globe is threatened by souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing up their land.
Pillay said Seychelles is experiencing millions of dollars of damage as a result of storms and floods, despite contributing little to increased global warming.

He said a U.N. fund created for compensating for climate-related loss and damage needs to be urgently strengthened. “Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt.”

Speaking at the talks, Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific Island of Niue, said the El Niño conditions which have driven up global temperatures are a warning of what might happen if planet heating is not controlled.
“Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now," Tagelagi said.
The comment came as a report said the world has failed to slow global warming trends in the past five years because plans weren’t realized and efforts that would have helped were canceled out.

“Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the report said.

Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned. Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, called nationally determined contributions. The speed of reductions and ways to achieve them are different by country.

Because collective efforts of countries haven't significantly reduced global emissions, the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, which is the warming threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report.

The report said if the nations of the world fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than preindustrial times.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the appointment of a special representative to deal with security risks from the climate crisis, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world.
“Climate is a national security issue,” Burnham said at the summit. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere."
He said Britain would place climate resilience high on the agenda when it assumes the G20 presidency next year.

The appointment of Madeleine Alessandri as special representative for climate security follows a British government assessment earlier this year warning that damage to ecosystems, driven partly by climate change, could disrupt food supplies and fuel conflict and migration since the island-nation imports about 40% of its food.
Climate activists said, however, that Burnham’s policies do not fully align with the sense of urgency he expressed in his speech.
“Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action,” said Ami McCarthy of Greenpeace UK in a statement.

“The future we feared has become the present we are living. Climate change knows no borders. No nation can face it alone. Solidarity must mean real action,” said Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

Sharif, like many other leaders from countries ravaged by climate impacts, said adequate financing needs to be made available to deal with climate disasters, such as the 2022 floods in Pakistan that submerged over a third of the country and resulted in thousands of deaths and over $30 billion in damage.
A day earlier, Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine described fossil fuel expansion as "something to fear."

“Every new oil well drilled, every piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country’s future," Heine said. “No one has the right to pollute their neighbors.” She said the response of the world to the inevitability of passing the 1.5-degree warming limit target “must be overwhelming or the world we know is over.”
Meanwhile, climate activist Greta Thunberg, attending her first U.N. climate summit since 2021, said those in power were failing to address the climate crisis.
“We are heading toward a future of more genocides and ecocides where basic necessities become luxury,” Thunberg said at a news conference on the sidelines of the summit.
“The planet is not dying, it is being killed," she said. "And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue.”
The last time Thunberg attended a climate summit was the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.”
Webber reported from Chicago, Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland, and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.
