title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: World shares log modest losses as investors assess impact on AI sector from the Nvidia scandal
summary: Shares are mostly lower in Europe and Asia, but losses remain modest as investors assess how Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO might affect the global artificial intelligence industry
story: Shares are mostly lower in Europe and Asia, but losses remain modest as investors assess how Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO might affect the global artificial intelligence industry

HONG KONG -- Shares were mostly lower Friday in Europe and Asia, but losses remained modest as investors assessed how Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO might affect the global artificial intelligence industry.
A global outage for Microsoft web services disrupted email accounts and some other applications worldwide but appeared to have scant direct impact on markets.

Microsoft said in an update Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
U.S. futures were little changed.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX edged 0.1% lower, to 26,748.60 and the CAC 40 in Paris also shed 0.1%, to 8,353.98. Britain's FTSE 100 fell 0.1% to 10,856.66.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.5% to 61,142.35. Shares of chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron were up 1.7%, while memory chip maker Kioxia Holdings dropped 2.3%. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 5.1%.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index declined 1% to 5,290.53. Samsung Electronics, one of South Korea’s most valuable companies, was down 1%. Memory chipmaker SK Hynix fell 3%.
Taiwan’s Taiex gained 1.4%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., adding 0.4%.

The departure of Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and has been a key architect of its role at the center of the AI boom, has raised questions about the company's future. Its shares fell 4% after his resignation was announced. Huang had been the face of Nvidia and was deemed by some in the industry as bigger than Nvidia itself.
Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns. Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO.

A lynchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street’s most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Market watchers will be keeping a keen eye out for what Nvidia's woes might mean for pending public debuts of AI companies, such as Anthropic’s pending IPO, valued at $1.3 trillion.
Share prices for many Asian companies that make the computer chips, servers and other hardware used for AI have been closely linked to the speed of AI infrastructure development in the U.S.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index gave up 1.6% to 23,637.60. The Shanghai Composite index slid 0.6% to 3,634.35.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.7% to 9,082.20.
India’s Sensex fell 0.6%.
On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 slipped 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.4%, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite also declined 0.4%.
Shares of some of Nvidia’s rivals rose on Thursday. That includes AMD, or Advanced Micro Devices, whose stock rose 5.9%.
Stocks were also under broad pressure as oil prices climbed after U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday the U.S. didn't “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he posted on social media. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
Early Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was up 0.3% at $96.07 a barrel. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.
Benchmark U.S. crude edged 0.1% higher, to $88.08 a barrel.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.92 Japanese yen from 159.84 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1066, up from $1.1055.

title: Microsoft struggles to restore services as outage hits companies and governments worldwide
summary: Microsoft is dealing with a major outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams
story: Microsoft is dealing with a major outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams

HONG KONG -- From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue.

Microsoft said in an update Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.”
The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website.
Roughly 130,000 users from dozens of countries Downdetector reported problems on outage tracker with accessing Outlook on Thursday although new reports have since fallen from that peak.
A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control.
Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.
Its most recent post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution.
“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote.
In a more recent update Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

In July 2024, a massive global tech outage grounded flights, disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers, with Texas-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike blaming a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer machines.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts could not receive updates from their U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that they were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.
AP journalists Adam Schreck in Bangkok, Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Australia, Sheikh Saaliq in New Delhi and Mayuko Ono in Tokyo contributed.

title: A Romanov sapphire bracelet sells for $4.9 million at a Geneva auction
summary: Sotheby’s says a Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet has sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs or $4.9 million at auction
story: Sotheby’s says a Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet has sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs or $4.9 million at auction

GENEVA -- A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby's said.

The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia's imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday.
The buyer, a private collector, wasn't identified.

The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia's imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court.

Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II's mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — "widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said.
After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby's said.

title: Portugal closes all schools and non-essential services ahead of a major Atlantic storm
summary: Portugal has closed all schools and non-essential public services as a major Atlantic storm approaches the mainland
story: Portugal has closed all schools and non-essential public services as a major Atlantic storm approaches the mainland
LISBON, Portugal -- LISBON, Portugal (AP) — Portugal closed all schools and shuttered non-essential public services on Wednesday as a major Atlantic storm headed for the country's mainland.

Streets remained largely deserted ahead of the arrival of Storm Charles after the government told people to stay at home as heavy rain and rough seas were expected to batter the Portuguese coast, with wind gusts of up to 140 kph (85 mph).
It was the first time in living memory that Portugal’s roughly 8,000 schools had canceled classes nationwide over a storm forecast.

Buses without passengers drove through the country's capital, Lisbon, where some streets flooded due to clogged drains. A national supermarket chain closed its stores, while an international technology conference in Lisbon attended by around 70,000 people called off the day's events.

In January, the country's center-right government faced harsh criticism for its weak response when Storm Kristin hit central Portugal, felling thousands of trees and causing widespread property damage that is still being repaired.

The brunt of Storm Charles was expected to hit the Atlantic coast on Wednesday afternoon and evening, coming from the southwest after it had struck the Portuguese island of Madeira on Tuesday with 130 kph (81 mph) winds.

title: Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy

She was building a career in Chinese finance before turning to tech with a leadership role at a data center company in Singapore. He is the high-profile CEO of Nvidia, the California-based company that makes computer chips relied upon by advanced artificial intelligence systems.
An affair between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who reportedly was suspected of working as a spy for Beijing, has rocked the tech and political worlds.

The Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to reports over the past month by the New York Times. The newspaper also reported that top policymakers were informed in a memo that intelligence indicated she was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.

In one widely shared photograph of the pair, Jensen Huang and people surrounding him are holding drinks in Taipei, while Alice Huang sits behind him, apparently watching him in conversation. The picture was posted in 2024 by software company NetThunder to its LinkedIn page.
It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Publicly available information about Alice Huang is scant.
She was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips.

In 2023, she became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which describes itself as an “NVIDIA cloud partner.” Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. over its alleged skirting of U.S. export restrictions and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips for Chinese users.

Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 in Singapore with the name 7Road International, after being spun off as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, according to corporate registration records.
Filings show that in March 2023, it renamed itself Megaspeed International, with all of the shares transferred to Huang Le Limited, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, Alice Huang became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security.
But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan.

While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations.

Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database.
Her roles at Hexi included deputy general manager, executive director and member of the investment committee, according to Hexi's social media posts, among possible other roles.

Hexi's founder Kang Wei, who appeared on some records alongside Alice Huang, was fined in 2018 by China's securities regulator 400,000 yuan ($60,000) over financial misconduct behaviors while Hexi was fined 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Before that, Alice Huang worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her employment history.
Beijing has refuted claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Its Foreign Ministry said this week that the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.”
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again under the spotlight.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.

Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”

Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at prediction market Kalshi
summary: Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday
story: Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday
NEW YORK -- Donald Trump Jr. is no longer a paid adviser for Kalshi, the prediction market company said Thursday.

Kalshi described the decision as a mutual business decision between the two parties that followed a decision by Trump Jr.'s investment firm, 1789 Capital, to increase its investment in Kalshi's biggest competitor Polymarket.

But the announcement comes a week after Democrats were able to take control of both the House and Senate in the midterm elections. Democrats have said they planned to investigate the Trump family's investments, including their business relationships with both prediction markets.

“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer," said Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi. “We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers.”

The president's eldest son became a paid “strategic adviser” for Kalshi shortly after President Trump was sworn into office for his second term in January 2025 and has been an investor in Polymarket since August 2025. Both companies have seen their popularity and use jump significantly in the past two years.

At the same time, both companies have received favorable treatment from the White House. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has backed the industry's efforts to expand their products nationwide, including allowing their customers to trade sports-related contracts.
Both companies have adamantly denied that the financial relationship between Polymarket, Kalshi and the Trumps played any role in how the industry has been regulated under this administration.

1789 Capital increased its investment in Polymarket this past August, as part of Polymarket's latest fundraising round. It was this investment that started the conversation about ending Trump Jr.'s advisory role with Kalshi.

title: Spain’s workers hold a general strike over housing costs ahead of a national election
summary: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs
story: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs

BARCELONA, Spain -- Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and snarled transport in a massive protest Wednesday over housing costs that the government hopes to leverage ahead of a national election later this month.
The walkout — under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years.

In Barcelona, the country’s second-largest city, most storefronts on a main shopping boulevard were boarded up in anticipation of violence during protests later in the day. Some retail chains were open to business while public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays.
The subway opened only for the rush hour.

Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course.
“Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something," he said.

Rain pelted the capital, Madrid, as strikers marched down main streets and blocked off Gran Vía, the city’s main thoroughfare, where big brand stores remained open although some were also boarded up. Unions have called for workers to march through the city center later Wednesday, and protests are also planned in more than 50 cities and towns.
Manuel Gómez, a 19-year-old student in Madrid, welcomed the protests, which he said marked a change for the country.
“In Spain, we have a serious problem, which is that when we don’t like something, we never go out to protest,” he said.
About 5% of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across the country, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA.
“The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike. “It has been a success in terms of turnout.”

Earlier, the two unions — CCOO and UGT — reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said the stoppages amounted to 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Tires were set on fire at roadblocks in Barcelona, and scuffles with police were reported near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against the strikers in some places.

Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, this added to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago demanding better working conditions. In southwestern Spain, classes were suspended due to bad weather.

“It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told national radio, RNE.

The strike brought workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

The anger reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can’t even dream of homeownership.
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions.

The housing activists are seeking the elimination of pricey tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters. Unions demand more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.

The nationwide protests over Maricarmen's eviction propelled Spain’s government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them, claiming they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then doubled down and called an early election, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29.

Then, in late October came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year — that killed 69 people. The aftermath of the tragedy has dominated Spanish news and created a drag on Sánchez's campaign just when he had hoped to build momentum.
The strike now offers a much-needed opportunity for Sánchez’s Socialists and other parties on the Left seeking to stay in power, analyst Oriol Bartomeus said.

“The Socialists need for the strike to be a success and for there not to be any violence so that the election campaign can swing back to being about housing,” Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press.
On Thursday, Sánchez's government will again try to have a reduced interim Parliament ratify the two housing decrees that the full lower chamber rejected last month.

Sánchez posted a long video on social media this week, lauding past social policies like the 40-hour work week and national health insurance, which were the fruit of the workers' movement and the right to strike.
“It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said, warning that right-wing parties would bring austerity and underfunded social services if they took over.
The traditional conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox oppose any government intervention in the housing market, other than incentivizing construction of new homes.
The two also argue that the unions are trying to help Sánchez stay in office, with months of polling showing voters leaning toward the right.
If the strike descends into violence or has a low turnout, right-wing parties, which already have joined forces to govern in some Spanish regions, could benefit, Bartomeus said.

“The Popular Party and Vox both want the strike to be a flop and to end in scenes of burning dumpsters and shattered shop windows,” Bartomeus added, so that the next morning, "they can say, ‘This is chaos and we are coming to establish order.’”
Associated Press journalists Hernán Muñoz in Barcelona, Spain, and Iain Sullivan in Madrid contributed to this report.

title: PGA Tour in no hurry to decide on future of LIV players
summary: The PGA Tour is not in a rush to figure out whether LIV Golf players can return
story: The PGA Tour is not in a rush to figure out whether LIV Golf players can return
The PGA Tour board had “thoughtful discussions” on Monday about the future of players at LIV Golf but otherwise seemed to be in no hurry to decide if there is room for them next season.
CEO Brian Rolapp only repeated his position that rules exist for a membership organization to ensure fairness and a competitive balance.
“Rules matter and they will be enforced,” he said.
Rolapp said the “ returning member program ” that allowed Brooks Koepka to return to the PGA Tour this year with financial penalties was not on the table.
“There are no plans for that currently, no,” Rolapp said in a conference call to discuss the tour's changes to its developmental system.

LIV Golf, which loss the financial support of Saudi Arabia and filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 8, told a bankruptcy court earlier this month it had abandoned plans for a new version of the league and had begun winding down its business.
It hopes to finalize the bankruptcy plan sometime in January.

“We engaged in thoughtful discussion on the top of LIV players with both boards today,” Rolapp said, referring to the PGA Tour and the commercial PGA Tour Enterprises. “As far as we have read, bankruptcy proceedings are ongoing and the process is complex. I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the new year.”
Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau are the most attractive stars. DeChambeau has yet to indicate his plans while Rahm, who won two weeks ago in Abu Dhabi, remains a European tour member.

Rahm has said he has yet to speak with the PGA Tour but would take the deal Koepka got if offered. Rolapp in January offered that deal to Rahm, DeChambeau and Cameron Smith — before there was any indication Saudi Arabia would stop funding the rival league — and said there was no guarantee the offer would be available in the future.

Rahm told the Spanish site “Ten Golf,” “I imagine they have their boards, their meetings to hold for whatever is coming at the end of the year, and I imagine one of those points will be me. I just don't know if it'll be this November or December. I have no idea.
“At the very least, I'll be here in January, here in Dubai,” Rahm said. “So I jokingly tell everyone this: I will either be here or in Palm Springs in January, one of the two.”
The 2027 season on the PGA Tour starts with The American Express in the California desert.

Several players, such as Joaquin Niemann, are planning to play in Australia, where the two biggest events are co-sanctioned with the European tour. DeChambeau had already said he would be playing the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa, also co-sanctioned by the European tour.

Rolapp said the PGA Tour is still discussing a renewed alliance with the European tour. That alliance would determine how many players — currently 10 — will be awarded PGA Tour cards from the season “Race to Dubai” points list.

title: PGA Tour makes changes to feeder system as it wraps up work on new competition model
summary: The PGA Tour is eliminating the PGA Tour Americas in 2028 to create a vast network of feeder tournaments with a unified ranking system
story: The PGA Tour is eliminating the PGA Tour Americas in 2028 to create a vast network of feeder tournaments with a unified ranking system

The PGA Tour is doing away with the PGA Tour Americas in 2028 as it moves to create a vast network of feeder tournaments that will have one ranking system to reward players trying to make it to the big leagues.

The changes were approved Monday as the Future Competition Committee, which CEO Brian Rolapp created in 2025 with Tiger Woods as the chairman, wrapped up its work on the new competitive model that starts in 2028.

Missing from the announcement were more pieces to the PGA Tour puzzle in the new model, particularly the rest of the tournaments in the upper-tier Championship Series and which ones will be part of the lower Challenger Series.

The board also selected Adam Scott to remain as a player-director. Scott's term expires this year. He takes over for Patrick Cantlay, whose three-year term that ends this year was chosen by the board instead of the entire membership.
The Korn Ferry Tour will have at least 20 tournaments with $1 million purses, and the leading 20 players will be promoted to the Challenger Series.

Previously, the top players from the PGA Tour Americas — events held in Canada and throughout Latin America — were promoted to the Korn Ferry Tour. Instead, there will be a network of PGA Tour-sanctioned events — but not necessarily run by the tour — to provide tournaments throughout the year.

Those players will be part of a unified priority ranking that can help them advance. The tour believes this will allow the feeder system to be more connected and allow for emerging talent to be more quickly identified.
“Having been on this Tour for almost 30 years, I can confidently say the PGA Tour is in the best position it has ever been,” Woods said in a news release.

“We set out last year to build the strongest possible version of the PGA Tour, and by listening to our fans, players and partners, we created a competitive model grounded in meritocracy, built to last and that offers the best opportunity for the next generation of players.”

title: Mauricio Pochettino splits US staff ahead of final match before Manchester United move
summary: Mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his final match with the U.S. national team before taking over at Manchester United
story: Mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his final match with the U.S. national team before taking over at Manchester United
CINCINNATI -- Mauricio Pochettino has split up his staff as he prepares to coach his final match for the U.S. national team before heading to Manchester United.

Goalkeeper coach Toni Jiménez, top assistant Jesús Pérez and fitness coach Sebastián Pochettino left for England after the Americans defeated Haiti 6-0 on Saturday in the first leg of the Nations League quarterfinals.

Assistant coach Miguel D’Agostino, fitness coach Sylvia Tuyà Viñas and analyst Alex Scott are still on the U.S. staff until after Tuesday night's match, when they also head to Manchester with Pochettino.

“That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the national team. They are preparing all there because Wednesday when we arrive, it’s going to be nonstop, and then start with playing games," Pochettino said Monday before the U.S. held a training session at TQL Stadium. “We are focused here into finishing the best way.”

Pochettino will have a couple days to work with his new squad before United travels to Liverpool on Sunday. Pochettino — who previously coached in the Premier League at Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea — is United’s eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
The one area Pochettino tried to steer clear of is whether he would persuade United's management to sign any of the players on the national team when the winter transfer window opens on Jan. 1.

“All the good players always have dreams to reach the (highest) level, and United is one of the teams in that level," he said. “In case some decisions need to be made, we are going to pay attention to the players we know really well.”
U.S. midfielder Weston McKennie, who has played in Italy with Juventus for six years, also raised the possibility of one or two Americans eventually heading to Old Trafford.

“We have a lot of guys on our team that are due to probably make moves soon or within the next year, and so I think it’s kind of inevitable,” McKennie said. "You never know what’s going on in a coach’s mind and what players that he’s looking for. But I think he could potentially see some of the guys from here being talked about and potentially it happening.”

The U.S. is in excellent shape to reach Nations League semifinals after a 6-0 win over Haiti in Saturday's first leg in Miami. Five players scored in the rout, including two goals by Christian Pulisic.

Even though the Americans have a large lead in the quest to qualify for the semifinals in Los Angeles in March, Pochettino might be leery to make sweeping lineup changes in his final game or use it as a showcase for younger players.

“It’s important to keep growing and the team keeps evolving. I don’t want to think too much tomorrow because it’s normal to get emotional, but I think to be very focused in preparing the best way,” he said.
The Americans are 16-3-5 in matches in Ohio and unbeaten in four matches at TQL Stadium, which opened in 2021 and is the home of MLS team FC Cincinnati.

title: Philip Rivers takes the reins as coach of the NC State program where he starred as QB
summary: N
story: N

RALEIGH, N.C. -- Philip Rivers walked to the podium for the first time at N.C. State's football coach, back to the place where he forged himself into a beloved figure in a record-setting playing career.
The emotions and excitement were bubbling so much he could barely contain it.
“Oh boy,” Rivers said with a big grin as he pulled out his notes.

N.C. State formally introduced the former Wolfpack and longtime NFL quarterback as its coach Monday afternoon, three days after the school's trustees approved his five-year contract to make the hiring official. That marked the transition for Rivers from retired NFL player and high school head coach in Alabama to first-time college coach.
The 44-year-old Rivers seemingly reveled in all of it, from enthusiastically talking about taking on the job to being choked up by emotion multiple times during the session.

“We all have many gifts, right?” Rivers said. “I do feel like God has given me the gift to serve and impact through this game. And I've got a lot still to give. And there ain't no better no place, or any place, that I'd really would want to give it besides right here at N.C. State.”

The news conference was a festive event, with numerous former Wolfpack players, school officials and donors in attendance. There were large video screens on either side of the stage, showing highlights and images before the start from Rivers' playing career from 2000-03 — when he became the Atlantic Coast Conference's all-time leading passer before a long NFL career.

title: Michigan State up to No. 2 behind Gators in AP Top 25 basketball poll, Kentucky drops out
summary: Michigan State has moved up to No. 2 in the AP Top 25 men's basketball poll after an impressive win over Duke
story: Michigan State has moved up to No. 2 in the AP Top 25 men's basketball poll after an impressive win over Duke
Michigan State has moved up to No. 2 following an impressive win over Duke, Virginia moved into the top five and Texas Texas crashed the top 10 in the AP Top 25 men's basketball poll released Monday.
The Spartans received three first-place votes from a 59-person media panel, climbing three places from last week. Florida remained at No. 1 and had 56 first-place votes.
UConn climbed one place to No. 3, with Virginia and Duke rounding out the top five.
No. 25 LSU moved into the poll for the first time since the 2021-22 season after beating No. 22 Gonzaga 81-80 in Spokane on Donovan Dent's last-second 3-pointer.
Michigan State entered coach Tom Izzo's 32nd season with high expectations behind a loaded roster led by preseason All-American Jeremy Fears.

The Spartans (4-0) blew out Quinnipiac and Toledo to open the season before facing their first big test against then-No. 2 Duke in Chicago. Michigan State pushed around the Blue Devils and Fears was superb, finishing with 18 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds in a rugged 79-73 win.
“I really believe that we played our best basketball of the year, but we’re three games into the year, so big deal,” Izzo said.

UConn had an impressive home win over Ohio State despite playing without forward Nik Khamenia, who will miss several weeks after undergoing foot surgery. The Huskies also blew out Wagner last week, before Khamenia's injury, and welcomed back Solo Ball to full-contact practice this week after offseason wrist surgery.
Virginia has its highest ranking since reaching No. 2 in 2022-23 after beating Bucknell and Maryland last week.
No. 7 UCLA continued its rise from No. 22 in the preseason poll, moving up two spots this week after setting a school record for margin of victory in a 106-37 win over Arkansas-Pine Bluff.
Several big-name programs took big falls in the poll following losses last week.
Louisville moved into the top 10 last week, but a 20-point loss to Memphis sent the Cardinals plummeting down the poll, losing 13 places to No. 23 this week.

No. 22 Gonzaga opened the season with a hard-fought win over Purdue in Las Vegas, but a collapse dropped the Zags eight places this week. Gonzaga led LSU by 13 with about eight minutes left in, but the Tigers rallied to set up Dent's winning 3-pointer with 1.5 seconds left.

Illinois opened the season with high expectations after reaching the Final Four last season, but an 84-78 loss at Texas Tech dropping the Illini from No. 3 last week to No. 10. The Red Raiders climbed seven spots to No. 9 by beating Illini for their nonconference home winning streak to 49 games.
Kentucky dropped out of the poll from No. 24 after losing by 20 to No. 11 Kansas in Chicago and needing Alex Wilkins' 3-pointer with 2.1 seconds left to beat Northern Arizona i n Lexington.

Memphis was the first team outside the poll last week and remained there despite beating a top-10 team. Texas A&M was the next team just outside the top 25 following a lopsided win over Oklahoma State.

The Southeastern Conference has seven teams in the Top 25 after LSU moved in and Kentucky dropped out. The Big Ten was next with three of the top 10 and six in the poll. The Big 12 had five ranked teams, the ACC had four, the Big East had two and Gonzaga gave the new-look Pac-12 one team in the Top 25.

title: Sweden beats Finland 2-1 in shootout to win bronze at women's world hockey championship
summary: Hilda Svensson scored the decisive shootout goal, and Sweden medaled at the women’s world hockey championship for the first time since 2007 by defeating Finland 2-1 in the bronze medal game
story: Hilda Svensson scored the decisive shootout goal, and Sweden medaled at the women’s world hockey championship for the first time since 2007 by defeating Finland 2-1 in the bronze medal game

HERNING, Denmark -- Hilda Svensson scored the decisive shootout goal and Sweden medaled at the women’s world hockey championship for the first time since 2007 by defeating Finland 2-1 in the bronze medal final on Monday.

Sweden rallied from a 1-0 deficit with Lina Ljungblom tying the score with a power-play goal from the slot with six minutes left in regulation. Svensson, a 20-year-old sophomore at Ohio State, had an assist on Ljungblom’s goal.

Svensson then scored Sweden’s second shootout goal by driving in from the right wing and beating Sanni Ahola with a snap shot inside the far post. Ebba Svensson Traff sealed the win by stopping Finland’s final two attempts, including a right pad save on Emmi Juusela.
Defending world and Olympic champion United States plays cross-border rival Canada in the gold-medal final later in the day.
Svensson Traff stopped 29 shots through overtime and four of five shootout attempts.

Michelle Karvinen opened the scoring with a power-play goal with 3:05 left in the second period, and Noora Tulus scored Finland’s lone shootout goal. The 36-year-old Karvinen's goal was her team career record 27th in world championship play, moving her one ahead of Petra Nieminen.
Ahola finished with 35 saves through overtime and also allowed a shootout goal by Tilde Grillfors.

Sweden was making its first tournament medal-game appearance since a 4-1 loss to Finland in 2009. Sweden won its third medal after also winning bronze in 2005. The Swedes were coming off a promising fourth-place finish at the Milan Games in February in which they lost the bronze-medal final to Switzerland.

title: Posey, Lester among 14 newcomers on Hall of Fame ballot while Utley, Pettitte top 13 holdovers
summary: Catcher Buster Posey and pitcher Jon Lester are among 14 newcomers on the Hall of Fame ballot for the Baseball Writers' Association of America
story: Catcher Buster Posey and pitcher Jon Lester are among 14 newcomers on the Hall of Fame ballot for the Baseball Writers' Association of America

COOPERSTOWN, N.Y. -- Catcher Buster Posey and pitcher Jon Lester were among 14 newcomers on the Hall of Fame ballot for the Baseball Writers' Association of America released Monday, while infielder Chase Utley and pitcher Andy Pettitte head 13 holdovers.

Pitchers Jake Arrieta and Andrew Miller and third baseman Pablo Sandoval also are on the ballot for the first time, joined by pitchers Wade Davis, Ervin Santana and Joakim Soria; infielders Asdrubal Cabrera, Starlin Castro, Kyle Seager and Ryan Zimmerman; and outfielders Jay Bruce and Brett Gardner.

Utley received 251 of 425 votes (59.1%) last year when Carlos Beltrán and Andruw Jones were elected, up from 39.8% in 2025. Pettitte appeared on 206 ballots (48.5%), an increase from 27.9% in 2025, and is on the ballot for the ninth time.
Shortstop Omar Vizquel is on the ballot for the 10th and final time after receiving 18.4% last year.

Other holdovers include pitcher Félix Hernández (46.1% last year), infielder Alex Rodríguez (40%), outfielder Bobby Abreu (30.8%), shortstop Jimmy Rollins (25.4%), pitcher Cole Hamels (23.8%), second baseman Dustin Pedroia (20.7%), pitcher Mark Buehrle (20%), third baseman David Wright (14.8%), pitcher Francisco Rodríguez (11.8%) and outfielder Torii Hunter (8.7%).

BBWAA members with 10 or more consecutive years of membership are eligible to vote. Ballots must be postmarked by Dec. 31 and results will be announced Jan. 19. Any players elected will be inducted on July 25 along with anyone chosen Dec. 6 by the hall's contemporary era committee for managers, executives and umpires. That ballot includes Bruce Bochy — Posey's former manager — along with Dusty Baker and Lou Piniella.

A seven-time All-Star, Posey was the NL Rookie of the Year in 2010 and won the Most Valuable Award in 2012, when he led the major leagues with a .336 average and became the first catcher to win the NL batting title since the Boston Braves’ Ernie Lombardi in 1942.

He finished with a .302 career average, 1,500 hits, 158 homers and 729 RBIs in 12 major league seasons with San Francisco from 2009-21, helping the Giants win World Series titles in 2010, ‘12 and ’14.

Posey's fibula was broken in a collision at the plate with the Florida Marlins' Scott Cousins in May 2011, prompting Major League Baseball ahead of the 2014 season to prohibit a runner from deviating from his direct pathway to the plate in order to initiate contact with the catcher.
Now 39, Posey was hired as the Giants' president of baseball operations in September 2024.

Lester, a left-hander who is now 42, was 200-117 with a 3.66 ERA over 16 seasons with Boston (2006-14), Oakland (2014), the Chicago Cubs (2015-20), Washington (2021) and St. Louis (2021). A five-time All-Star, he won World Series titles with Boston in 2007 and 2013, and with the Chicago Cubs in 2016.

His rookie season was cut short when he was diagnosed with lymphoma in August 2006. Lester underwent chemotherapy, said that December he was cancer free and returned to the Red Sox rotation in July 2007. He pitched a no-hitter against Kansas City on May 19, 2008.

title: Louisville up to No. 3 in women's AP Top 25 after UConn win; South Carolina, Michigan still 1-2
summary: Louisville climbed to No. 3 in the Associated Press Top 25 women’s basketball poll after a big win over UConn
story: Louisville climbed to No. 3 in the Associated Press Top 25 women’s basketball poll after a big win over UConn
Louisville climbed to No. 3 in the Associated Press Top 25 women’s basketball poll on Monday after its biggest win over UConn ever.
The Cardinals (6-0) dismantled then-No. 4 UConn 69-51 on Sunday and moved up four spots in the poll for their best ranking since 2022. The Huskies fell to seventh.

South Carolina remained the No. 1 team after edging then-No. 3 USC 89-85 on Sunday. The Gamecocks were a unanimous choice from the 33-member national media panel. The Trojans dropped to fourth. Michigan stayed at No. 2 and Duke was still fifth.
Gamecocks coach Dawn Staley has already played three games against Top 25 teams and has five more non-conference matchups scheduled against Top 25 teams.

“These games, we’ve always played in November, December for March and April,” Staley said. “We’ve always done it. A lot of times when you play these games, you see these same teams in the NCAA Tournament and familiarity is a really good thing. ... We’re not going to be the same team but you get a feel for how your team plays and it’s really important for us to do that.”
Texas was ahead of the Huskies in sixth. Iowa, LSU and UCLA rounded out the top 10.

Vanderbilt fell three spots to 11th after a loss at Iowa. Kentucky, Notre Dame, Oklahoma and TCU followed them. Washington was 16th with Minnesota, Maryland, Ole Miss and Ohio State next. The final five were Illinois, West Virginia, Nebraska, North Carolina and Oklahoma State. The Cowgirls dropped six spots after an overtime loss to Tulsa.

The Huskies are now 3-2 to start the year for the second time within the last four seasons and just the sixth time in Geno Auriemma’s 42-year tenure at the school. The 18-point loss to Louisville was the Huskies' worst since losing by the same amount to Oregon in 2020. They open Big East play on Friday, hosting Seton Hall. Then come games against No. 1 South Carolina and No. 5 Duke during Thanksgiving week.

The Big Ten has 10 teams in the Top 25, including four of the top 10. The Southeastern Conference has seven, including three in the top 10. The Atlantic Coast Conference has two in the top 10 and four overall, and the Big 12 has three ranked teams. The Big East has one.
No. 19 Ohio State vs. No. 6 Texas, Sunday. The two teams will play in Fort Worth, Texas, as part of the Lone Star Series, an event to showcase premier national matchups in women's basketball.

title: France’s Diallo enters race to challenge Infantino in FIFA presidential election
summary: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo emerges Monday as an unexpected opponent to Gianni Infantino in what shapes to be a FIFA presidential election of three candidates
story: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo emerges Monday as an unexpected opponent to Gianni Infantino in what shapes to be a FIFA presidential election of three candidates
GENEVA -- French soccer leader Philippe Diallo emerged as an unexpected opponent to Gianni Infantino on Monday in what shapes to be a FIFA presidential election of three candidates.
UEFA proposed Diallo at a short-notice meeting of its 21-member executive committee that includes the French Football Federation president.
“Philippe Diallo has accepted the invitation to stand,” UEFA said in a statement citing the 63-year-old official's “extensive experience across all levels of the game.”
Diallo is set to join veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima as official entries in the March 18 contest by a FIFA-set deadline of midnight Swiss time (2300 GMT) on Wednesday.

Infantino seeks a fourth presidential term amid the biggest crisis of his near 11-year presidency, sparked by his divisive plan in July to sell stakes in future World Cup profits for $4.2 billion to private investors led by Joshua Kushner.
The furor that provoked, even after the project was dropped within days, deepened unease with Infantino’s leadership in Europe and parts of North America and Asia, including Japan.

After Tashima's declaration this month, UEFA still was expected to field its own candidate while also pursuing legal action in U.S. courts. UEFA seeks discovery of evidence for a possible criminal complaint against Infantino in his and FIFA's home country Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement.
FIFA accused UEFA of a “smear campaign” against its president in a court filing in Colorado.

Those concerns include Infantino seeming to act alone in creating a peace prize for U.S. President Donald Trump last year and, at the World Cup, letting United States forward Folarin Balogun avoid a mandatory ban for a red card after Trump intervened.

“Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community,” UEFA said. “They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition.”
Diallo’s candidacy must be confirmed on Tuesday at a meeting of the French federation, UEFA said.

When the World Cup ended on July 19 in the U.S., Infantino was set to be reelected unopposed effectively by a coronation. FIFA said he had about 200 letters of support from among the 211 member federations who will vote in March in Rabat, Morocco.

One of those letters was from France which Diallo formally withdrew in September, citing that trust in Infantino was broken by the World Cup sell-off plan. It had been secretly devised with Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“We feel that his approach to the management of world football no longer matches our own,” Diallo said two months ago.

Candidates must have letters of support from five of the 211 FIFA members. They then must pass eligibility and integrity checks by a FIFA-appointed panel to be confirmed by Feb. 18 on the ballot papers.
Infantino built widespread global support for hugely raising FIFA's revenue and adding more and bigger tournaments to the soccer calendar.

FIFA earned billions of dollars more in revenue from the 48-team men's 2026 World Cup in North America compared to a 2022 edition of 32 teams in Qatar. Infantino has promised at least $25 million in development funds to each member federation through 2030.
Diallo is a long-time soccer administrator with French clubs and the league who entered the inner circle at the French federation in 2021.

He was first its treasurer then rose to interim president in January 2023, before being fast-tracked in an election of UEFA member federations several weeks later to join the European body’s executive committee.
Diallo has worked for FIFA as a judge on its Dispute Resolution Chamber, typically handling contract disputes between players and clubs.

During Diallo’s presidency of French soccer, FIFA and Infantino have had close ties to Paris with offices looking out at Place de la Concorde as a base for liaising with member federations in Europe and Africa.

He would become the 10th elected FIFA president since 1904, the third from France and the first full-time president who is Black. FIFA had a Black interim president for a few months before Infantino was first elected in February 2016, when Issa Hayatou of Cameroon took over from the suspended Sepp Blatter.
Since Aug. 1, hours after Infantino withdrew his private equity plan, European soccer leaders have committed to removing him and finding a candidate to oppose him.

Some early speculation focused on Qatari soccer and broadcast executive Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, the president of Champions League titleholder Paris Saint-Germain and a member of UEFA's executive committee. The former tennis professional, who would have had wider appeal in Asia, eventually said in late September he would not run against Infantino, who has backing from Qatar.
UEFA also wooed French coaching great Arsène Wenger to run against his current boss Infantino. FIFA hired former Arsenal manager Wenger in 2019 to be its global head of developing the game.
Once the 77-year-old Wenger made clear privately in recent days he would not stand, UEFA stayed in France to find its preferred in-house candidate to lead FIFA.

title: Louisville's Clark, UNC's Smith suspended, other penalties issued for postgame brawl
summary: There was an on-field brawl at the close of Saturday night's game
story: There was an on-field brawl at the close of Saturday night's game

The Atlantic Coast Conference has issued half-game suspensions for Louisville linebacker Stanquan Clark and North Carolina defensive back Greg Smith III, along with fines and public reprimands for the schools following an on-field brawl between the teams at the end of Saturday night's game.

The ACC announced the penalties Monday morning, saying “the unsportsmanlike behavior displayed was unacceptable” and the suspensions are in accordance with NCAA rules for fighting. Clark and Smith, both starters, will sit out the first half of Saturday's games; the Cardinals host Pittsburgh while the Tar Heels visit Virginia.
The league didn't specify the amount of the fines for each school and said it would have no further comment.

The suspensions come as the Cardinals (7-3, 6-2 ACC) try to stay in the chase for a trip to the Atlantic Coast Conference championship game as the only two-loss team in the league standings. The Tar Heels (5-5, 2-4) are attempting to become bowl eligible in NFL coaching icon Bill Belichick's second season in Chapel Hill.
Clark leads the Cardinals in tackles (74) while tallying 7.0 tackles for loss, 1.5 sacks and an interception. Smith is fourth in tackles (56) for the Tar Heels with a team-best three interceptions.

The brawl began as Louisville knelt out the final seconds of a 16-14 road win, with Tar Heels defensive tackle Xavier Lewis and Cardinals offensive lineman Johnnie Brown III continuing to jostle in a testy exchange on the final snap.
More players stepped in and tempers flared, escalating into multiple skirmishes and players in pileups spreading across the field before the teams were eventually separated.

title: Lewis Hamilton says Formula 1 has 'much still to do' on diversity in employment
summary: Formula 1 has “much still to do” to improve its record on diversity, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton says in a report published by the Mission 44 charity he founded
story: Formula 1 has “much still to do” to improve its record on diversity, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton says in a report published by the Mission 44 charity he founded
LONDON -- Formula 1 has “much still to do” to improve its record on diversity, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton said Monday in a report published by the charity he founded.

The report from the Mission 44 charity concludes that F1 and its teams have made progress in offering scholarships and outreach programs which aim to broaden access to employment in the sport in areas such as engineering.
However, the report also highlights a lack of data about diversity in the broader workforce and whether people stay in the sport and progress in their careers.

“When I walk through the paddock now, I see more women, more Black and Brown faces, more people who look like the fans in the grandstands than at any point since I started. That is heartening, and the people behind it deserve credit,” Hamilton wrote in a foreword to the report.
“And yet, there is much still to do. We have opened the door, but we have not yet learned to count how many people walk through it, or how many stay.”
Hamilton, F1's only Black driver, has worked to set up diversity initiatives at his former team, Mercedes, and since joining Ferrari in 2025.
He has also been vocal on a range of global issues and visited Rafah in Egypt last week to meet organizations sending humanitarian aid to the war-torn Gaza Strip.
Hamilton is fourth in the championship standings ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix this week.

title: AI cheating fears spook South Korea ahead of high-stakes college entrance exam
summary: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology
story: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology

SEOUL, South Korea -- Days before South Korea comes to a standstill for its all-important college entrance exam, the nation is reeling after the top scorer on its tax accountant test was found to have cheated with a hidden camera and artificial intelligence.

The scandal has left authorities scrambling to prevent cheating on the exam, which will be taken Thursday by more than 500,000 students, as concerns grow that AI and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Monday rejected calls by some lawmakers to postpone the exam until stronger anti-cheating measures are in place, telling a legislative hearing that a delay would cause “even a larger disruption” to students.

Choi said that he was confident that proctors could spot AI-powered smart glasses, which typically have thick, horn-rimmed frames. Education authorities are also offering guidance on detecting devices such as microcameras, Education Ministry officials said.

Worries about cheating deepened over the weekend after a 34-year-old man who scored the highest on a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden microcamera and smartphone to get answers from AI.

Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.

In a video posted Sunday on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, Han said that he used a concealed camera to capture the questions, fed the images to a generative AI tool and received answers on a smartphone. He said that he would cooperate with police, who are investigating the case.

Han had previously said that he scored 397.5 out of a possible 400 points on the first-stage, multiple-choice test in April, and 663 out of 800 on the second-stage essay exam in July, unusually high marks that one Korean newspaper likened to “running a 100-meter sprint in under five seconds.”

The national college entrance exam, known as “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a high-stakes annual event in a country notorious for intense academic competition, where prospects for jobs, social standing and even marriage can depend on which university a person attends.

South Korea goes to great lengths each year to create an ideal testing environment, effectively bringing the country to a standstill by delaying the start of the workday and stock market trading to ease traffic for test-takers and pausing flights during the English listening section of the exam. Police officers often use cars and motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training in areas near testing sites.

But it’s difficult for authorities to come up with equally sweeping measures to prevent cheating with AI devices, which the Seoul-based Hankyoreh newspaper warned in an editorial Monday could threaten “the very foundations of the examination system.”

Education authorities had focused for months on preventing the use of AI-powered glasses, but Han’s case has raised doubts about whether they are prepared for cheating involving other, less conspicuous devices.

Education authorities will deploy at least one specially trained supervisor at each of the 1,300 test sites nationwide to identify such glasses. Officials also are considering requiring test takers to hand over their smart devices and shutting down public Wi-Fi connections at test sites, according to Prime Minister Han Seongsook's office.

Song Geun-hyeon, another senior Education Ministry official, said that the ministry has provided proctors with new guidance on detecting test-takers using hidden cameras and other devices, including watching for suspicious movements involving “their sleeves, collars or buttons, and certain gestures.”
The ministry was working with the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology on anti-cheating measures for the college entrance exam, which are due to be announced on Tuesday.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that the discussions with the science ministry also include temporarily restricting telecommunications at test sites. It wasn't immediately clear whether that's feasible, considering laws prohibiting electronic signal jamming, or concerns that it could interfere with communication in surrounding areas.

Song said that metal detectors and radio detectors would be limited, while deploying thermal cameras would be highly unlikely because of privacy concerns. Supervisors can't search belongings without the consent of the test-takers.

“At the government-wide level, we would also need to give further consideration to measures that will make it easier to identify (AI) smart devices,” said Song, adding that officials are debating whether to require manufacturers to design the devices to emit “flashing lights or sounds” while in use.

title: Microsoft says services fully restored after hourslong global outage
summary: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
story: Microsoft says services are fully restored after a massive, global outage that lasted for hours
Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored after a massive outage that lasted for hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company said in an update on X.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.

The outage affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had impacted some of their operations.
Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems started appearing around midday Thursday in the U.S.
The Redmond, Washington-based company apologized on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents.
It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” following a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.
“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.

Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”

The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.
Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.
As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.
For Outlook, many users said they couldn’t send or receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.
In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.
The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.

British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff’s office in Colorado’s Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.

Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.
Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.

And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.

OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: Meta fined $887M in Italy over Android gallery photos, videos on Facebook
summary: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.
story: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.

ROME -- Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law. The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
Meta made no immediate comment.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit, caught by launch pad arms in dramatic first
summary: It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for.
story: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.
