title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
summary: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29
story: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29

In a comeback tale like one from Harry Potter battling back his nemesis or a “Heated Rivalry” hockey hero rebounding from injury, a top global fandom site that was sidelined by a security incident is now on the mend.

The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.
“AO3 is now up!” said a status page for the Organization for Transformative Works, an activist group behind the platform, on Sunday.

The outage sent fans of the platform — readers and authors alike — into a desperate void for the past two weeks with a “Bad Gateway” message stirring frustration. The return drew many expressions of joy Sunday.

The organization, in a summary it posted on Instagram of its 2025 results, said nearly 2.6 million AO3 works were created, with nearly 40 billion page views. Nearly 2 million accounts have been created, it said.
AO3 hasn't been without its critics, who have warned about sexual content that could be available to minors and fandom racism through the platform.

The group said some features like user icons have been disabled and importing of external work isn’t available, while downloads are currently only possible in the web-language HTML format. It promised those features will ultimately return.

The team predicted that the security incident would take up to four weeks for AO3 to get back up, while floating the prospect of a partial revival “in a degraded state” — which appears to be what was taking place on Sunday.

The organization said contributors’ “works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe” and that no drafts were deleted during the outage — but it couldn’t rule out that the user database might have been compromised.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the status update said.

AO3 is a hub of content from fans who have produced content that riffs off fiction, art and other culture and entertainment: Imagine a repository of sequels, prequels and derivatives dreamt up by adoring aficionados of some of the world’s best-known titles.
The result is catchy products like “fanfic” — fiction from fans — and similar fanart, as well as “podfics,” readings of narratives shared in audio form.

A recent listing of “ship stats” — or the number of references to relationships of stars from literature — shows that pairings of characters featured in the Harry Potter, Heated Rivalry and anime fandoms were the most prominent this summer.
The reaction from fans of the fandom platform was swift and exuberant.
“So, we've all agreed we don't need to sleep tonight, now that AO3 is finally back, right? Right!?” quipped yet.another.loon on the Threads social media site.
User Verkielos gushed: “Just got email from AO3 about a fic update. The world is healing!”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025, company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout
summary: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.
story: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn't matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.

“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel's “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of 'catastrophic' risks
summary: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development
story: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development

NEW YORK -- A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies to halt further development, alleging the tech giants can’t prevent their own creations from causing “catastrophic” harm.

The lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court follows a midterm election that could bring a moment of reckoning for the fast-moving AI industry, as Democrats who won back control of Congress stress the need to regulate the technology.

The filing, first reported on by The Associated Press, asks a judge to stop Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI from developing or deploying new AI models, pointing to documented examples of cyberattacks and other harmful actions by AI systems and the companies’ own alarming acknowledgments that their technology has the potential to someday destroy humanity.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” reads the complaint from the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. “Plaintiffs bring this suit to stop Defendants from continuing their unlawful path to disaster.”

The AI industry has generated excitement and stock market gains, but also deep fears that the technology could go rogue and escape human control. Recent incidents of AI agents hacking government websites and companies — including when OpenAI's ChatGPT hacked into another AI company on its own in July — have accelerated those concerns.

President Donald Trump, a proponent of rapid AI development to keep the U.S. ahead of foreign competitors like China, has so far encouraged the companies to police themselves on matters of safety, though he has expressed openness to more guardrails. Congress also has stopped short of regulating the technology, but that may change with its Democratic takeover.

Some CEOs of major AI companies, meanwhile, have voiced support for slowing development of the technology to give safety measures a chance to catch up. They also haven't held back in recognizing the risks. Anthropic's Dario Amodei, for example, last year said he thinks there’s a 1 in 4 chance AI’s future goes “really, really badly,” compared with a 3 in 4 chance it goes well. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, told Fox News in 2023 that AI could lead to “civilization destruction.”

The plaintiffs, all nonprofits, allege that the companies named in the lawsuit have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property such as computer systems. They claim they’ve had to divert resources away from other planned work to address the acute harms threatened by each of the companies’ advancing AI models.

They also warn that the companies' goals of creating AI systems that are broadly as smart as humans and can increasingly manage tasks and learn things autonomously could result in a permanent loss of control of the technology and heighten existential risks to humanity.
The companies named in Thursday's lawsuit didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
story: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.

The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.

But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.

It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.

Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S.

Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.

The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.”
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.

The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.

“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”

Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump's second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.

Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week's midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.

While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.

Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.

Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related."

Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: SpaceX’s Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
summary: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad
story: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad

SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.

It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk's company missed out on a double catch.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.

This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday's launch.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.

During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

title: Anthropic promises to pursue humanity's benefit. Its IPO filing gives it wiggle room
summary: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence
story: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence

When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity's benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.

The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it's benefiting society, experts say.

Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.

“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.

In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80% of their wealth.

Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind.
Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter in 2021 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law.

“Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.”
Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company.

There aren't many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021.
Anthropic's idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, "will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?”
The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders.

Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That's particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity's problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity.

“There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured.
A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.

Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic's board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don't see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can't sell it.

“The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said.

Three of the company's board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1% voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders.
Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company's broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said.

The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company," he said. "If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.”

As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly.
The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic's corporate structure, Gadinis said.

“I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community," he said.

title: Tech consultant sentenced to 16 years to life in stabbing death of Cash App founder
summary: The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee has been sentenced in San Francisco to 16 years to life to prison
story: The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee has been sentenced in San Francisco to 16 years to life to prison
SAN FRANCISCO -- The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee was sentenced in San Francisco on Tuesday to 16 years to life to prison.

A jury in December 2024 found Nima Momeni guilty of second-degree murder, rejecting the defendant's claim that he had acted in self-defense. He has remained in custody since his arrest nine days after the April 4, 2023, killing.
Before imposing the sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon rejected Momeni’s request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal.
Members of Lee’s family addressed the court on Tuesday, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni.
“You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports.
Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee’s family that he understood their loss.
“Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said.
Lee, a renowned tech mogul, was found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. Lee, 43, later died at a hospital.

Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack on Lee, driving him to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister's kitchen. They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer she says gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her.

But Momeni testified on the stand that Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night. Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn't realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt.

Lee had created mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died. He had recently moved to Miami from the San Francisco Bay Area, where his ex-wife Krista Lee lives with their two children, and had returned to California for a visit.

Jurors in the end rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully and with premeditation. Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation.

title: US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, FBI says
summary: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
story: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
WASHINGTON -- The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.

The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.

Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: Europe's Hera spacecraft begins close inspections of asteroid rammed by NASA
summary: A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of a harmless asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test
story: A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of a harmless asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of an asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test.
The European Space Agency announced Wednesday that the Hera spacecraft is now studying Didymos and its moonlet Dimorphos from just 15 miles to 18 miles (25 kilometers to 30 kilometers) away.
NASA’s Dart spacecraft deliberately slammed into little Dimorphos in 2022 to see whether such a defensive move might help save Earth from a killer space rock one day.
The impact shortened the moonlet's orbit around Didymos. More importantly, it nudged the moonlet into a slightly different path around the sun.
Next month, the small car-sized Hera, launched in 2024, will venture even closer — just 12 miles (20 kilometers) away.

ESA officials consider this a "crash site investigation" worthy of its finest robotic detective. Hera is carrying 25 science instruments as well as a pair of shoebox-sized Cubesats to survey Dimorphos even more closely and attempt to land on it.

The Dart spacecraft — short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test — sent rubble and even boulders flying off Dimorphos, providing an extra kick to the impact’s momentum. The debris trail extended thousands of miles (more than 10,000 kilometers) into space for months.
Some of that debris could still be in the vicinity, according to scientists.
Dimorphos is an estimated 500 feet (151 meters) in diameter. Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet (780 meters) in diameter.

title: Southeast Asian leaders, with US and Chinese counterparts, will renew alarm over online scams
summary: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams
story: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams

MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders and their key counterparts, including from the United States and China, will renew their alarm over the escalating threat of online scams, according to a draft statement seen by The Associated Press on Friday.

Such transnational crimes, which have swindled billions of dollars from people in Asia to the United States and elsewhere, will be high in the agenda when leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gather in an annual summit with their Asian and Western counterparts on Tuesday in the Philippine capital.

The Philippines currently holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, an 11-nation bloc in a poverty-stricken region where criminal groups have used technology and resorted to human trafficking to expand their illicit and lucrative operations to other parts of the world.

The leaders of the expanded ASEAN bloc, called the East Asia Summit, will express their “grave concern over the escalating threat posed by transnational criminal organizations inflicting harm through online scams, including those originating from scam center operations and associated criminal conduct such as human trafficking,” according to a draft of their joint statement to be issued after their summit.

They acknowledged “the exploitation of digital and other advanced technologies and digital financial platforms, by increasingly sophisticated criminal actors and the need to strengthen financial and digital systems, as well as the severe human consequences associated with scam centers.”

Authorities in Southeast Asia have reported in recent years how large numbers of workers, who were lured by recruitment syndicates into working in online scam centers, including in the Philippines and Cambodia, have been subjected to threats and even torture when they tried to escape or defy orders.

Aside from sharing of information and strengthening law enforcement coordination, the leaders will encourage “the sharing of threat assessments and best practices" as well as strengthening cooperation between relevant authorities in dismantling scam centers, the leaders said in their draft statement, without elaborating.

In July, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reported how Southeast Asia-based criminal groups have increasingly used integrated networks and technology to expand to other regions. The scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, according to the report.
Criminals are using new technologies to launder money through global financial systems and using artificial intelligence to steal from victims worldwide, the U.N. report said.

East Asian crime syndicates are running businesses that use malware, generative AI and deepfakes for sexual extortion and exploitation in a trend that increases the risks of in-person as well as livestreamed abuse. Apart from outright trafficking for the sex industry, victims can be sold into domestic servitude, forced begging and forced labor, among other forms of exploitation, the report said.

The East Asia Summit leaders meeting in Manila will underscore “the need to address underlying drivers and other related factors of online scams," such as poverty, lack of social protection interventions, outdated domestic laws, private and public coordination gaps, corruption and limited economic opportunities.
They will stress that government responses to online scams must be consistent with international law and respect human rights.

title: Trump Asia trip live updates: Logistical hurdles with a Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting
summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
story: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

3 hours and 44 minutes agoAir Force One refueling stop diverted because of weather3:18 PM ESTLogistical hurdles with Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting3:01 PM ESTTrump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un
3 hours and 44 minutes agoAir Force One refueling stop diverted because of weather
3:18 PM ESTLogistical hurdles with Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting
3:01 PM ESTTrump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un
Air Force One refueling stop diverted because of weather

President Donald Trump landed at Alaska’s Fairbanks International Airport after a planned refueling stop at Elmendorf Air Force in Anchorage was diverted because of weather, the White House told travel pool reporters on the trip.
Air Force One landed around 4:30 p.m. ET for the refueling stop on its way to the Philippines.
After taking off from Alaska Monday evening, Air Force One is expected to arrive at Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila early Tuesday morning ET for the ASEAN Summit.
-ABC News Isabella Murray
Logistical hurdles with Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting

President Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in reviving diplomacy with North Korea, but beyond the apparent lack of developed plans, there are logistical barriers that could make an impromptu meeting between the leaders on the sidelines of APEC unlikely.

Kim Jong Un has traveled internationally by plane before, but the last publicly documented time he did so was all the way back in 2018 -- when he borrowed a Boeing 747-400 from China to meet President Trump in Singapore.

Since then, he has traveled either by car for a couple short, cross-border trips or via notoriously slow armored trains. North Korea’s rail fleet travels at an average speed of around 35 mph -- topping out at 50 mph on China’s more advanced tracks.
While it is technically possible to travel by armored train from Pyongyang to Shenzhen, a one-way journey is projected to take as long as 60 hours.

Kim made a quick and quiet visit to China last month, taking a car over a newly opened bridge connecting the countries, according to Chinese state media. He did not meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the short trip.
South Korea's top diplomat previously said he believed there was little chance of Kim attending the APEC summit. North Korea is not a member of APEC, and Kim has never attended an APEC meeting.
-ABC News' Shannon Kingston
Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
As he departed the White House Monday morning, Trump said he "may" meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China as well, though he said it would ultimately be Xi's decision.
"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump said of Kim Jong Un.

Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, senior U.S. officials said. The president is expected to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. However, he does not intend to discuss Ukraine during the trilateral meeting, officials say.
Read more about what to expect from Trump's trip.

title: United Airlines briefly has 'systemwide' disruption to departing flights
summary: United said there is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.
story: United said there is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.
United Airlines said Monday a "technology issue" delayed some departing flights.
The issue has since been resolved, the airline said.
The union representing United pilots said United experienced a "systemwide operational outage" that affected pilot applications, "including crew communications and messaging systems."

"The outage has also impacted the Company's ability to provide final aircraft weight information for departing flights," the union, the Air Line Pilots Association, said in a memo obtained by ABC News.
United said there is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.
"While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights," United said.
The incident comes days after a nationwide ground stop resulted in thousands of cancelled flights and thousands more flight delays.
Though the worst of the flight cancellations is over, more than 340 flights were still cancelled in the U.S. as of late Monday afternoon, according to FlightAware, with more than 5,000 delayed.

title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond. A look back at his other franchises
summary: Some fans lauded Pattinson's casting as the next 007 on social media, while others pointed out that Bond is the latest franchise on his resumé that includes "Twilight."
story: Call Robert Pattinson Bond. James Bond.
On Monday, Amazon MGM Studios announced that Pattinson will play the legendary British spy in the studio's highly anticipated film directed by Denis Villeneuve.
The actor, who is a dad and shares a daughter with his fiancée Suki Waterhouse, called the role the "honour of a lifetime" in a statement shared by Amazon MGM Studios.
Some fans celebrated Pattinson's casting as the next 007 on social media, while others pointed out that Bond is the latest franchise on his resumé that already includes "Twilight" and "The Batman."
Here's a look at all the film franchises that Pattinson has appeared in.

Many were first introduced to Pattinson when he starred in the 2005 film "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" as Hogwarts student Cedric Diggory. The film also marked Pattinson's theatrical film debut.
In an interview with GQ in 2022, he reflected on the role, saying it was "so terrifying."

"I remember the first scene I ever shot on that, which was in the magical maze at the end," he said. "And I've never done anything with special effects and stunts and it was a big deal at the time. It felt very, very intimidating."
When he was cast as vampire Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" franchise, it transformed Pattinson from a recognizable face into a global superstar.

"I was 21 and kind of wanted to make it as arty as possible," Pattinson told GQ in 2022. "I was kind of -- so we had this strange tension where the studio was kind of a little bit scared to make things a little bit too emo and stuff and I thought that was the only way to play it."

He would go on to play Edward Cullen in all the "Twilight" films, including "The Twilight Saga: New Moon," "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse," "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn - Part 1" and "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn - Part 2."
In 2022, Pattinson took on the role of Bruce Wayne in "The Batman." The film was nominated for three Oscars and was Pattinson's first superhero role.
Earlier this month, Pattinson said in an interview with BAFTA that he never thought playing a superhero was "in reach at all."
"It's a kind of universally acknowledged fact (Batman) is the coolest superhero by a million miles," he said. "If I was to do a superhero movie I want to do that one."
Next month, Pattinson will star in Villeneuve's "Dune; Part Three" as the villain Scytale, a genetically engineered shapeshifter and a major antagonist in Frank Herbert's novel, "Dune Messiah."
Ahead of its theatrical release on Dec. 18, Pattinson told BAFTA that he "can't believe I got a part" in the franchise, sharing it was something he wanted for some time.
When he was doing "The Drama" with Zendaya, Pattinson asked her, "How do you get in one of those 'Dune' movies?"

"And then just randomly, Denis called me totally out of the blue and said, 'Oh, do you want to get on a call?'" he said. "I somehow found out that there were rumours of two new characters and I hadn't read 'Dune Messiah' at that point and I just saw the character brief. I just googled who Scytale was and I'm like, 'Oh, if that's the part that he's asking me if I was interested in it, then I'm like I'm in, immediately.' That's literally my ideal part."
Pattinson added, "The experience was just beyond anything I could have hoped for."

title: 'Everybody's shell-shocked': GOP operatives face 2028 prospects after midterm defeats
summary: GOP sources told ABC News the party leaned on culture wars over costs and lost key Latino voters. Some doubt JD Vance is still the presumptive 2028 nominee.
story: Some argued JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee.
On Election Day, many Republicans were bracing for a tough outcome, but not what has been described as a blue tsunami.

"I thought that we were going to keep the Senate," former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel told ABC News. "I didn't think that Democrats could make inroads in states like South Carolina and Kansas and even Texas."

Democrats did more than make inroads. They flipped eight GOP-held Senate seats and as of Monday, Democrats hold 256 House seats to the GOP's 170. There are still some outstanding races as of Monday: nine House races and one Senate race.

Over a dozen Republican donors and operatives told ABC News that the Republican Party is still in shock after the sweeping midterm losses. They pointed to a message that focused on culture wars and failed to reach voters squeezed by costs tied to the war in Iran and a Latino coalition that slipped away. Some argued Vice President JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee. Vance, who has not formally announced he is launching a presidential bid for 2028, has acknowledged "there's a chance" he won't run in 2028.
The president’s record-low approval ratings were also difficult to ignore, some said.

"The losses are all about Trump," said one Republican consultant who worked on races out West and spoke to ABC News on the condition of anonymity. "This was a total rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his politics."

RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement that Republicans will "continue to put America first,” highlighting that the RNC raised $130 million, sending more than $60 million directly to Republican campaigns.
When reached for comment, the White House emphasized Trump’s signature tax legislation and said that Trump will continue to work for the American people.

"Under President Trump’s leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, secured the border, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals. President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told ABC News in a statement.
Vance's office, when asked for comment, deferred to the White House.
The donors and operatives who spoke to ABC News agreed Republicans lacked a clear message on affordability -- a key issue for voters.
"We need to talk about pocketbook issues. We didn’t do that,” said Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, a group that fundraises for moderate Republicans.

T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist who worked on Republican Darline Graham’s Senate race, said Democrats were talking about affordability "in a more tangible way than we were … We have conservative solutions to these issues, we just didn’t deliver."

A GOP strategist involved in many 2026 races said the party's turnout operation will likely take much of the blame. ABC News' analysis of early voting in Texas and Georgia a week before Election Day showed greater Democratic enthusiasm.
"We just weren't hitting the numbers we needed to hit of just sheer Republicans voting. A lot of them stayed home, and we knew that was happening," the strategist said.
The Republican consultant who worked on races out West added that Republicans had "no choice" but to run on culture war issues because of the high costs brought on by the Iran war.
"You can't tell people to ignore your lying eyes,” the source said. "[Republicans] had no choice but to go down the culture-war road because we couldn't talk about the economy."

Trump said in a phone interview with Fox News on election night that he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm results and added that part of the reason was the Iran war, directly linking it to gas prices.
In a social media post after the election, Trump wrote that Republicans would have been more successful had he been on the ballot.
Reversal among Latino voters
According to the ABC News Voter Poll, in 2026, Latino voters nationally supported Democratic House candidates by a 30-point margin. In 2024, it was a 13-point margin.
Trump acknowledged his mass-deportation policies may have been "too tough" in an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes" after the midterms.
Mike Madrid, a GOP consultant who studies Latino voting behavior, said "there is no question that the ICE stuff and deportations played a role."
"There’s also no question that the economy was the No. 1 factor. But in some districts, like south Texas, they're one and the same. Immigration is the economy there," Madrid said.
Democrats swept every congressional district along the southern border, flipping several Republican-held seats in Texas.
Billionaire donor John Catsimatidis told ABC News that the losses came down to the war in Iran and "ICE being too tough on waiters and busboys."

Immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has reached local businesses and restaurants. ABC News reported last May that in D.C., federal law enforcement officials visited dozens of restaurants, carry-out spots and bars across several neighborhoods.
RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie announced on Nov. 5 that she's challenging RNC Chair Joe Gruters, saying the party should "be willing to confront where we fell short."
A source close to Gruters confirmed to ABC News that he is running for reelection.
While Trump has since reaffirmed his support for Gruters, some Republicans questioned Gruters' competence.
“Joe Gruters failed the Republican Party, and I find it puzzling that he believes he deserves to be reelected,” said an RNC member.

Florida GOP Chairman Evan Power said in a statement, however, that "Gruters was a key partner in our fight to keep the Free State of Florida red, and he’s the leader I trust to keep our party on offense and ready to win in 2028."
McDaniel said "the committee should support whoever the president wants to be the RNC chair."
She added that donors who may be discouraged from giving in the future need an autopsy from the party over what went wrong.

"People are still wondering what happened, and the sooner that a plan is put forward, and they get in the field and they get data … That's going to be what’s going to bring donors back. But right now, I think everybody's shell-shocked."
While Vance hasn't ruled out a run in 2028, some donors told ABC News that his proximity to Trump may be a liability.
But a Vance ally who spoke to ABC News cautioned against writing off Vance, comparing it to the 2016 and 2024 election cycles, when different parts of the Republican Party wrote Trump off.

And although Vance is still undecided about a 2028 presidential run, many of Vance's allies expect that he will run for president in 2028, sources confirmed to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl.
Vance's allies say he will decide whether to pursue a White House bid on his own timeline.
But some Republicans see an opening for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028 following the midterm elections.
Rubio has said he has no plans to run for president in 2028, adding that he would support Vance if he mounted a presidential run.
Catsimatidis said his family has been supporters of Vance, but he has known Rubio for 15 years and considers the nomination "still open."
A Texas-based GOP donor said the next nominee must appeal to "most all Republicans, a majority of independents and a reasonable group of conservative Democrats."
"We're in like stage two with a five-stage model of grief or something. We're not at the writing-checks-for-new-people yet stage," said one donor. "America doesn't want more MAGA."

title: Iran live updates: Tankers attacked in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: Two tankers reported fires in their engine rooms, the UKMTO said.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
