title: Trump heads to Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
summary: President Trump set off on a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit.
story: Washington — President Trump set off Monday for a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 1/2-year war in Ukraine during the summit.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.

Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

title: Top federal prosecutor in Houston accused of breaking ethics rules
summary: A nonprofit watchdog group filed an ethics complaint on Monday against the top federal prosecutor in Houston, alleging he has violated professional conduct rules by threatening to prosecute Democratic lawmakers.
story: A nonprofit watchdog group filed an ethics complaint on Monday against the top federal prosecutor in Houston, alleging he has violated professional conduct rules by threatening to prosecute several Democratic lawmakers for undertaking congressional oversight.

The complaint, filed by the Campaign for Accountability, asks the Texas state bar to investigate Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, over confrontational letters he sent to lawmakers including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

In those letters, Reitz cited public comments they made about their intentions to investigate the Trump administration and some of its backers, and insinuated that their comments may run afoul of several criminal civil rights laws.
He also ordered them to preserve all their records, a step that prosecutors sometimes take ahead of a criminal investigation.

Reitz sent a similar letter on Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. He pointed to several comments by Garcia vowing intense investigations into the Trump administration, including an election night statement encouraging people to "lawyer up," which Reitz called "little more than a call for political punishment against American citizens and businesses."

The letters from Reitz came after White House counsel Will Scharf warned Garcia last week that some congressional investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," and if lawmakers issue "unlawful subpoenas," the executive branch may launch investigations of its own.
Blumenthal replied to Reitz with his own letter, in which he ordered Reitz to preserve his own records, and said that Reitz's "implied threat of an investigation is baseless."
CBS News has reached out to Warren's and Garcia's offices for comment.
In the ethics complaint, the Campaign for Accountability asks the Texas state bar to investigate Reitz over possible violations of three different rules.

One such rule prohibits prosecutors from threatening to bring charges not supported by probable cause, while another rule prohibits lawyers from taking actions that serve "no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay or burden" someone else.
A third rule, meanwhile, prohibits attorneys from committing a serious crime. The complaint suggests that Reitz may be unlawfully obstructing a congressional inquiry.

"Officials who hold prosecutorial power have long been tempted to abuse it for political gain. A federal prosecutor's threat to bring criminal charges against United States Senators for conducting oversight strikes at the separation of powers and at public confidence in the fair administration of justice," the group wrote in its complaint.
"If left unaddressed, Mr. Reitz's conduct signals to every prosecutor that the threat of criminal process may be wielded against those who investigate the executive branch," it added.
In a statement, Reitz called the complaint "harassing" and "frivolous."

"I will continue my preliminary inquiry unfazed to determine whether certain members of Congress have unlawfully stepped outside the legitimate legislative purpose of their planned committee activities, and to ensure Americans' constitutional rights are protected. I'll always do the right thing by following the facts and the law," he said.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department called the complaint "nothing more than selective barfare against an administration official, which is a dangerous and illegitimate tactic."
"Oversight is not a license to threaten private citizens for exercising their First Amendment rights," the spokesperson added.
It is not clear exactly why a U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas has been targeting lawmakers from other states over their comments about oversight investigations.
Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at a press conference last week that "any office" could investigate this type of matter.
At the same time, however, he also told reporters there were "no ongoing criminal investigations into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said."

title: "Tiger team" formed to head off another nationwide ground stop
summary: Members of the new tiger team include officials from the FAA, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, Defense Department and Transportation Department.
story: The White House has organized a "tiger team" to work on preventing another incident like the one that caused the nationwide ground stop last week, U.S. officials told CBS News.

Members of the team include officials from the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, Defense Department and Transportation Department. A tiger team is a small group of experts or specialists who work together on solving a specific problem that isn't easily addressed by normal operations.
The tiger team's first meeting was held Monday at the White House, one of the sources said.

The four-hour ground stop just after 3:30 p.m. last Friday caused the cancellation of thousands of flights and occurred while 3,500 flights were in the air. A preliminary investigation by the FAA indicated that a router that was being replaced in Arkansas was the cause of the problem.

In September, the Government Accountability Office issued a report analyzing the Transportation Department's effort to modernize the air traffic controller systems. It found that the "FAA has made progress implementing this initiative, but it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is not ruling out the possibility of another ground stop as the system continues to be updated. Asked about the GAO's report, Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday, "We are going, I think, at the right speed. We have to get off old network, old telecom."

The GAO also said the FAA lacks an overall cost estimate and "master schedule for related projects," and warned that without them, the FAA "could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems." Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion to make the necessary updates.
"Let's finish the job. Let's not see what happened on Friday. Let's not let it happen again," he told "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan.
Trump administration officials have blamed the problem on the FAA's antiquated technology, and have pressed lawmakers to approve more funding to modernize the air traffic control system.
President Trump told reporters the outage was caused by "very, very old equipment that had a heart attack."

Intelligence agencies preliminarily ruled out any nefarious activity on Friday after they didn't find any concerning chatter or pings, CBS News previously reported. But key questions still remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:58 p.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Ex-staffers claim lack of enforcement, "chaos" under Lutnick
summary: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of computer chip smuggling.
story: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of highly sensitive computer chip smuggling.

A key national security responsibility of the department is investigating and enforcing bans on the export to China and other U.S. adversaries of advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated weapons.
"There was an inexplicable refusal to use the tools at their disposal for national security over the last year," one former Commerce official told CBS News.

Scrutiny of Lutnick's tenure has heightened in recent days with Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of spying, calling it "an attempt to smear China."

As the scandal has unfolded, senior officials and members of Congress have questioned how Nvidia was permitted to sell chips to companies with deep ties to China, and whether the Commerce Department policed those exports effectively.
The answer, according to some of Lutnick's former staff, was not at all.
Four ex-Commerce officials spoke with CBS News, asking to remain anonymous, fearing professional reprisals for discussing their recent experience in government.

"We weren't able to add entities to the Entity List. That was just a complete stop," one former Commerce employee said, referring to the federal list of firms that the U.S. government has banned from buying the most advanced chips due to the belief they would route them to China or other adversaries.

Another former Commerce official said a whole year passed with no companies added to the list, noting that this was the first time that had happened in 18 years. The Federal Register shows the last time entities were added was Oct. 9, 2025, and the last yearlong gap in additions was in 2008.

The first former staffer said the agency's own enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips had been delivered, but that Commerce directors allegedly took no action.
Placement on the list triggers more stringent license requirements and creates a higher threshold to prevent sensitive products from getting where they shouldn't, the ex-official said.
Instead, "nothing happened," the ex-official said.

The Biden administration issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023, and in January 2025 issued an interim final rule to block China and other adversaries from obtaining the most advanced AI chips, both directly and through third-party countries.

In May 2025, President Trump's Commerce Department rolled back the rule, arguing it "would have stifled American innovation." Instead, the department said it would strengthen export controls for AI chips by issuing guidance to the industry and public.
There are growing signs that bans on exporting advanced U.S. computer chips have been circumvented in large quantities, according to published reports.

An April 2026 study by AI research nonprofit Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025, comprising "roughly a quarter of the comput[ing power] China acquired through legal channels or domestic production."

Tech news site The Information reported that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips allegedly ended up with Chinese companies since 2023 just through companies linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese agent accused of an affair with Nvidia's ousted CEO. The report cited sources close to her for the estimate.

And a former researcher at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, published a paper last week claiming to have found digital forensic evidence that top Chinese AI models were trained using Nvidia chips banned in China.

One former Commerce staffer described the department under Lutnick as "very chaotic, very frantic," with staff sometimes learning of major policy changes via media reports, including a pivot to allow the sale of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China — the company's second-most advanced tier of GPUs.
"We found out about that in The New York Times," the ex-Commerce official said. "It was pretty clear that the decision was made between Trump and Jensen Huang."
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.  CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.

On Monday the department imposed a new rule requiring licenses for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand, aimed at closing a loophole through which chips were exported to China via an intermediary. But the Commerce Department suggested that its own involvement was limited, describing the rule as "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers."
The department lost two of its most senior and experienced experts shortly after Lutnick took office.
One was Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration. Borman had been with the department for over 30 years.

Another veteran official, Eileen Albanese, was let go from her longtime role as director of the Office of National Security Controls. Reuters first reported their departures in February 2025, the same month Lutnick started running the department.
"They kicked off the administration by essentially firing the two most respected people," said one former employee.

A profile on the website of law firm Akin Gump, where Albanese now works, says she played a "key role in the development of U.S. export control policy and regulations for advanced artificial intelligence chips and semiconductor manufacturing tools."
"Matt and Eileen were treasures of the U.S. government," one former Commerce staffer said.
Albanese did not respond to a request for comment. Borman declined to comment.
Former officials said subsequent changes under Lutnick helped prompt an "exodus" of up to 50 skilled staff members over the past 18 months.
Over time, those who departed were among the most experienced officials who dealt with key areas including chips and export control enforcement, the ex-staffers said.

"It was an exodus of the finest engineers and scientists, the key experts on AI, on Russia, on diversion, our key expert on chips. Decades of institutional memory and skill went out," an ex-employee said.

Key roles remain vacant in Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the department in charge of export controls, according to a registry of current senior federal employees. The principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, the same role for export enforcement and the chief of staff roles are all currently unfilled, the records say.

Some staff described a bottleneck at the Bureau of Industry and Security, accusing its chief — Jeffrey Kessler, a top deputy to Lutnick — of "micromanaging" and blocking enforcement against companies suspected of smuggling chips.

"He made everything go through him. Literally every possible decision, the most minor things. It's impossible for one person to manage that level of things," one former employee under Lutnick told CBS News.

"He didn't want to make any decisions on his own. He would want you to make a memo and he would say, 'Package it up with options for me to bring to a decision maker,' which always cracked me up. Because it's like, who are you? A concerned citizen?"

"The career workforce felt frustrated and stymied," said one former staffer from the previous administration, who is close to many who remained in the department. "They felt like they were unable to do their jobs because [Kessler and Lutnick] were standing in their way."
The former staff members told CBS News that the critical view of Lutnick and his deputy was widely shared in the department.

Cabinet members have even voiced criticism, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent telling CNBC last week that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department and others in the administration.
"Commerce has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told the channel.
"I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above" a certain sophistication, Bessent said.

title: Tennessee names new corrections chief after botched executions
summary: Josh Smith has been appointed to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee following the botched execution of Christa Pike last month.
story: Josh Smith, who unexpectedly left his role as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons in August, was appointed Monday to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee.
Smith, a pardoned drug offender, was named to the position by Republican Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn.

"Josh brings a distinctive combination of executive leadership, firsthand correctional experience, and an understanding of the challenges facing our prison system," Blackburn said in her announcement. "He has demonstrated the ability to lead large organizations, make difficult decisions, and tackle longstanding problems."
Smith said in a statement he is honored to have been selected.

"Tennessee's correctional system faces significant challenges, including staffing shortages, institutional safety, and the need to strengthen leadership throughout the organization," he said. "I believe we can address these challenges by empowering our employees, establishing clear expectations, developing leaders, and maintaining an unwavering commitment to public safety."
Smith is succeeding interim Director Christopher Hansen, who has been in office since Frank Strada resigned early last month following the botched execution of Christa Pike.

Pike was the first female inmate scheduled to be executed by the state of Tennessee in 200 years. All executions following Pike's were stayed by Gov. Bill Lee. The lethal drug injection of pentobarbital left Pike on a ventilator with her arms blistered and bruised, her attorneys alleged.

Her lawyers said in a court filing that Department of Corrections employees did not seem to realize that the IV was not placed correctly into Pike's veins, or that they were blown, allowing the lethal drug to enter her body.

Pike's botched execution follows the failed execution of Tony Carruthers, who was set to be executed in May. Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve after corrections staff spent more than an hour trying — and failing — to find a vein for the IV line for the lethal drug.
Blackburn has called for the state to explore alternative means of execution, such as the electric chair. There are 40 inmates on death row in Tennessee.

Smith was widely seen as an unconventional choice to serve as the No. 2 official at the Bureau of Prisons. He had a criminal record himself, after having pleaded guilty in 1998 to conspiring to possess and distribute cocaine and marijuana and serving a five-year sentence in a BOP prison camp in Kentucky.
He was later pardoned by President Trump, and he sought to use his prior experience as an incarcerated offender to press for reforms inside the federal prison system.
His approach to the job, however, led to disagreements among BOP staff, many of whom viewed him as caring more about the inmate population than employees.

Smith abruptly resigned from his post at the BOP in August, with some current and former BOP employees telling CBS News that there have been a number of questions raised about several government contracts awarded during his tenure as deputy director.

One such contract, for instance, was awarded to a Texas-based company called Securus Technologies to provide inmates with tablets that it said would be used to help facilitate academic coursework, career training, access to rehabilitation and healthcare information.
The contract was later canceled, however, after several competing companies filed a grievance challenging the decision, according to a BOP letter obtained by CBS News.

Another business deal previously reported by CBS News, meanwhile, involved a partnership with a startup company to sell nicotine pouches to inmates. That deal was scrapped after it came to light that the pouches were not authorized by the Food and Drug Administration.

In a prior interview with CBS News, Smith denied having any involvement in some of the controversial contracts. He said at the time of his resignation that his main goals while serving as deputy director were to overhaul staffing and strive to improve rehabilitative services for prisoners to help them prepare for their return to society.

"I believe we should really care about what kind of people we are turning back out into our neighborhoods," he said in August. "I'm a tough-on-crime person, but I'm restorative in nature because they're going to be my neighbor."

In response to Smith's appointment, Kit Thomas, co-counsel on the long-running challenge by Tennessee death row prisoners to the state's lethal injection protocol, said, "We are hopeful that Commissioner-designate Josh Smith will bring a renewed commitment to transparency and accountability at the Tennessee Department of Correction.
"We urge him to prioritize implementing the recommendations of the 2022 and 2026 independent Butler Snow investigations, including meaningful revisions to Tennessee's lethal injection protocol."

title: High court rejects challenge to Maryland gun ban in sensitive places
summary: The Supreme Court left in place a lower court decision that upheld the measure banning guns in sensitive places.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland laws that prohibit firearms in sensitive places like schools, parks and government buildings.
In rejecting the appeal from a group of Maryland residents and gun rights groups, the high court leaves in place a lower court decision that upheld the rules.

Justice Clarence Thomas said that while he agrees with the Supreme Court's decision not to hear the case, he is "skeptical" of the constitutionality of sensitive-place restrictions and urged the court to consider the scope of states' authority to ban firearms in those locations in a more "narrowly focused case."

"I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions," he wrote in a statement. "In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry."
The Supreme Court last year struck down a Hawaii law that required concealed-carry permit holders to receive permission before bringing their firearms onto private property open to the public.

At issue in the case was a set of Maryland laws that limit the places where guns can be carried in public.  The state prohibits firearms from being brought on school property, at public demonstrations and on public transit, as well as in parks, museums and casinos.

Another set of limits was enacted in 2023, in the wake of the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision that recognized for the first time that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry a gun outside the home. Under the new restrictions, people are prohibited from carrying firearms at daycare and medical facilities, government buildings or other places where the public gathers for "entertainment, educational enrichment or other collective social pursuits."
On the same day Maryland's latest restrictions were signed into law, two sets of plaintiffs filed lawsuits arguing they violated the Second Amendment. The suits targeted 10 categories of places.

The two cases were consolidated, and a federal district court declined to block the limits on museums, healthcare facilities, public transit, state parks, entertainment venues, school grounds and government buildings. But the district court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs as to public demonstrations and places that sell alcohol for on-site consumption.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit went on to rule that all of the challenged restrictions are consistent with the Second Amendment. The appeals court applied the Supreme Court's new test for evaluating the constitutionality of gun regulations, which it laid out in its 2022 decision. Under that framework, the government must show that a firearms restriction is consistent with the nation's historical tradition.

In addition to pointing to historical analogues of some of Maryland's regulations, the 4th Circuit said the Supreme Court has twice, in decisions from 2008 and 2010, asserted that laws forbidding guns in government buildings and on school grounds are allowed.

The Maryland residents and gun rights groups appealed to the Supreme Court and argued that its intervention is needed to help lower courts better define the historical limits on the right to have guns in public as more and more states are enacting location-specific limits.

"The constitutionality of these so-called 'sensitive place' bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of" the Supreme Court's 2022 decision, they wrote in their petition. "If, as Maryland maintains and the Fourth Circuit below held, the right to carry a firearm 'in public' does not include public locations that are owned by the government, or where First Amendment protected activity is being carried out, or where people go to eat and to drink or gather for amusement and recreation, then it is hard to know what the right to carry a firearm 'in public' actually protects."

But Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown argued that the state's sensitive-place laws are consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearms regulation, and therefore constitutional. He noted that there is a "rich American tradition" of barring guns in certain locations, including those that are "confined and crowded."
"This Court endorsed such 'longstanding' bans in schools, legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses, while recognizing that this list was non-exhaustive," Brown wrote in a filing.

In the years since the Supreme Court laid out its new test for determining the legality of gun regulations, it has been confronted with a number of challenges to longstanding firearms laws. In 2024, the Supreme Court upheld a federal law that prohibits people subject to domestic violence restraining orders from having guns.

In an opinion authored by Chief Justice John Roberts, the eight-justice majority said the "appropriate analysis" under its new historical tradition standard "involves considering whether the challenged regulation is consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition."
Then, in its last term, a unanimous Supreme Court said the Second Amendment does not allow the government to prosecute a person who is an occasional marijuana user.

title: These are the last midterm races to be decided
summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
story: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.

The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in a few races. Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:
Senate Battlegrounds
Democrats are set to enter next year with at least 55 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44.

Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results weren't expected until 15 days after Election Day.
Democrats on Defense

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of election night, but a few Republican House candidates tried to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate won a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it will go to a runoff between Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.
GOP-Held Battlegrounds
Several races held by Republicans didn't have projections in the immediate aftermath of election night — including in districts that Democrats were hoping to flip.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is facing off against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount.
Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.
North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans.

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.
North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.
North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.
Please hold...

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed.
California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate.

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts. Roblox CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify but has declined to appear.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."
This story published first on CBS News at 1:58 p.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Trump says he "would not mind" if Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang
summary: According to a source directly familiar with the Nvidia board's thinking, the company is not interested bringing Jensen Huang back to the company as CEO or in any other position.
story: Washington — President Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, after he resigned last week amid allegations of two affairs. The president said he doesn't know if Alice Huang, one of the women allegedly involved with Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy.
"I would not mind. I would not mind that," the president told reporters Monday as he departed for a trip to the Philippines and China, and he said "that certainly isn't a bad idea."

He also floated the name of the former Apple CEO as a possible Huang replacement at Nvidia, saying, "I like, you know, I do have the name of Tim Cook." Mr. Trump added, "But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement — I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."
According to a source directly familiar with the Nvidia board's thinking, the company is not interested bringing Jensen Huang back to the company as CEO or in any other position.

Mr. Trump also said that the U.S. has banned Nvidia from selling the "important chips, the modern-day chips," in particular, the most powerful AI chip in the world, the company's Blackwell chip. And just before the president left, the Trump administration announced a new rule that's intended to curb efforts by China to bypass the restrictions by remotely accessing the chips through data centers in third countries.

The president also dismissed concerns that Alice Huang may be spying for China. She's a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a former gaming company that is now an AI infrastructure and cloud computing company and is one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers.

"Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Mr. Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
The president said he may speak with Xi about Alice Huang and whether she was a spy. Mr. Trump and Xi will be meeting in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
Last week, Attorney General Todd Blanche said he "certainly" hasn't said Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

Elon Musk, tech executives and Nvidia employees have signed a petition calling for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. The former CEO resigned last week amid reports of two extramarital affairs — one with Alice Huang and one with an Nvidia employee.

title: Commerce Department moves to curb remote access to AI chips
summary: U.S. announces a temporary rule to limit foreign countries' access to advanced chips via data centers in other countries.
story: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.

The federal government is stepping up scrutiny of semiconductor exports to ensure that such shipments don't bypass existing regulations prohibiting their sale to certain U.S. competitors, such as China. The temporary regulations follow last week's shock resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company.
Huang's exit has heightened concerns that China and other nations could access Nvidia's advanced chips by renting computing resources through data centers in Southeast Asia.

"The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement on Monday. "The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten U.S. national security."

In addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, the new rule will require licenses for exporting, re-exporting, or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand. BIS said such nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

The interim rule notes that advances in cloud computing have made it easier for foreign nations to access American AI computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers in countries not subject to U.S. export restrictions.

The Commerce Department wants to "ensure that computing power, based on U.S. technology located in foreign data centers, is not used in a manner contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests," the rule states.
The rule aims to align remote-access protections with existing controls governing physical access to sensitive American technology, the Commerce Department said.

Existing regulations on chip exports apply only to the most advanced semiconductors. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing," President Trump said in remarks at the White House on Monday.

Mr. Trump is heading to Asia on Monday, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Chinese officials have said the country was not involved in Huang's affair with the suspected spy.

title: How Trump administration responded to FAA ground stop
summary: President Trump was informed within 30 minutes after the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, according to U.S. officials.
story: President Trump was informed within 30 minutes after the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, according to U.S. officials.

The ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers across the U.S. The FAA announced that all planes would be grounded at 3:36 p.m. ET — while 3,500 flights were in the air.

Within minutes, the FBI, director of national intelligence, Department of Homeland Security, Transportation Department, Justice Department, Defense Department, Joint Chiefs of Staff, U.S. Cyber Command, FAA and Federal Emergency Management Agency began looping each other in.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement at 4:16 p.m. ET that the ground stop was necessary due to "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," and that FAA technicians were investigating. Within minutes, the White House led a call with the agencies to determine what had happened. A game plan was put in motion.
The intelligence community soon preliminarily ruled out the likelihood of nefarious activity after searching through its various channels for chatter or pings. Nothing came up.

Senior staff briefed Mr. Trump, who was in an economic policy meeting, one U.S. official said. The staff relayed his directives to others on the multi-team call, led by White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Later Mr. Trump met with Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Mr. Trump started calling congressional leaders on Friday to work on getting the FAA more funding. The White House congressional team called key congressional members to work with them on air traffic controller modernization.

The Homeland Security Council invited key members of the government and some outside stakeholders to a meeting Monday to discuss the next steps and what should be done to prevent a recurrence as modernization efforts continue.

The council is an interagency government body responsible for coordinating national homeland security policy. Established by President George W. Bush in 2001, under the current White House structure, the Council operates through the National Security Council framework and can draw on senior officials from agencies like the Transportation Department, FAA, DHS and Defense Department.
But not all planes were grounded during the four-hour stop: medical services flights were green-lighted to proceed to their intended destinations.
By the fourth hour, the problem in the system had been identified, and the grounding was lifted. Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware.

At a news conference on Saturday, Duffy said the trouble apparently began as FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies performed maintenance updates at a remote facility, replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. During that work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming routers across the entire FAA network.

Mullin and Duffy were more than 30 minutes late for a 7:45 p.m. ET press conference on the ground stop Friday because they were close to getting the grounding lifted and didn't want to interrupt the effort to hold the presser, U.S. officials said.
While federal officials have identified a likely sequence of events behind Friday's disruption, key questions still remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

On Monday morning, speaking to reporters at the White House before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump said the ground stop wasn't his fault, or Duffy's. The president said he was at the White House having meetings at the time of the ground stop.
"I don't take any responsibility," he said. "They did a great job. Secretary Duffy — they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe, nobody was hurt, no crashes, no nothing."
The president placed all the blame on what he described as an outdated system.
"Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," Mr. Trump said.

title: Supreme Court rejects case on Trump's bid to cut grants related to DEI
summary: Two federal agencies had moved to cancel grants to researchers at the University of California that they said did not align with President Trump's policies on DEI.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a case involving the Trump administration's termination of grants awarded to University of California researchers that it said did not align with President Trump's priorities, including on diversity, equity and inclusion.

By turning away the appeal from the Trump administration, the Supreme Court leaves intact a lower court decision that found the cancellation of the millions in academic funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and National Science Foundation likely violated the First Amendment.

The Justice Department had warned that if the high court allowed the decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit to stand, as it now has done, it would clear the way for taxpayer dollars to go to research projects promoting DEI initiatives.

The case stems from the first days of Mr. Trump's second term, when he signed executive orders that instructed federal agencies to cancel grants related to certain topics, including DEI. The legal fight involves grants from the NEH and the NSF to University of California researchers, which the Trump administration terminated because they were not consistent with the president's priorities on DEI.

Lawyers for the University of California said that from January to June 2025, the Trump administration cut off more than $324 million in grants to that university system alone. They said the two agencies carried out Mr. Trump's executive orders on funding for DEI-related programs by conducting keyword searches of grant applications, and then canceled awards that used words like "diversity," "climate change" and "gender ideology."

Grant recipients began receiving letters informing them that their funding had been terminated in April 2025. Several months later, six researchers at the University of California who received grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, NSF and NEH filed a lawsuit and sought a court order requiring their grants to be reinstated.

A federal district court sided with the plaintiffs in a June 2025 decision and certified a provisional class covering University of California researchers who had grants terminated under Mr. Trump's executive orders targeting DEI-related initiatives.

U.S. District Judge Rita Lin said that the Trump administration had terminated the grants en masse for touching on issues it said were prohibited and ruled that the funding was likely terminated based on the perceived viewpoint expressed in the research. She ordered the Trump administration to reinstate grants from the NSF, NEH and EPA.
The 9th Circuit upheld the district court's preliminary injunction in May and agreed that the grant terminations likely violated the First Amendment's prohibition on viewpoint discrimination.

The Trump administration, it said, "has not merely exercised its power to choose the programs it funds but has instead terminated individual grants in existing programs based on the perceived viewpoints of individual speakers."

While the case proceeded, the plaintiffs reached a settlement related to the EPA grants, leaving only the awards from the NSF and NEH at issue. The Trump administration said there was approximately $59 million remaining on the grants, which will expire as late as November 2029.

title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
summary: President Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on his China trip this week.
story: Washington — President Trump said he may meet with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia this week.

As he left the White House Monday morning for a summit in the Philippines, which will be followed by a trip to China, Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting with Kim would take place in China — if it happens. No meeting with Kim has been confirmed by the White House. The president said whether the meeting happens is up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump will meet with Xi, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, later this week.

"We'll be with President Xi," the president told reporters on the White House South Lawn. "He was here a month ago. And we're also going to meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un, also. So that'll be good. We could — we have a chance to accomplish a lot."
The president said he doesn't know if Kim will come.
"He may come," Mr. Trump said of Kim. "I don't know. That's up to President Xi."
Mr. Trump has met with the North Korean leader in person three times, all during his first term in office. He is the only sitting U.S. president to have met with Kim.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Fewer foreign students studying at U.S. universities, study shows
summary: Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, a study shows.
story: Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.

Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

"No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.," said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
"It feels like an unsafe place. That's the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they're listening."

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practical training program.
Although the rule hasn't been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.
Other factors in foreign enrollment decline

Politics aren't the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

"They're saying to themselves, 'Too much uncertainty in the United States. It's too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?'" Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students' contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
Schools' coffers feeling the effects
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F-1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

"I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career," said Sridhar, who is from India. "So international education is personal to me."

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall's data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
"Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there's not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes," Spreitzer said.

title: Officials received years of warnings before FAA ground stop
summary: For years, audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns.
story: Government watchdogs have warned for years of the risk of technical failures involving decrepit air travel systems like the one that grounded all planes across the country on Friday, according to federal audits and past congressional testimony.

Audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault that led to Friday's five-hour halt may trace back to one router that was supposed to be replaced in 2006.
"We're investigating that right now," Duffy said Sunday on CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." "This goes back decades."
One company that has been in charge of the aging telecommunications infrastructure for the last quarter-century is L3Harris.

The Federal Aviation Administration has poured billions of dollars into the company's contracts since 2020. A 2024 audit by the Office of the Inspector General found that since awarding the original contract in 2002, the FAA made 10 extensions that were "improperly authorized" (as well as one that was proper), adding 57 months and $1.5 billion in spending.

The inspector general warned the FAA "may be repetitively using these noncompetitive extensions for convenience and administrative ease," adding that it "risks paying more than the Agency should and receiving less than the best-quality results."

These concerns by government watchdogs can be traced back two decades. Just four years after Harris Corporation, now part of L3Harris, was awarded the contract in 2002 to modernize and operate the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure, an audit warned that the program was falling behind schedule. A follow-up report in 2008 identified continuing concerns about reliability problems that disrupted air traffic control operations.

A year later, in 2009, more than 800 flights were delayed after a telecommunications outage. The DOT IG investigated the incident and found that the FAA had failed to adequately oversee Harris Corporation and also had not developed sufficient safeguards for overseeing privately operated systems despite increasingly shifting more services to the private sector to reduce costs.

Despite these issues, the FAA awarded Harris another $291 million contract in 2012 to update its outdated air traffic control voice communications equipment. The project was ultimately terminated in 2018, after running into repeated delays and technical problems, with $160 million spent on the unsuccessful program.

Duffy acknowledged in a press conference following last week's outage that the government could not immediately move away from L3Harris, saying he was "stuck with L3Harris" until a new system could be built.

"Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us," Duffy said, as he raised questions about whether the outage was caused by contractor error or faulty equipment.

Eric Soskin, transport inspector general under the Biden Administration, told CBS News that some of the FAA's equipment was now so old that one manufacturer of replacement parts had been out of business for over a decade.

"When you have systems as old as the ones that we have in place now, the knowledge of how those systems work… may even have been lost to retirements or memory," he said. "If only we had succeeded in getting a full rollout of next-gen technologies a decade ago, I bet whatever the cause was here wouldn't have happened."
But a September report from the Office of the Inspector General also warned that moving ahead with upgrades too quickly could also cause disruptions.

L3Harris did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment regarding the inspector general's criticisms, but said in a statement on Saturday that the company is working "in close coordination with the FAA" and has completed 70% of the switch from old copper lines to fiber cables for the Agency's communications.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Even as L3Harris faced scrutiny over its performance, the company spent millions seeking to influence federal policy, including efforts to secure additional funding for modernizing the infrastructure it has operated for more than two decades.

It has paid $23.9 million to lobbyists since 2020, including $2.51 million this year, according to Senate records. Disclosures show it lobbied Congress on FAA modernization funding every year. L3Harris has also lobbied the FAA directly.

Ballard Partners, which has had deep ties to the White House, has at times been among the lobbying firms it retained. Other firms employed lobbyists who previously worked on congressional appropriations committees that play a large role in decisions on FAA funding, the records show.

Last April, L3Harris penned a letter urging congressional leaders of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to advance an air traffic control modernization proposal that initially called for $15 billion in federal spending.

Two of the lawmakers addressed in the letter had previously received campaign contributions from the company's political action committee, including Chairman Rep. Sam Graves, a Missouri Republican, whose campaign received $10,000 during the 2021-2022 election cycle, and Democrat Rick Larsen, of Washington, whose campaign received $5,000 during the 2023-2024 cycle.

Four days after the letter was sent, Graves publicly unveiled the committee's proposal to provide billions in additional funding for air traffic control modernization. Congress ultimately approved $12.5 billion for FAA modernization as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including $4.75 billion for telecommunications upgrades.
Graves and Larsen did not respond to CBS News' requests for comment.

In testimony to the House Appropriations Committee this March, Deputy Inspector General Mitch Behm cited a repeated pattern across 50 audits of cost increases and schedule overruns, largely blaming a failure to nail down design decisions and a lack of a clear plan.
Other government watchdogs have also been calling out crumbling infrastructure around aviation communications.

In 2024, the Government Accountability Office found 51 of the FAA's 138 air traffic systems unsustainable, citing outdated functionality and missing spare parts, with 54 more potentially unsustainable.

The Transportation Department says it is putting its $12.5 billion to good use, including replacing handwritten paper systems with electronic ones at 25 control towers, upgrading five facilities from using floppy disks, and modernizing 469 tower radios, but says that the funds are narrowly allotted by Congress with little room to choose what it spends on.

Soskin told CBS News that Friday's outage "confirms the importance of pushing ahead with the technology upgrades," but added that "FAA and DOT need to supervise these projects carefully, and make sure they are getting highly capable systems that are reliable, and that are procured properly so that they're good value for taxpayers."

"The transfer needs to be handled carefully," the former inspector general said. "It may be that some disruptions like this are unavoidable, in which case FAA and other leaders need to do a good job of explaining to travelers why they happen, and why the end result is worth the trouble."

title: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising lags
summary: After a quiet 2025, Biden's presidential library foundation landed two $5 million gifts, but some allies are said to be frustrated donors haven't come calling.
story: The foundation building Joe Biden's presidential library is nearing a decision on a site in Delaware, as it tries to gain fundraising momentum after bringing in less than $1.5 million in 2025, according to sources familiar with the planning and a copy of its most recent tax filing obtained by CBS News.

The Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation spent about $2.1 million last year, mostly on staff, consultants and legal fees, running a deficit of around $600,000, according to the filing. The document, which covers the foundation's first full calendar year and does not cover 2026 activity, was submitted to the IRS and has not been made public.

Board members met last week to discuss the library, and an announcement on the site is expected in the next couple of months, the sources said. In 2026, the foundation stepped up its fundraising, securing several multimillion-dollar donations, including two $5 million gifts, one of the sources said. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal planning and fundraising.

Last week, the Biden library foundation added five new board members, an official for the foundation said. They include Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, Biden's former ambassador to Brazil and a longtime Democratic fundraiser; Bijan Sabet, a venture capitalist who served as his ambassador to the Czech Republic; event planner Bryan Rafanelli; Wilmington nonprofit leader Logan Herring; and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff who will remain the group's co-executive director.

The official for the foundation declined to share an estimate of the expected cost of the library, but said the group expects to do so when it announces its site. It finished 2025 with about $3.4 million in net assets, the filing shows.

The fundraising push is an early test of Democratic donors' appetite for a project meant to further shape the legacy of Biden's presidency and a political career that spanned more than half a century. Biden is out with a memoir, "Promise Me, America," to be published on Tuesday. He announced that he would be scaling back the book tour amid his cancer treatment.

Modern presidential centers cost hundreds of millions of dollars and rely on large checks from individual and corporate donors. The foundation is now courting donors after a midterm cycle that drew heavily from ultra-wealthy Democrats.

The nonprofit's fundraising pace stands in stark contrast to President Trump's library foundation, which has already raised tens of millions of dollars, including from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. That includes large donations from Meta, Elon Musk's X, and Paramount, which paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. (Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.)

The official for the Biden library foundation said it wasn't actively fundraising in 2025, describing it as a "building and infrastructure year." The money for this came from Biden's presidential inaugural committee, his transition fund and two individual donors whom the foundation official declined to name also made unsolicited donations.

The filing shows the foundation paid about $250,000 last year to consultants for "fundraising counsel." This was meant to lay the groundwork for its fundraising push in 2026, including a feasibility study on its donor base and advice on how to structure its fundraising team, the official for the foundation said.

Biden, who served one term, waited until the final weeks of his presidency to set up a library foundation, while several predecessors began theirs during their second terms. The foundation was incorporated in December 2024 and listed $4 million in contributions, which the foundation official described as seed money, on its first tax filing.

By comparison, former President Barack Obama's foundation was formed in early 2014, nearly three years before he left office, and raised $5.4 million that year, even as Obama capped donations at $1 million and did not solicit publicly. It raised a staggering $232 million in 2017, his first year after leaving the White House. Former President George W. Bush's foundation raised $27.5 million from 2006 to 2008, while he was still in office, and $152 million in 2009.

The Biden library foundation did not receive tax-exempt status from the IRS until March 2025, about two months after Biden left office. It announced its board in September of that year and said the library would be in his home state of Delaware.

Some of Biden's close allies have privately been frustrated with Democratic donors for not proactively reaching out to support his library, according to a source familiar with the matter. That frustration has grown amid reports of the haul by President Trump's library, which includes $50 million from SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant.

Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," the source said. Former first lady Jill Biden is expected to help out on fundraising while also caring for Biden as he gets treated for prostate cancer that has metastasized to his bones, they added.
An official for the Biden library foundation said it is "not comparing" itself to Mr. Trump's library. "We're running very different types of organizations," the official said.

Mr. Trump's library is facing scrutiny from Democrats, who take control of Congress in January and have vowed to investigate its finances. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who has said donors "will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," opened an inquiry over the summer into SoftBank's donation — which came two months before the Trump administration announced a federal land lease for a SoftBank data center in Ohio.

The Energy Department has said the lease was signed in February and that a local group first proposed the project in October 2024. SoftBank referred CBS News to its July statement confirming the donation, which said the company "is proud of its support for institutions dedicated to preserving American history while continuing its commitment to investing in America's future."

The Trump library foundation is also fundraising through a donation platform run by PublicSquare — a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr., CBS News reported. The library foundation's trustees include Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, corporate records filed in Florida show.

An official for the Biden library foundation said its staff has worked to ensure there are "no conflict issues," noting that no members of the Biden family, including the former president and Jill Biden, sit on its board. The board is chaired by Rufus Gifford, a prolific Democratic fundraiser and former ambassador to Denmark under Obama. The board also includes former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and Biden adviser Steve Ricchetti, both of whom worked with Biden over a long stretch of his public life.

The tax filing shows that the Biden library foundation paid over $221,000 each in compensation to its co-executive directors, Tomasini and Anthony Bernal, a longtime senior adviser to Jill Biden. Their combined pay made up roughly a fifth of the foundation's spending last year.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:00 a.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.
