title: United Airlines says it resolved a system outage
summary: A memo from the union representing United Airlines pilots indicated the issue was with the airline's weight and balance calculation system.
story: United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" it was dealing with Monday afternoon, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said Monday evening. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights." The outage lasted about 90 minutes.
Earlier, United said it was "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights."

A memo from the union representing United Airlines pilots indicated the issue was with the airline's weight and balance calculation system, noting: "The Company cannot provide outbound flights with final weights."
A United spokesperson said there's no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity issue.

The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 715 delayed flights late Monday afternoon, although it was unclear how many of those were the result of the short-lived tech issue. About an hour and a half after the outage was resolved, it didn't appear that the brief outage was having a major impact on the carrier's flights, with delays and cancellations roughly in line with its competitors.

The disruption for the Chicago-based carrier came less than 24 hours after the Federal Aviation Administration said airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal following Friday's hourslong ground stop.
The United computer problem was just the latest high-profile technology meltdown.
Earlier in the day, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.

On Friday, the FAA ordered every U.S. flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email services. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: Top federal prosecutor in Houston accused of breaking ethics rules
summary: A nonprofit watchdog group filed an ethics complaint on Monday against the top federal prosecutor in Houston, alleging he has violated professional conduct rules by threatening to prosecute Democratic lawmakers.
story: A nonprofit watchdog group filed an ethics complaint on Monday against the top federal prosecutor in Houston, alleging he has violated professional conduct rules by threatening to prosecute several Democratic lawmakers for undertaking congressional oversight.

The complaint, filed by the Campaign for Accountability, asks the Texas state bar to investigate Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, over confrontational letters he sent to lawmakers including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

In those letters, Reitz cited public comments they made about their intentions to investigate the Trump administration and some of its backers, and insinuated that their comments may run afoul of several criminal civil rights laws.
He also ordered them to preserve all their records, a step that prosecutors sometimes take ahead of a criminal investigation.

Reitz sent a similar letter on Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. He pointed to several comments by Garcia vowing intense investigations into the Trump administration, including an election night statement encouraging people to "lawyer up," which Reitz called "little more than a call for political punishment against American citizens and businesses."

The letters from Reitz came after White House counsel Will Scharf warned Garcia last week that some congressional investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," and if lawmakers issue "unlawful subpoenas," the executive branch may launch investigations of its own.
Blumenthal replied to Reitz with his own letter, in which he ordered Reitz to preserve his own records, and said that Reitz's "implied threat of an investigation is baseless."
CBS News has reached out to Warren's and Garcia's offices for comment.
In the ethics complaint, the Campaign for Accountability asks the Texas state bar to investigate Reitz over possible violations of three different rules.

One such rule prohibits prosecutors from threatening to bring charges not supported by probable cause, while another rule prohibits lawyers from taking actions that serve "no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay or burden" someone else.
A third rule, meanwhile, prohibits attorneys from committing a serious crime. The complaint suggests that Reitz may be unlawfully obstructing a congressional inquiry.

"Officials who hold prosecutorial power have long been tempted to abuse it for political gain. A federal prosecutor's threat to bring criminal charges against United States Senators for conducting oversight strikes at the separation of powers and at public confidence in the fair administration of justice," the group wrote in its complaint.
"If left unaddressed, Mr. Reitz's conduct signals to every prosecutor that the threat of criminal process may be wielded against those who investigate the executive branch," it added.
In a statement, Reitz called the complaint "harassing" and "frivolous."

"I will continue my preliminary inquiry unfazed to determine whether certain members of Congress have unlawfully stepped outside the legitimate legislative purpose of their planned committee activities, and to ensure Americans' constitutional rights are protected. I'll always do the right thing by following the facts and the law," he said.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department called the complaint "nothing more than selective barfare against an administration official, which is a dangerous and illegitimate tactic."
"Oversight is not a license to threaten private citizens for exercising their First Amendment rights," the spokesperson added.
It is not clear exactly why a U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas has been targeting lawmakers from other states over their comments about oversight investigations.
Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at a press conference last week that "any office" could investigate this type of matter.
At the same time, however, he also told reporters there were "no ongoing criminal investigations into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said."

title: New James Bond is announced after rampant speculation
summary: After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced who the new 007 will be.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond.
He will be the seventh actor to play the role since the first Bond film, "Dr. No," was released in 1962.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The naming of Pattinson comes five years after the beloved franchise's last film, 2021's "No Time to Die," which marked the first time in Bond's 64-year history on the silver screen to end with the character's death.
But 007 will be reborn in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve. It will be the first since Amazon MGM took over the franchise.
For months, fans had been debating the merits of other potential 007s, including names like Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists.

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."

Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
The British royal family responded to the news on social media, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Now in the Bond role, Pattinson follows in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.

title: U.S. loses measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, researchers with knowledge of the decision confirmed to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. The agency is set to hold a news conference on Tuesday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.

But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading. "They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.
Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities.

"It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50."

"I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before."
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.

There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles."

title: "Tiger team" formed to head off another nationwide ground stop
summary: Members of the new tiger team include officials from the FAA, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, Defense Department and Transportation Department.
story: The White House has organized a "tiger team" to work on preventing another incident like the one that caused the nationwide ground stop last week, U.S. officials told CBS News.

Members of the team include officials from the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, Defense Department and Transportation Department. A tiger team is a small group of experts or specialists who work together on solving a specific problem that isn't easily addressed by normal operations.
The tiger team's first meeting was held Monday at the White House, one of the sources said.

The four-hour ground stop just after 3:30 p.m. last Friday caused the cancellation of thousands of flights and occurred while 3,500 flights were in the air. A preliminary investigation by the FAA indicated that a router that was being replaced in Arkansas was the cause of the problem.

In September, the Government Accountability Office issued a report analyzing the Transportation Department's effort to modernize the air traffic controller systems. It found that the "FAA has made progress implementing this initiative, but it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is not ruling out the possibility of another ground stop as the system continues to be updated. Asked about the GAO's report, Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday, "We are going, I think, at the right speed. We have to get off old network, old telecom."

The GAO also said the FAA lacks an overall cost estimate and "master schedule for related projects," and warned that without them, the FAA "could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems." Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion to make the necessary updates.
"Let's finish the job. Let's not see what happened on Friday. Let's not let it happen again," he told "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan.
Trump administration officials have blamed the problem on the FAA's antiquated technology, and have pressed lawmakers to approve more funding to modernize the air traffic control system.
President Trump told reporters the outage was caused by "very, very old equipment that had a heart attack."

Intelligence agencies preliminarily ruled out any nefarious activity on Friday after they didn't find any concerning chatter or pings, CBS News previously reported. But key questions still remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:58 p.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Lindsay Clancy to be retried on first-degree murder charges in March
summary: Prosecutors plan to retry Lindsay Clancy on first-degree murder charges, after her first Massachusetts murder trial ended in a mistrial.
story: Prosecutors plan to retry Lindsay Clancy on first-degree murder charges, after her first Massachusetts murder trial ended in a mistrial. The judge set a jury trial date for March 29, 2027.

Clancy was back in Plymouth Superior Court Monday morning as prosecutors addressed how they plan to proceed with her case in what was a brief but tense hearing. The commonwealth argued for a later trial date in May, citing other cases on the docket, but Judge William Sullivan, who is retiring in June 2027, was firm in seeking a March date.

Clancy was charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. In her first trial, Clancy's attorney admitted she killed 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, but argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.
Prosecutors said Clancy knew right from wrong and planned to strangle her children. The jury ended up deadlocked and a mistrial was declared on Sept. 4.
Judge Sullivan has already made a number of rulings since the last hearing in the case on Nov. 9, when he denied Clancy's motion to dismiss the murder charges.

Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz has the power to decide to retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges again, which would require another jury trial. Cruz, who was not in court Monday, could also have tried Clancy on a lesser charge, such as second-degree murder or manslaughter.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington has said in the past that he would never accept a plea deal that puts her in jail at all. If Clancy was re-tried on lesser charges she would have had the choice to have either a judge or a jury decide the outcome of this case.

Reddington said Monday he plans to once again request that the trial is split in two - one trial to prove guilt and another to prove her mental state at the time. That request was denied by Judge Sullivan last time.

"It's not guilty. They still have to prove that their investigation - using the term loosely - proved that she's guilty," Reddington said. "The jury then has to look at the issue of criminal responsibility or lack thereof, which is very, very strong for the defense."
WBZ-TV legal analyst Jennifer Roman said the prosecution's choice to pursue first-degree murder charges again does not come as a surprise.

"They came out pretty strongly after the first trial that they wanted justice for these three children, and the prosecution has made it clear that justice for them is a conviction on first-degree murder," she said.
Roman said the prosecution "needs to do a better job of telling their narrative this time around."

"I think that's where they fell short the first time and it hurt them ultimately when we had this hung jury," she said. "I think they really need to be clear as to what the theory of their case is, right from the outset."
Finding another jury for Clancy's second trial will not be easy, Roman said.

"This has gotten national, worldwide coverage. Everybody has heard of this case, even if they didn't follow the trial, they've certainly heard about it now," she said. "I think we are going to see an extended jury empanelment period of time for them to get the 14 or 15 members of that jury pool."
The next status hearing in the case is scheduled for Dec. 30.

title: Kalshi to start offering stock and ETF trading in coming months
summary: The announcement follows Kalshi's acquisition of a New York-based broker, FB Securities, in July.
story: Kalshi plans to enable customers of the prediction market to trade stocks and exchange-traded funds, a person familiar with the matter confirmed.
The company expects to roll out the services later this year, following its July acquisition of the New York-based broker FB Securities, which will facilitate stock trading on Kalshi.
The Wall Street Journal was the first to report Kalshi's plan.
Kalshi's platform allows people to bet on the outcomes of sports, political elections, weather and many other events. The expansion aligns with the company's push to diversify its offerings.

In May, Kalshi began allowing users to trade cryptocurrency perpetual futures and later expanded its offerings to include precious metal perpetual futures in September. Perpetuals are contracts with no expiration date that allow traders to speculate on the price of an asset without owning the underlying asset. The platform also launched perpetuals for dozens of individual stocks earlier this month.

Kalshi, which skyrocketed in popularity during the 2024 presidential election, has been at the center of an ongoing regulatory battle. The platform is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, an independent federal agency. But multiple states allege the sports contracts it offers amount to a form of illegal gambling and should be regulated at the state level.
Experts say the legal battle is likely to reach the Supreme Court.

title: Tennessee names new corrections chief after botched executions
summary: Josh Smith has been appointed to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee following the botched execution of Christa Pike last month.
story: Josh Smith, who unexpectedly left his role as deputy director of the Bureau of Prisons in August, was appointed Monday to lead the Department of Corrections in Tennessee.
Smith, a pardoned drug offender, was named to the position by Republican Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn.

"Josh brings a distinctive combination of executive leadership, firsthand correctional experience, and an understanding of the challenges facing our prison system," Blackburn said in her announcement. "He has demonstrated the ability to lead large organizations, make difficult decisions, and tackle longstanding problems."
Smith said in a statement he is honored to have been selected.

"Tennessee's correctional system faces significant challenges, including staffing shortages, institutional safety, and the need to strengthen leadership throughout the organization," he said. "I believe we can address these challenges by empowering our employees, establishing clear expectations, developing leaders, and maintaining an unwavering commitment to public safety."
Smith is succeeding interim Director Christopher Hansen, who has been in office since Frank Strada resigned early last month following the botched execution of Christa Pike.

Pike was the first female inmate scheduled to be executed by the state of Tennessee in 200 years. All executions following Pike's were stayed by Gov. Bill Lee. The lethal drug injection of pentobarbital left Pike on a ventilator with her arms blistered and bruised, her attorneys alleged.

Her lawyers said in a court filing that Department of Corrections employees did not seem to realize that the IV was not placed correctly into Pike's veins, or that they were blown, allowing the lethal drug to enter her body.

Pike's botched execution follows the failed execution of Tony Carruthers, who was set to be executed in May. Lee granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve after corrections staff spent more than an hour trying — and failing — to find a vein for the IV line for the lethal drug.
Blackburn has called for the state to explore alternative means of execution, such as the electric chair. There are 40 inmates on death row in Tennessee.

Smith was widely seen as an unconventional choice to serve as the No. 2 official at the Bureau of Prisons. He had a criminal record himself, after having pleaded guilty in 1998 to conspiring to possess and distribute cocaine and marijuana and serving a five-year sentence in a BOP prison camp in Kentucky.
He was later pardoned by President Trump, and he sought to use his prior experience as an incarcerated offender to press for reforms inside the federal prison system.
His approach to the job, however, led to disagreements among BOP staff, many of whom viewed him as caring more about the inmate population than employees.

Smith abruptly resigned from his post at the BOP in August, with some current and former BOP employees telling CBS News that there have been a number of questions raised about several government contracts awarded during his tenure as deputy director.

One such contract, for instance, was awarded to a Texas-based company called Securus Technologies to provide inmates with tablets that it said would be used to help facilitate academic coursework, career training, access to rehabilitation and healthcare information.
The contract was later canceled, however, after several competing companies filed a grievance challenging the decision, according to a BOP letter obtained by CBS News.

Another business deal previously reported by CBS News, meanwhile, involved a partnership with a startup company to sell nicotine pouches to inmates. That deal was scrapped after it came to light that the pouches were not authorized by the Food and Drug Administration.

In a prior interview with CBS News, Smith denied having any involvement in some of the controversial contracts. He said at the time of his resignation that his main goals while serving as deputy director were to overhaul staffing and strive to improve rehabilitative services for prisoners to help them prepare for their return to society.

"I believe we should really care about what kind of people we are turning back out into our neighborhoods," he said in August. "I'm a tough-on-crime person, but I'm restorative in nature because they're going to be my neighbor."

In response to Smith's appointment, Kit Thomas, co-counsel on the long-running challenge by Tennessee death row prisoners to the state's lethal injection protocol, said, "We are hopeful that Commissioner-designate Josh Smith will bring a renewed commitment to transparency and accountability at the Tennessee Department of Correction.
"We urge him to prioritize implementing the recommendations of the 2022 and 2026 independent Butler Snow investigations, including meaningful revisions to Tennessee's lethal injection protocol."

title: High court rejects challenge to Maryland gun ban in sensitive places
summary: The Supreme Court left in place a lower court decision that upheld the measure banning guns in sensitive places.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday turned away a challenge to Maryland laws that prohibit firearms in sensitive places like schools, parks and government buildings.
In rejecting the appeal from a group of Maryland residents and gun rights groups, the high court leaves in place a lower court decision that upheld the rules.

Justice Clarence Thomas said that while he agrees with the Supreme Court's decision not to hear the case, he is "skeptical" of the constitutionality of sensitive-place restrictions and urged the court to consider the scope of states' authority to ban firearms in those locations in a more "narrowly focused case."

"I harbor serious doubts that our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation supports many of these sweeping restrictions," he wrote in a statement. "In an appropriate case, this Court should consider whether particular sensitive-place laws are consistent with the right to public carry."
The Supreme Court last year struck down a Hawaii law that required concealed-carry permit holders to receive permission before bringing their firearms onto private property open to the public.

At issue in the case was a set of Maryland laws that limit the places where guns can be carried in public.  The state prohibits firearms from being brought on school property, at public demonstrations and on public transit, as well as in parks, museums and casinos.

Another set of limits was enacted in 2023, in the wake of the Supreme Court's landmark 2022 decision that recognized for the first time that the Second Amendment protects the right to carry a gun outside the home. Under the new restrictions, people are prohibited from carrying firearms at daycare and medical facilities, government buildings or other places where the public gathers for "entertainment, educational enrichment or other collective social pursuits."
On the same day Maryland's latest restrictions were signed into law, two sets of plaintiffs filed lawsuits arguing they violated the Second Amendment. The suits targeted 10 categories of places.

The two cases were consolidated, and a federal district court declined to block the limits on museums, healthcare facilities, public transit, state parks, entertainment venues, school grounds and government buildings. But the district court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs as to public demonstrations and places that sell alcohol for on-site consumption.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit went on to rule that all of the challenged restrictions are consistent with the Second Amendment. The appeals court applied the Supreme Court's new test for evaluating the constitutionality of gun regulations, which it laid out in its 2022 decision. Under that framework, the government must show that a firearms restriction is consistent with the nation's historical tradition.

In addition to pointing to historical analogues of some of Maryland's regulations, the 4th Circuit said the Supreme Court has twice, in decisions from 2008 and 2010, asserted that laws forbidding guns in government buildings and on school grounds are allowed.

The Maryland residents and gun rights groups appealed to the Supreme Court and argued that its intervention is needed to help lower courts better define the historical limits on the right to have guns in public as more and more states are enacting location-specific limits.

"The constitutionality of these so-called 'sensitive place' bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of" the Supreme Court's 2022 decision, they wrote in their petition. "If, as Maryland maintains and the Fourth Circuit below held, the right to carry a firearm 'in public' does not include public locations that are owned by the government, or where First Amendment protected activity is being carried out, or where people go to eat and to drink or gather for amusement and recreation, then it is hard to know what the right to carry a firearm 'in public' actually protects."

But Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown argued that the state's sensitive-place laws are consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearms regulation, and therefore constitutional. He noted that there is a "rich American tradition" of barring guns in certain locations, including those that are "confined and crowded."
"This Court endorsed such 'longstanding' bans in schools, legislative assemblies, polling places, and courthouses, while recognizing that this list was non-exhaustive," Brown wrote in a filing.

In the years since the Supreme Court laid out its new test for determining the legality of gun regulations, it has been confronted with a number of challenges to longstanding firearms laws. In 2024, the Supreme Court upheld a federal law that prohibits people subject to domestic violence restraining orders from having guns.

In an opinion authored by Chief Justice John Roberts, the eight-justice majority said the "appropriate analysis" under its new historical tradition standard "involves considering whether the challenged regulation is consistent with the principles that underpin our regulatory tradition."
Then, in its last term, a unanimous Supreme Court said the Second Amendment does not allow the government to prosecute a person who is an occasional marijuana user.

title: Epstein's death may not have been suicide, new analysis suggests
summary: Forensics expert Dr. Michael Freeman says multiple images and overlooked details about Jeffrey Epstein's death contradict the conclusion that he died by suicide.
story: Warning: This article and video contain graphic images that may be disturbing.
Across the political spectrum, a large chunk of Americans believe, despite a lack of evidence, that Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide.
Now one forensics expert, working with photos and files provided by Epstein's brother, is weighing in to contend that this suspicion might be right.

Dr. Michael Freeman, who is editor-in-chief of the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine, spent months reviewing never-before-published autopsy records provided to him and CBS News by Epstein's brother. The 2019 ruling by the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner was that Epstein died by suicide. But Freeman has concluded that Epstein's death was more likely a homicide.

Freeman — who worked with Anders Eriksson, a professor of forensic medicine at Umea University in Sweden, and Itiel Dror, a researcher specializing in identifying bias in forensic decision making — presented their findings Monday in London. Freeman said he believes that in August 2019 the world's most notorious sex abuser was likely attacked and killed by another person.

"The injuries that were documented by the medical examiner were not consistent with the suicidal hanging. And the injuries that were attributed to something other than potentially a physical struggle or assault were just overlooked," Freeman told CBS News, based on his review of the autopsy records, photos and a biomedical reconstruction he produced.

The report is the second by an outside forensic expert to question the official findings of suicide. In 2020, Epstein's brother hired forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden to look into the death, as first reported by "60 Minutes." At the time, Baden said injuries to Epstein's neck raised doubts about the official ruling. He told "60 Minutes" the evidence he saw pointed more to murder than suicide.

Freeman's report was rejected for publication from an academic journal, he acknowledged. He said reviewers for the journal thought it wasn't appropriate to criticize a medical examiner's findings in a peer-reviewed publication. Freeman plans to resubmit, he said.
Freeman, a professor of forensic medicine, said he was struck by the first image he examined, depicting the right side of Epstein's upper body and face, with ligature wounds visible on his neck.
"When I saw this photograph, my first reaction was that that is a very unusual looking injury for a hanging on the neck," Freeman said.

Freeman has testified as a forensic expert in high-profile court cases and was a member of the Maryland attorney general's audit team that reviewed dozens of in-custody deaths last year.  Still, forensic pathology is not an exact science. Credible experts often interpret the same evidence very differently. Neck injuries from hanging or strangulation can be especially ambiguous. And Epstein's death investigation was marked by added uncertainty because of a cascade of blunders in the hours, days and weeks after his body was discovered in his Manhattan federal jail cell.

The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner — which conducted the autopsy on Aug. 11, 2019, the day after Epstein was found dead — declined an interview request, and did not reply directly to Freeman's findings when pressed by CBS News.
"Our office stands by its determination," a spokesperson for the medical examiner said.

There has been support for that finding. In June, The New York Times conducted an investigation that it said relied on tens of thousands of pages of newly released documents, as well as Epstein's own notes handwritten in jail. That report said there were indications Epstein was intent on ending his own life. And the newspaper reported that, of the forensics experts they interviewed, "almost none of them believed that his manner of death  — suicide or homicide — could be conclusively settled based on the medical evidence alone."
"That's not what suicidal hangings do"
Freeman believes the official investigation missed key details.
"The injury pattern was described as a sloped or as a peaked injury that was a perfect description for a hanging. But that's not what we saw when we saw the photos," Freeman said.
While one mark fit that description, he noticed a second mark in the ligature wounds on Epstein's neck, beneath and angled differently than the mark above it.

"There is no mechanism to produce a second mark that would be lower. Even if the ligature was tied with two loops, both loops would go up to the point where it was tied because that's the anchor point," Freeman said.

Asked if the two markings, present on each side of Epstein's neck, could have been indicative of him stopping and starting — trying twice to kill himself — Freeman said available research into suicidal hanging indicates that's unlikely. Epstein would have had to make "a false start that was strong enough to break his hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage and give him a deep abrasion and then maintain consciousness," Freeman said.
It's an explanation that doesn't make sense, he said.

"That's not what suicidal hangings do," Freeman said. "The body becomes unconscious and then it is the weight of the body that produces the abrasion, not any kind of running jump at it. That opportunity really isn't there. That's not a realistic scenario for any hanging described in any of the literature throughout the world."

None of the prison guards on duty when Epstein died spoke to medical examiner investigators, according to Justice Department records. Some of them falsified records and lied about their activities the night before and morning of Epstein's death. Corrections officer Michael Thomas is credited with finding Epstein's body. He only agreed to be interviewed by investigators after he was charged with crimes two years later.

There's no indication that the medical examiner's office revisited its determination after Thomas agreed to share his account. Freeman, however, based his reconstruction of the scene of Epstein's death on Thomas' later description, in which he said he found Epstein hanging from a bedpost.
Freeman constructed a biomechanical analysis, or series of three-dimensional models, based on Thomas' description of the scene, as well as wounds and abrasions visible in images of Epstein's body.
"The biomechanical analysis was designed to be able to map the injuries on a model that was…as close to the anatomy and size and shape of Epstein as possible," Freeman said.

The 3-D model allowed Freeman to test the suicide hypothesis. What the model showed is that some of the abrasions and injuries visible on Epstein's neck were indicative of suicidal hanging, but some on his neck, and elsewhere on his body including an injury to his shoulder, weren't.

"We have too many other injuries that are not explained by any suicidal hanging. Because I don't care how this guy is found, where did these other injuries come from?" Freeman asked. "How do you get the deep soft tissue hemorrhage in his left shoulder? How do you get the injury on his back?"
His conclusion will add fuel to the fire of conspiracy theories that have consumed much of the popular discourse around Epstein's death.
The alternate theory: Strangulation
"The alternative scenario is that there was a strangulation that occurred," Freeman said. In particular, horizontal marks on Epstein's neck point to ligature being pulled from behind him, he said.

Epstein's cell was littered with piles of torn orange fabric, the bedding used in cells at the Manhattan Correctional Center. Freeman says an image shows one knotted fabric that he believes appears to support the strangulation theory.

"That is a double knotted, looped, narrow ligature that was found in the cell that was dropped in a corner near the desk. And if we put those together in a format in which the knot, one of these knots, is applied as pressure to produce this irregular abrasion at the back of the neck, we actually have a fairly good explanation for all the injuries," Freeman said.
He also noticed what he claims are signs of an assault and struggle, including blunt force trauma to the face and the left shoulder.

"And we see what appeared to be consistent with fingernail marks above the ligature," Freeman said. "And if you put it all together, it is most consistent with a homicidal strangulation from behind using a narrow knotted fabric ligature."
The fabric Freeman believes matches Epstein's injuries wasn't collected for the medical examiner.

"What you see in this front view of the ligature pattern is that it is ragged looking," Freeman said, referring to the markings on Epstein's neck. "It is segmented looking. It's not smooth. This certainly would not be consistent with the noose that was taken from the room."

Epstein's death drew global headlines and promises from the top levels of the Justice Department that it would be among the most scrutinized inmate deaths in history. Instead, it was marked by a series of failures.
A flawed investigation?
The issues with Epstein's death scene began almost immediately on Aug. 10, 2019.
Thomas reported finding Epstein's body, cold to the touch, around 6:30 a.m.
"The fact that to touch, Epstein's body was cold, would indicate he had been dead for at least a few hours," Freeman said.

Epstein's body was moved out of the cell within minutes of being discovered, preventing accurate photography of the scene when investigators first arrived that day. The cell was never sealed off for forensic investigation, and much of the evidence at the scene wasn't properly preserved, a 2025 CBS News investigation found.

To make matters worse, most of the closed-circuit cameras in Epstein's wing of the prison were not functioning. And Justice Department documents show investigators who reviewed footage from the nearest working camera — one that looked over a common area connecting multiple tiers of cells — did not follow up on some details, including an unexplained orange blur seen ascending a staircase toward Epstein's block the night of his death.

It took two years for federal investigators to interview Thomas, who had been charged with lying and falsifying prison records, and provided a statement in exchange for leniency. It took another year for those same investigators to talk to the medical examiner who examined Epstein's body.

And Freeman said the medical examiner may have misinterpreted key details on Epstein's body. She noted that there were no broken fingernails or defensive wounds on the hands. An abrasion on Epstein's arm was probably from convulsing during hanging, the medical examiner said.

"When she talks about the fact that there's only a little scratch on the arm, she completely overlooks the fact that there was deep intramuscular hemorrhage in the left shoulder that was undoubtedly due to blunt force trauma," Freeman said.
To Freeman, the mystery of Epstein's death is not how he died, but who killed him.

"I'm comfortable saying that's a mystery. Who did it? Exactly how they did it. What happened? All the other things. Why the cameras [were] off? All a mystery, yes," Freeman said. "Was this a suicide? Not a mystery."

title: Hawley, Durbin introduce Roblox safety bill ahead of hearing
summary: The legislation would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration.
story: Missouri Republican Josh Hawley and Illinois Democrat Dick Durbin are introducing new legislation targeting sexual abuse on Roblox and online gaming platforms, CBS News has learned.

The legislation, titled the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, would allow families of individuals harmed by tech products to take their claims to court even if they agreed to the company's terms of service for private arbitration. Roblox is being sued by dozens of families and state attorneys general who claim online predators have been able to groom, extort and exploit kids they meet on the platform.

The measure is being rolled out ahead of an inaugural congressional hearing Tuesday into the popular gaming portal. The hearing, chaired by Hawley, will feature witness testimony from two abuse survivors and a pair of experts. Roblox CEO Dave Baszucki was invited to testify but has declined to appear.

"I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators," Hawley said in a statement. "This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox's practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online."

The bill would close loopholes to ensure a child's rights aren't limited in click-through agreements, allow class-action lawsuits and let survivors and families choose whether to bring a claim in public court or through confidential arbitration.

"In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have," said Durbin. "Therefore, an 'agreement' buried in the terms of service shouldn't limit a child's or family's rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I'm proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won't stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law."
In August, Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation by the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism into child safety on Roblox.

"Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny," the Senators wrote in a letter to the company at the time.

Roblox has 138 million daily active users, ranging in age from five to over 25, according to its latest shareholder letter released at the end of October. The company currently faces nearly 200 lawsuits in federal court and has reached settlements with at least six states over online child safety issues.

This month, Roblox chief safety officer Matt Kaufman wrote that the company continues to partner with law enforcement and "aggressively look for bad behavior and report it through the appropriate channels."

Last year, the company announced it would strengthen its age verification protections for minors. Roblox CEO David Baszucki described the guardrails in an interview with "CBS Mornings" as "what we believe will become the gold standard for safety and civility on the internet."
This story published first on CBS News at 1:58 p.m. on Nov. 16, 2026.

title: Nvidia's board of directors opposes restoring Jensen Huang as CEO
summary: Nvidia's board isn't considering rehiring Jensen Huang as CEO despite an online petition that has drawn more than 180,000 signatures.
story: Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, according to a source directly familiar with their thinking.

Huang stepped down from Nvidia on Thursday amid an investigation into his extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. His departure from the chipmaker he co-founded more than three decades ago came within days of the relationship becoming public.

At the same time, thousands of Nvidia employees and technology executives, including Elon Musk, have signed a petition asking the chipmaker to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, with the organizers arguing that he "may have been forced out without due process and without even a few days to make his case."

The push to reinstate Huang comes as the company named Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as its interim CEO and said it would seek a permanent replacement. Nvidia's stock has tumbled in the past week amid the controversy, chopping more than $500 billion from its market valuation.

"For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," according to the petition, which described itself as an "independent, volunteer campaign" that is "not affiliated with, authorized by or endorsed by Nvidia Corporation or Jensen Huang."

The petition added, "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes ... That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now."

The petition has gained more than 180,000 signatures, including from what it says are more than 9,000 Nvidia employees representing about one in five company workers. Executives, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, have also signed the petition, according to its website.
"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," Musk wrote on X on Friday.
At the same time, Huang is said to be discussing his return to Nvidia with allies, the Financial Times reported on Sunday.
President Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.
Long-shot bid

Huang's return to Nvidia is a long shot, according to Wall Street analysts. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for the chipmaker to hire its next CEO from outside the company, arguing that the company needs a major leadership shakeup amid questions about whether sales of its chips to companies in Singapore and other Asian countries circumvented U.S. export controls and ended up in China.
"We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday.

Given Bessent's push for Nvidia to look outside the company for its next leader, Huang's return appears unlikely, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli, who told investors in a research note that the "odds of him being reinstated seem quite low."
Dan Ives, a well-known tech stock analyst at Yorkville Ives, downplayed the likelihood that Huang would resume his duties at Nvidia.

"Any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles," he said in a note to investors. "For the company, the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette [Kress]."
Prediction market users aren't giving much credence to the idea of Huang's return, with Kalshi traders assigning only a 10% chance of the former CEO returning to that role.
Nvidia shares are poised to continue their decline on Monday, with the stock down $2.39, or 1.5%, to $160.46 in early trading.
Investors will be tuning into Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon to hear more about the company's guidance in the wake of Huang's departure.

"The critical question in the immediate term is what management has to say about the 70% sales growth guidance for next fiscal year — does Nvidia reiterate confidence in that or withdraw it given uncertainty about export rules in Washington," Crisafulli said.

title: Trump says he "would not mind" if Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang
summary: According to a source directly familiar with the Nvidia board's thinking, the company is not interested bringing Jensen Huang back to the company as CEO or in any other position.
story: Washington — President Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, after he resigned last week amid allegations of two affairs. The president said he doesn't know if Alice Huang, one of the women allegedly involved with Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy.
"I would not mind. I would not mind that," the president told reporters Monday as he departed for a trip to the Philippines and China, and he said "that certainly isn't a bad idea."

He also floated the name of the former Apple CEO as a possible Huang replacement at Nvidia, saying, "I like, you know, I do have the name of Tim Cook." Mr. Trump added, "But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement — I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."
According to a source directly familiar with the Nvidia board's thinking, the company is not interested bringing Jensen Huang back to the company as CEO or in any other position.

Mr. Trump also said that the U.S. has banned Nvidia from selling the "important chips, the modern-day chips," in particular, the most powerful AI chip in the world, the company's Blackwell chip. And just before the president left, the Trump administration announced a new rule that's intended to curb efforts by China to bypass the restrictions by remotely accessing the chips through data centers in third countries.

The president also dismissed concerns that Alice Huang may be spying for China. She's a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a former gaming company that is now an AI infrastructure and cloud computing company and is one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers.

"Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Mr. Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
The president said he may speak with Xi about Alice Huang and whether she was a spy. Mr. Trump and Xi will be meeting in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
Last week, Attorney General Todd Blanche said he "certainly" hasn't said Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

Elon Musk, tech executives and Nvidia employees have signed a petition calling for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. The former CEO resigned last week amid reports of two extramarital affairs — one with Alice Huang and one with an Nvidia employee.

title: How will Nvidia stock fare after Huang's exit? Data provides clues.
summary: Other companies whose CEOs have left due to personal conduct issues often lag financial markets for a year, research shows.
story: Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as Nvidia's CEO last week dealt a hammer blow to the chipmaker's stock price, vaporizing more than $550 billion in its market value. If history is any guide, meanwhile, the company's shares could be in for a rough road.

Other companies whose chief executives departed due to personal conduct reasons have underperformed the S&P 500's average return in the year following the executive's exit, according to financial services firm StoneX.

For example, shares of HP (formerly Hewlett-Packard) tumbled nearly 29% in the 12 months after former CEO Mark Hurd resigned in 2010 for concealing a relationship with a former contractor, while the S&P 500 rose 9% over that period.

"Removing a CEO over personal conduct has more often than not been followed by a difficult year for shareholders," StoneX said in a recent report that analyzed the stock performance of 12 major companies, including Boeing, CNN and McDonald's, after their CEO exited under a cloud.

Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares plunged the following day and are now down more than 30% from a recent peak on Oct. 6.

Of the companies StoneX analyzed, seven lagged the average S&P 500 returns the year after their CEO left. Cody Acree, an equity research analyst at StoneX, thinks Nvidia shares could also struggle as the chip giant searches for a new leader and amid uncertainty over the AI sector.

Already, several Wall Street analysts have downgraded their price forecasts for Nvidia's stock, citing the leadership vacuum left by Huang's departure and questions about Nvidia's future. Truist, an American bank holding company, lowered its price target last week from $346 per share to $174. Yorkville Ives and Co., led by noted tech analyst Dan Ives, also reduced its estimate from $300 to $225.
In morning activity on Wall Street, Nvidia shares were down 2.1% to $159.31.

Of the companies StoneX analyzed, five outperformed the S&P 500, according to StoneX. However, those examples may offer "little comfort" to Nvidia, given that those companies had a successor lined up to replace the departing CEO.
"They had heirs apparent," Acree told CBS News. "They had people that were kind of ready to take the position."

In Nvidia's case, Huang's sudden departure has made for a more chaotic succession plan. The company's board tapped Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Wall Street analysts said the company's board will be eager to find someone with the dealmaking prowess and technical know-how to lead the world's leading chipmaker.
How much will Nvidia change?

In the meantime, Nvidia will have to reassure investors about who will handle responsibilities that once rested with Huang, including engaging with officials in Washington and managing relationships with Nvidia's customers and partners, StoneX said in its report.

Nvidia will also have to assuage concerns about possible restructuring efforts, Acree added. Huang had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that kept him at the center of Nvidia's decision-making.
"If you come in with a more standard CEO, does he try to implement that structure that he's maybe more used to, or does he try to reproduce what Jensen already had in place?" Acree said.
Already, some are calling for Huang's return, with a petition to reinstate him garnering more than 170,000 signatures.

Nvidia also faces other challenges, including heightened competition in the chip industry and the possibility that the U.S. could tighten export controls on AI chips, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli.

Still, Nvidia retains powerful competitive advantages. The company already has a roadmap for chip production over the next two years created by Huang, Acree noted. Demand for Nvidia chips and related equipment is also expected to remain robust, given the rapid growth of AI services.
"There's still going to be demand that outstrips even that ability to supply for the next couple of years," Acree said.
The next major test for Nvidia will come on Tuesday, when the company is scheduled to announce its quarterly earnings.

title: Bodycam shows party with hundreds of teens, leading to charges for parents
summary: Police body camera footage captured a chaotic Virginia house party that led to charges for the parents of twin 13-year-old boys.
story: Police body camera footage captured a chaotic Virginia house party that led to charges for the parents of twin 13-year-old boys. Officers said as many as 300 people showed up to the party, where, they allege, there was underaged drinking and fireworks.
The twins' mother, Lisa Vaughan, 45, can be seen in the footage talking to a Fairfax County police officer who questioned her about the possible presence of alcohol.
"No, we haven't had any alcohol. We've been making sure," she told the officer, who proceeded to ask her: "Are you joking?"
Vaughan said she wasn't joking, and that she and her husband, Aubrey Vaughan, had "been making sure nobody has any backpacks or anything."
"You don't smell it in the air right now?" the officer asked. "No I don't smell anything in the air," she responded.

Suddenly, a loud bang and the sounds of cheering interrupted their exchange, which was recorded by the officer's body camera. Police headed toward what sounded like fireworks coming from the other side of the house.
As police made their way around the property, the mingling teenagers scattered, and officers could be heard telling them to "go home."

Aubrey Vaughan, 55, told CBS News he was expecting up to 50 guests at the party, which he and his wife hosted for their twins earlier this month. But, after the location went viral on Snapchat, hundreds showed up, including older teens.
"It was surprising to us that 9th-, 10th-, 11th- and 12th-grade kids just crashed our home, trespassing, unallowed, sneaking in from the egress areas and other areas that weren't allowed," he said.

Aubrey Vaughan also said the invitation that he and wife sent out ahead of the party specifically noted that guests could not bring alcohol or bags to their home. He said there was no alcohol in the Vaughan's home or backyard on the night of the event, and "no visible alcohol in any of the body cam footage."

He told CBS News he was in the backyard when officers arrived. "And when I first realized that we should have [shut the party down], it was just the massive influx of kids that we didn't, like bigger kids that we saw just coming to the front of our yard. And I was like, we've got to shut this down," he said.

The Vaughans turned themselves into police after the incident and have since been released on bond. They maintain their innocence. According to Fairfax County police, both were charged with contributing to the delinquency of a minor and maintaining a common nuisance.

title: Diesel prices dip below $6 a gallon for first time since September
summary: Diesel around the U.S. now averages $5.99 a gallon, down from a record high of $6.53 in September, according to AAA.
story: The national price of diesel in the U.S. fell below $6 a gallon on Monday, the first time it has been below that level in over two months.
Diesel now averages $5.99 a gallon, according to AAA, down from a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.

Diesel prices surged past $6 a gallon in September as the wars in Iran and Ukraine squeezed global refining capacity and disrupted oil flow. The run-up in prices rippled across the economy, increasing costs for the diesel-dependent transportation, construction and agriculture industries and keeping inflation elevated.
Prices ease as oil supplies stabilize
Diesel and gasoline prices have fallen in recent weeks after President Trump signaled he wouldn't escalate the war in Iran, according to Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy.
At the same time, the global oil market is also showing signs of stabilization.
"Oil prices slipped to start the week as expectations of a coming supply surplus outweighed fresh security incidents around the Strait of Hormuz," De Haan said in a report on Monday.
Brent crude, the international standard, traded on Monday at $93.56 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $86.72.
Last week, the International Energy Agency raised its oil production forecast, predicting a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the organization said in its November report.

While tanker attacks continue in the Strait of Hormuz, traffic through the strategically vital waterway has picked up. Shipments have largely returned to levels before the war erupted in late February, according to De Haan. Gasoline prices have also dropped, falling below $4 a gallon last week for the first time in nearly four months.
A brief reprieve?

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, said November is typically a good time to rebuild diesel inventory, given that demand in the agriculture sector fades after the summer. At the same time, demand for heating oil, also derived from crude oil, hasn't fully ramped up.
"It's too early for severe winter demand to remove diesel molecules for the heating oil business," he told CBS News in an email.
Kloza expects diesel and heating oil prices to ebb over the next six weeks, but warned that they could tick up around the new year as colder winter temperatures drive demand for heating oil.
"There is plenty to worry about between Christmas week and February 15 or so," he said.
