title: Supreme Court rejects case on Trump's bid to cut grants related to DEI
summary: Two federal agencies had moved to cancel grants to researchers at the University of California that they said did not align with President Trump's policies on DEI.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear a case involving the Trump administration's termination of grants awarded to University of California researchers that it said did not align with President Trump's priorities, including on diversity, equity and inclusion.

By turning away the appeal from the Trump administration, the Supreme Court leaves intact a lower court decision that found the cancellation of the millions in academic funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and National Science Foundation likely violated the First Amendment.

The Justice Department had warned that if the high court allowed the decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit to stand, as it now has done, it would clear the way for taxpayer dollars to go to research projects promoting DEI initiatives.

The case stems from the first days of Mr. Trump's second term, when he signed executive orders that instructed federal agencies to cancel grants related to certain topics, including DEI. The legal fight involves grants from the NEH and the NSF to University of California researchers, which the Trump administration terminated because they were not consistent with the president's priorities on DEI.

Lawyers for the University of California said that from January to June 2025, the Trump administration cut off more than $324 million in grants to that university system alone. They said the two agencies carried out Mr. Trump's executive orders on funding for DEI-related programs by conducting keyword searches of grant applications, and then canceled awards that used words like "diversity," "climate change" and "gender ideology."

Grant recipients began receiving letters informing them that their funding had been terminated in April 2025. Several months later, six researchers at the University of California who received grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, NSF and NEH filed a lawsuit and sought a court order requiring their grants to be reinstated.

A federal district court sided with the plaintiffs in a June 2025 decision and certified a provisional class covering University of California researchers who had grants terminated under Mr. Trump's executive orders targeting DEI-related initiatives.

U.S. District Judge Rita Lin said that the Trump administration had terminated the grants en masse for touching on issues it said were prohibited and ruled that the funding was likely terminated based on the perceived viewpoint expressed in the research. She ordered the Trump administration to reinstate grants from the NSF, NEH and EPA.
The 9th Circuit upheld the district court's preliminary injunction in May and agreed that the grant terminations likely violated the First Amendment's prohibition on viewpoint discrimination.

The Trump administration, it said, "has not merely exercised its power to choose the programs it funds but has instead terminated individual grants in existing programs based on the perceived viewpoints of individual speakers."

While the case proceeded, the plaintiffs reached a settlement related to the EPA grants, leaving only the awards from the NSF and NEH at issue. The Trump administration said there was approximately $59 million remaining on the grants, which will expire as late as November 2029.

title: Officials received years of warnings before FAA ground stop
summary: For years, audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns.
story: Government watchdogs have warned for years of the risk of technical failures involving decrepit air travel systems like the one that grounded all planes across the country on Friday, according to federal audits and past congressional testimony.

Audits flagged billions of dollars thrown at non-competitive contracts beset with delays, amid repeated technology breakdowns. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the fault that led to Friday's five-hour halt may trace back to one router that was supposed to be replaced in 2006.
"We're investigating that right now," Duffy said Sunday on CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." "This goes back decades."
One company that has been in charge of the aging telecommunications infrastructure for the last quarter-century is L3Harris.

The Federal Aviation Administration has poured billions of dollars into the company's contracts since 2020. A 2024 audit by the Office of the Inspector General found that since awarding the original contract in 2002, the FAA made 10 extensions that were "improperly authorized" (as well as one that was proper), adding 57 months and $1.5 billion in spending.

The inspector general warned the FAA "may be repetitively using these noncompetitive extensions for convenience and administrative ease," adding that it "risks paying more than the Agency should and receiving less than the best-quality results."

These concerns by government watchdogs can be traced back two decades. Just four years after Harris Corporation, now part of L3Harris, was awarded the contract in 2002 to modernize and operate the FAA's telecommunications infrastructure, an audit warned that the program was falling behind schedule. A follow-up report in 2008 identified continuing concerns about reliability problems that disrupted air traffic control operations.

A year later, in 2009, more than 800 flights were delayed after a telecommunications outage. The DOT IG investigated the incident and found that the FAA had failed to adequately oversee Harris Corporation and also had not developed sufficient safeguards for overseeing privately operated systems despite increasingly shifting more services to the private sector to reduce costs.

Despite these issues, the FAA awarded Harris another $291 million contract in 2012 to update its outdated air traffic control voice communications equipment. The project was ultimately terminated in 2018, after running into repeated delays and technical problems, with $160 million spent on the unsuccessful program.

Duffy acknowledged in a press conference following last week's outage that the government could not immediately move away from L3Harris, saying he was "stuck with L3Harris" until a new system could be built.

"Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us," Duffy said, as he raised questions about whether the outage was caused by contractor error or faulty equipment.

Eric Soskin, transport inspector general under the Biden Administration, told CBS News that some of the FAA's equipment was now so old that one manufacturer of replacement parts had been out of business for over a decade.

"When you have systems as old as the ones that we have in place now, the knowledge of how those systems work… may even have been lost to retirements or memory," he said. "If only we had succeeded in getting a full rollout of next-gen technologies a decade ago, I bet whatever the cause was here wouldn't have happened."
But a September report from the Office of the Inspector General also warned that moving ahead with upgrades too quickly could also cause disruptions.

L3Harris did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment regarding the inspector general's criticisms, but said in a statement on Saturday that the company is working "in close coordination with the FAA" and has completed 70% of the switch from old copper lines to fiber cables for the Agency's communications.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

Even as L3Harris faced scrutiny over its performance, the company spent millions seeking to influence federal policy, including efforts to secure additional funding for modernizing the infrastructure it has operated for more than two decades.

It has paid $23.9 million to lobbyists since 2020, including $2.51 million this year, according to Senate records. Disclosures show it lobbied Congress on FAA modernization funding every year. L3Harris has also lobbied the FAA directly.

Ballard Partners, which has had deep ties to the White House, has at times been among the lobbying firms it retained. Other firms employed lobbyists who previously worked on congressional appropriations committees that play a large role in decisions on FAA funding, the records show.

Last April, L3Harris penned a letter urging congressional leaders of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to advance an air traffic control modernization proposal that initially called for $15 billion in federal spending.

Two of the lawmakers addressed in the letter had previously received campaign contributions from the company's political action committee, including Chairman Rep. Sam Graves, a Missouri Republican, whose campaign received $10,000 during the 2021-2022 election cycle, and Democrat Rick Larsen, of Washington, whose campaign received $5,000 during the 2023-2024 cycle.

Four days after the letter was sent, Graves publicly unveiled the committee's proposal to provide billions in additional funding for air traffic control modernization. Congress ultimately approved $12.5 billion for FAA modernization as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including $4.75 billion for telecommunications upgrades.
Graves and Larsen did not respond to CBS News' requests for comment.

In testimony to the House Appropriations Committee this March, Deputy Inspector General Mitch Behm cited a repeated pattern across 50 audits of cost increases and schedule overruns, largely blaming a failure to nail down design decisions and a lack of a clear plan.
Other government watchdogs have also been calling out crumbling infrastructure around aviation communications.

In 2024, the Government Accountability Office found 51 of the FAA's 138 air traffic systems unsustainable, citing outdated functionality and missing spare parts, with 54 more potentially unsustainable.

The Transportation Department says it is putting its $12.5 billion to good use, including replacing handwritten paper systems with electronic ones at 25 control towers, upgrading five facilities from using floppy disks, and modernizing 469 tower radios, but says that the funds are narrowly allotted by Congress with little room to choose what it spends on.

Soskin told CBS News that Friday's outage "confirms the importance of pushing ahead with the technology upgrades," but added that "FAA and DOT need to supervise these projects carefully, and make sure they are getting highly capable systems that are reliable, and that are procured properly so that they're good value for taxpayers."

"The transfer needs to be handled carefully," the former inspector general said. "It may be that some disruptions like this are unavoidable, in which case FAA and other leaders need to do a good job of explaining to travelers why they happen, and why the end result is worth the trouble."

title: Trump heads to Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
summary: President Trump set off on a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit.
story: Washington — President Trump set off Monday for a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
Ahead of his departure, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first between the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

The president will first head to the Philippines, where the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit is being held. Mr. Trump will meet with Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking. Mr. Trump is not expected to speak about the 4 1/2-year war in Ukraine during the summit.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.

Both Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

title: U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
summary: Britain's government will consider adopting staggered ages for sexual consent in the wake of "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men."
story: London —  Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.

British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.

Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.

Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

There is plenty of precedent: In eight U.S. states —   Idaho, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota and Florida, where Brand was living before he was jailed — the age of consent varies depending on the age gap between the two people.

In Idaho, for example, if one person is under 16 and the other is 18 or older, or if the victim is 16 or 17 years old and the perpetrator is at least three years older, it is classed as rape. "Lewd contact with a child" younger than 16 is a crime regardless of the perpetrator's age.
In most U.S. states, the age of consent has a "close-in-age" exception for people under 18 who engage in mutually consentual sexual acts.

In Canada, where the age of consent is 16, the staggered-age system includes more detailed, age-dependent exemptions. For people aged 12-13, the partner must be less than two years older; age 14-15, the partner must be less than five years older, and between 16-17, people are generally seen as able to give consent, unless their sexual partner is in a position of trust or authority toward them.
Austria, Belgium, France, Ireland and South Africa also have close-in-age exemptions.
Mia Latter, now 37, has accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in Britain.

Latter, whose allegations were not part of the case that saw Brand convicted last week of raping and sexually assaulting other women, abandoned her anonymity as an accuser of the celebrity in an interview published over the weekend by The Sunday Times. She told the newspaper she was speaking out to help "protect teenagers from being groomed by older men or women."

"I don't want to criminalize teenagers having sex with each other," she said. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offense."
Brand protested his innocence from jail on Sunday in a statement read out by his wife Laura.

The prime minister's office said Monday that the comments were under investigation, as "prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

title: Drawing China close, is Kim Jong Un bracing to confront the U.S.?
summary: As North Korea and China draw closer together, is Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation with the U.S.?
story: Dandong, China — With a pair of binoculars and a camera hanging around his neck, retired Chinese government official Mr. Yang leaned against a fence on a boardwalk that meanders through the city of Dandong, peering across the wide Yalu River that separates China from North Korea.

He came to visit from Dalian, about 200 miles away, despite the temperature hovering just above freezing, to catch a glimpse of life inside China's heavily sanctioned, nuclear armed neighbor nation. But the main attraction he came to see is the massive new bridge towering over Dandong, which now links the two countries.
"The bridge is good, but it's only for trucks and cars, not for the trains," he complained. "But this is good for trade, and I do hope this means relations improve with North Korea."

At almost two miles long and four lanes across, the new Yalu River Bridge is a feat of engineering. The Chinese side was finished 12 years ago, but North Korea only recently completed its section, with leader Kim Jong Un making a surprise appearance for the official opening on Oct. 24.

As CBS News visited the new river crossing, a large group of tourists arrived from Fujian province, more than 1,000 miles to the south, to pose for photos in front of the impressive piece of infrastructure.

"This will enhance the friendship between China and North Korea for sure, but we hope that North Korea will open up to the West," tour group leader Mr. Sun told CBS News. "North Korea was an isolated country, and this shows they're trying to join the world."
That may be a message China's government is keen to encourage, but the recent actions and rhetoric from the Kim regime in Pyongyang suggests otherwise.
Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation?
Since the beginning of October alone, North Korea has test-fired more than a dozen missiles — the most concentrated series of such launches by Pyongyang since 2023.
Kim has personally observed some of the launches, accompanied by his teenage daughter Kim Ju Ae, widely viewed as his potential successor.

Former U.S. State Department official Robert Carlin, who has half of a century of experience as a North Korea analyst, believes Kim could be preparing to take steps that will inevitably end in confrontation with the U.S.

"It's part of a pattern of preparations to get ready for what he (Kim) thinks he wants to do. So he's testing new systems, and there's been a flurry of them. They can test in private — they do it all the time —   so they want to make these visible for some reason," Carlin told CBS News. "When you put that together with the pretty aggressive probing along the demarcation line, the high-level statements with warnings and threats … we have to take seriously the possibility that KJU [Kim] is preparing something, putting himself into position for the moment he thinks the winds are at his back, the situation is ripe for him to make some sort of move against U.S. assets in the region and against South Korea."

President Trump has been pushing for a new meeting with Kim for months, citing what he considers his good personal rapport with the North Korean leader, and there has been speculation the two leaders could meet while Mr. Trump is in China this week to attend the APEC summit.

He fueled that speculation himself Monday as he departed for Asia, saying it would be up to the Chinese hosts of the summit, but telling reporters when asked about a possible meeting: "Yes, we might have Kim Jong Un."

Mr. Trump met three times with Kim during his first term, including two historic summits aimed at getting the North Korean leader to agree to steps toward his nuclear-armed country denuclearizing, but the discussions went nowhere.

Since then, Kim has only expanded his nuclear arsenal. South Korean intelligence agencies believe Pyongyang could now have as many as 120 nuclear warheads. Kim has made it clear, meanwhile, that he will only agree to a new round of negotiations if the U.S. first and formally recognizes North Korea as a nuclear state.
Burgeoning ties with Russia and China

While longstanding international sanctions against his country over its nuclear weapons program remain in place, since the failed talks with Mr. Trump, Kim has projected a sense of being emboldened — of no longer leading a nation ubiquitously dismissed as an international pariah.
The relationship with China, while at times strained, has been a constant, and it has helped Kim push the image of North Korea as a global player, rather than a "hermit kingdom."

Since Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago, Pyongyang has also proven a dependable ally to Russia. North Korea has sent a constant stream of munitions to replenish Moscow's depleted stocks, as well as thousands of soldiers to fight on the front lines. In return, Moscow has sent financial and technological assistance, helping North Korea further develop its nuclear weapons program.

The city of Dandong is a symbol of the China-North Korea bond. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops marched across the original Yalu River bridge to fight alongside North Korean soldiers in the Korean War. Almost 3 million Chinese soldiers were deployed to fight in that conflict between 1950 and 1953.

The city was bombed by U.S. forces due to its strategic position on the vital North Korean supply line, and the old Yalu River Bridge was destroyed. Renamed "Broken Bridge," it became a war relic and tourist attraction in its own right.

In the center of Dandong, overlooking the old Broken Bridge and the nearby Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a smaller piece of infrastructure that facilitates cross-border rail and one-lane road traffic with the North Korean city of Sinuiju, local businesses sell Korean outfits along with trinkets and souvenirs, cashing in on Chinese fascination with the neighbors.

Grocery stores sell liquor in bottles that look like grenades, mortars and bullets, while hotels positioned along the river, facing North Korea, offer telescopes and binoculars in bedrooms for guests to peer across the Yalu into apartments and farmland on the far side. On some sections of the river, North Korea is only about 1,000 feet away.

Using our own long lens, CBS News was able to see people in North Korean apartments at night. At first light, the North Korean side became a hive of activity as people headed out to the fields and greenhouses to work.
George, a 16-year-old student, said he was visiting Dandong because of his passion for Chinese and North Korean history.

"North Korea is trying to get better connections with China, and China is opening to Western countries more and more, and if those things continue to happen, maybe North Korea will be opening to Western countries the same as China," he said.
As for the increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula, George dismissed the concerns.
Kim Jong Un, he said, is just "trying to tell the Western countries and the whole world that the DPRK is powerful enough to join the global stage right now."

While in Dandong, CBS News visited a restaurant and met a North Korean waitress who said she had been living in China for a year — one of as many as 80,000 North Koreans living and working in the city, all of whom are strictly monitored and not permitted to assimilate with the local Chinese population.
She told CBS News she missed home and hopes to return one day to North Korea, and she praised Kim Jong Un as a father to her country.

title: Women in U.K. are getting automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records.
story: Women in the United Kingdom who were convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will receive automatic pardons on Monday, the government said.
This follows the passage of a landmark vote by Parliament last year to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section of the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons, and some will be issued posthumously.

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police have investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once "dragged from hospital beds to police cells" and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

"This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.

"While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice," said Heidi Stewart, with the British Pregnancy Advisory Service, according to CBS News partner BBC News.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for "compassion, not punishment."

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which was the legal limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge, with Packer's consent, told BBC News that the whole incident has been "incredibly traumatic."
She said it took five years of investigations before a trial eventually found Packer not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," Tumbridge said, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
summary: President Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on his China trip this week.
story: Washington — President Trump said he may meet with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia this week.

As he left the White House Monday morning for a summit in the Philippines, which will be followed by a trip to China, Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting with Kim would take place in China — if it happens. No meeting with Kim has been confirmed by the White House. The president said whether the meeting happens is up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump will meet with Xi, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, later this week.

"We'll be with President Xi," the president told reporters on the White House South Lawn. "He was here a month ago. And we're also going to meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un, also. So that'll be good. We could — we have a chance to accomplish a lot."
The president said he doesn't know if Kim will come.
"He may come," Mr. Trump said of Kim. "I don't know. That's up to President Xi."
Mr. Trump has met with the North Korean leader in person three times, all during his first term in office. He is the only sitting U.S. president to have met with Kim.

title: Drug lord who orchestrated murder of U.S. agent dies at 80
summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking, was known as "the boss of bosses."
story: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking known as "the boss of bosses," who transformed the global cocaine trade and orchestrated the murder of a U.S. agent, died Sunday at age 80, officials said.

The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
Felix Gallardo's health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was "in very poor health." A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989 and was serving a 40-year sentence.

He was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency officer, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States. Last year, Camarena's alleged killer,  Rafael Caro Quintero, was transferred to the U.S. along with 28 other prisoners requested by the U.S. government.

Camarena, a father of three sons, was living in Guadalajara, Mexico, with his family working as an undercover DEA agent, his son told CBS News in a 2017 interview. He had been stationed there for four years on the trail of the country's biggest marijuana and cocaine traffickers.
A memorial was created in Camarena's honor in Los Angeles in 2014.
His son Enrique, who became a judge in 2014 in San Diego, told CBS News he carries his father's lessons into the courtroom. "He taught us to treat everyone fairly."
Rise of the cartels
Felix Gallardo was a native of Sinaloa state, where he was born on Jan. 8, 1946, according to public records.
His involvement in crime went virtually hand in hand with his career in the state and federal police.
He even served as a bodyguard to a Sinaloa governor, a role that experts say may have helped him secure the complicity and protection of powerful politicians.
He partnered with another veteran kingpin, Rafael Caro Quintero. Together with other crime bosses, they united gangs trafficking drugs to the United States and formed the Guadalajara cartel.
The cartel was formed around a "hegemonic model" and laid "the roots for nearly all of today's drug trafficking activities," according to InSight Crime, a website specializing in the drug trade.
Felix Gallardo "partnered with Colombian traffickers like Pablo Escobar, and became Escobar's most important Mexico associate," the publication said.
The Guadalajara gang controlled the country's underworld, earning Felix Gallardo the nicknames "El jefe de jefes" and "El Padrino" -- which translate to "the boss of bosses" and "the Godfather."
Downfall
Felix Gallardo was convicted for the February 1985 murder of Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.
The agent's death remains an open wound for the United States.
Intense pressure from Washington led to the arrest in 1985 of Caro Quintero, who is now imprisoned in the United States on charges of drug trafficking and the agent's murder.
Felix Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to control the criminal business from prison, according to experts.
He was serving his sentence at Puente Grande prison in Jalisco state.

The Guadalajara cartel imploded in the 1990s, and its local leaders formed regional cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, built up by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman and Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, both sentenced to life in prison in the United States.

Felix Gallardo remained in the popular imagination through narcocorridos, or drug ballads, such as "El jefe de jefes," which is banned in public spaces, and Netflix dramas about drug trafficking, with Mexican actor Diego Luna portraying the kingpin.

Drug Cartels

title: Basketball player allegedly had 75 pounds of drugs in luggage
summary: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency said it had arrested an American professional basketball player with 33.95 kilograms of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at the main airport.
story: Nigeria's anti-narcotics agency on Sunday said it had arrested an American professional basketball player with 33.95 kilograms (about 75 pounds) of cannabis in his luggage on arrival at the main airport.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) named the player as 28-year-old Greene Da'monte Khiree, a native of Savannah, Georgia.

He was arrested on Wednesday at the main international airport car park in Lagos after he "was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," NDLEA said in a statement.

The bags bearing his name tags were filled with 16 packs of Loud, described as a "potent strain of cannabis," said NDLEA, which posted several images of the player with suitcases full of the purported drugs.
He had arrived in Lagos from Thailand, where he said he had lived and played professional basketball since October 2025, the agency said.

The agency said he claimed he was visiting Nigeria to "build networks for his basketball career" but examination of his mobile phone showed information suggesting his "knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
FIBA lists a player by the name DaMonte Greene, a point guard, one of whose recent appearances was at the Phuket Elite Cup in September.
Greene was the leading scorer for the semiprofessional Georgia Bombers during the 2023-24 season, averaging 26.3 points per game, according to the Basketball Job Market.
Nigeria has been considered a trafficking and production hub for drugs bound for other countries, but researchers say the contraband spills into local markets.
Recent busts of industrial-scale meth production labs have left authorities worrying that Mexican cartels are establishing links in Nigeria to produce and ship meth out of the country.
In a separate incident announced on Sunday, Nigerian officials said a man was arrested at the airport after more than 25 kilograms of meth were found concealed in packs of assorted breakfast cereals.

In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos, the BBC reported. In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28 million, which was allegedly destined for the U.K.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left company in 2025, denies wrongdoing
summary: The company denies wrongdoing after accusations that it smuggled Nvidia's AI chips into China.
story: The Singapore-based company at the center of the scandal that brought down Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Sunday that suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang left the company in 2025. It also denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."

In a statement to CBS News, Megaspeed International said Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, left the company in August 2025 and has no current role. It did not comment on the allegations that Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy.
"Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," the company's statement said.

Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed and is the woman with whom Jensen Huang was having an affair. She is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week.
U.S. investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China.
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

Now the company, which began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to the Nvidia chips, is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips into China.
In a statement to CBS News on Sunday, the company said that recent assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations are "not supported by verifiable evidence."

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
It added: "The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation."
President Trump said last week the FBI was investigating the romantic and business ties between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related.

CBS News reported on Friday that Singaporean authorities seized Alice Huang's passport in June 2025 while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into the suspected smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
The source added that the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington at the time.

title: Transcript: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 15, 2026
summary: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.
story: The following is the transcript of the interview with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 15, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: For more, we go now to the Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy. Good morning to you, Mr. Secretary. Will the country be back to fully operational with a full flight schedule by the end of today?

SEC. SEAN DUFFY: So we have some delays in the airspace right now, but as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity. What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So I know that there was a router in El Dorado, Arkansas, as I understand it, that became an issue on Friday. You said on another network this morning there was a second issue at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Are those two things related? And if so, why did they both become problems on Friday?

SEC. DUFFY: Yeah, so the- the Amarillo facility- that work had been done weeks ago, and so why- when we did the install in El Dorado, did that start to broadcast data into our network? But then also the- the facility in Amarillo- why did that happen? We're investigating that right now. We actually have both routers with L3Harris, who operates and owns our network. FAA is on site as well. FBI is offering support. We're looking at that right now, and when we know what the root cause of this issue was- was it- was it the install from L3Harris? Was it the router? I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, was the issue old infrastructure or was it new equipment?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, the- the- the telecom in El Dorado, it was an old copper wire that basically was- it was going to be decommissioned. They said it can't be used anymore. So we were forced by the telecom provider to actually update that copper to fiber, and we brought in our routers and did the work, and that's when we saw the- the flooding of the network. So this was- this is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network that was- I mean, this goes back decades. By the way, the rest of the world, every institution, every company, not just in the U.S. but around the world, they've all switched over to digital and fiber. It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the union that represents aviation safety specialists, PASS, as they're called, said the issue was isolated to two contractor-owned and maintained routers that were being updated in the middle of the day, and they said their technicians were not involved in the upgrades. So I wonder, did the FAA do a risk assessment in advance and know that something like this was- happened, or were you totally caught off guard?

SEC. DUFFY: So let's be clear, the union that works at the FAA, they'll do the work on the radios- our equipment, or the radar- our equipment. They do all of the work on FAA-owned equipment. This union doesn't do any work on telecom, and it's our telecom contractor and providers like L3Harris in this situation. They're the ones that actually do the work. So the FAA lets L3Harris into our- into our sites, and then L3Harris will do the telecom work. But our- this union only works on our equipment. This telecom is not our- is- that's not our equipment. It's L3Harris's network. So just to clarify that, this- this was done appropriately, which by the way, it's been done thousands of times by us, by others, and other companies. This has never happened, and so that's why when you have a remote location like this, we felt comfortable doing it in the middle of the day because it's been done thousands of times. We've never had this situation. We're going to have to reevaluate now when we do this work. Now, normally, if you have a big facility, a Newark or an Atlanta or an LA, we have work to do, we do that at night, but in a remote location, we can do it during the day because the risk historically has been very low. Obviously, on Friday we saw no, it flooded our network, and we had to take the extraordinary step of issuing a ground stop.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So there was not a risk assessment, or there was a risk assessment, and this was just not foreseen as an issue?

SEC. DUFFY: Oh no, no- listen, we do risk assessments on everything, right? And if you want to talk about a risk assessment, the GAO has done a risk assessment on my network, on all of the old equipment, and they'll say, "Hey, this is- this is risky America. Make the investments and fix American air traffic control systems." And by the way, the Congress gave me $12.5 billion dollars.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SEC. DUFFY: I've- I've got ordered new radar, new radios, new voice switches. We're doing all of that, but it's also risky to say we're operating on a 1980s network with copper wires. So we've done a risk assessment- assessment: How do you switch over from copper to fiber? We keep airplanes safe in the sky. That's our number one priority. We've done that, and which is why it's worked thousands of times when we've made the switch over.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when--
SEC. DUFFY: --this time it- it didn't- and the- go ahead.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. So you just mentioned the- the Government Accountability Office. They also, in a September report, concluded that there is a push to modernize quickly, and that the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions. So, should you have seen this coming?
SEC. DUFFY: Well, first off, with regard to the GAO, my number one priority is safety, which is why we shut down the airspace on Friday, right? We did the closure--
MARGARET BRENNAN: They're saying speed.

SEC. DUFFY: No, I'm going to get to that. But I want to make sure that- that Americans get from point A to point B safely. They get back to their loved ones. I want them to be on time, but I want them to be safe, which is why we issued the ground stop. In regard to speed, we are going I think at the- at the right speed, we- we have to get off old network, old telecom. By the way, that's why I've already switched over 70 percent of copper to fiber without incident, without issue. Almost 470 radios have been switched over. New- new- new electronic flight strips and towers. We're doing incredible work, and just- let's be clear about one thing.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEC. DUFFY: For decades, this work in the FAA has not been done. It hasn't been done because it's hard. I don't want to be dishonest. It's a hard problem to solve. The Trump administration, with my leadership, we are solving the problem. We're building and deploying new technology. One of the problems I have is I need more money to- to build a new--
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.
SEC. DUFFY: --telecom network. I need new software, but we're doing the right thing by- by way of the American people by fixing this really really old system that was left to us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But respectfully, the American people have put a lot of money into infrastructure upgrades. In 2021, it was $25 billion for upgrades under Biden. Under your administration, the Trump administration, as you just said, $12.5 billion for upgrades. Democrats say the lion's share of the money that was provided to you- you just have not obligated or spent. Why? And if the White House has allowed for reprogramming of funds, why do you keep saying Congress is stopping you from spending the money they're giving you?

SEC. DUFFY: So first off, there was a lot of money that was given to the FAA in the past, and I can't answer for other secretaries or other FAA administrators. A lot of money was given, not a lot of work was done. So when I asked for a massive amount of money to fix the system, what the Congress did is they said, "Okay, we'll give you a partial funding, $12.5 billion dollars," in One, Big Beautiful Bill. And they were very specific in how we spend it. Now I can't- I can't go buy radar off the shelf. This is a massive order. So we've asked those who won the contract, I want them to build the radar in America. They'll start to deliver those radar to us in the spring. All of them will be deployed by the end of 2028. So all that money hasn't been spent, but it's been obligated to radar. Radio is the same thing. I'm buying radios, but they're not on the shelf. They have to be built. They specifically said how I spend the money, and I've- and I've got it all spent, ready to be deployed by the end of the- the president's tenure in office. But what I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software. Those- those are critical pieces to the infrastructure, and it's been historically underinvested in. I'm making the case to the American people and the Congress. For the first time, the FAA is taking your money, and we're actually building with your money. Let me continue. Let's finish the job. Let's not see what happened on Friday. Let's not let it happen again
MARGARET BRENNAN: Is $50 billion the total ask?--
SEC. DUFFY: Let's make sure we keep the American people safe- yeah, $50 billion.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Mr. Secretary. I'm told you have to get to another network. Thank you for your time this morning. 'Face the Nation' will be back in one minute. Stay with us.

title: Company under scrutiny for ties to Nvidia and China
summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
story: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.

One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned.

In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.

Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.

Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.

In a statement on Nov. 12, Megaspeed said it "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously" and that it's "committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government."

The company also said that it "has cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and stands ready to cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority."
In a subsequent statement on Nov. 15, Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and denied any wrongdoing, saying it "conducts legitimate and lawful business."
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).

Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.

Nvidia's board said Sunday that it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. "The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.
However, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust Jensen Huang, a development that was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."

She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:

It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
The company grew rapidly.

"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.

Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.

"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.

But in its statement on Nov. 12, the company said it had "retained a leading U.S. law firm to ... independently verify its export control compliance practices. Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws."

Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.

By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.

But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.

The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.

When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.

Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

title: U.S. reportedly floated trading Ukrainian land for NATO membership
summary: The Ukrainian president said he would put the question of a potential exchange to the people if certain guarantees were in place.
story: U.S. negotiators asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to consider giving up a part of his country in exchange for NATO membership, the leader claimed.
Zelenskyy told journalists on Friday he had been asked for the first time whether he would withdraw from the eastern region of Donbas in exchange for membership in the military alliance.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," the Ukrainian president said.

Zelenskyy said he was discussing a "security package" for Ukraine which included security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, an "adequate number of troops, weapons" as well as financial support. The Ukrainian president said if these measures are offered, he would ask Ukrainians whether to accept the potential exchange.
He did not specify if he meant a referendum, but added, "I have no right to make that decision on my own."
Control over the Donbas region, much of which has been occupied by Russia since the start of the war, has been a recurring sticking point in negotiations to end the conflict.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine pull its forces out of the Donbas region as a precondition for a peace agreement.

After staging elections dismissed by most of the world as a sham in occupied parts of the Donbas region, Putin declared in September 2022 that four regions of eastern Ukraine had also been annexed by Russia. None of the annexations have been recognized by the U.S. or the United Nations, and most countries consider them illegal land grabs.

Zelenskyy said he told U.S. negotiators Ukraine would need security guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5 "as an absolute minimum." That article sets out a key principle for the military alliance, whereby an attack on one of the member states is considered an attack on all other members.
The Ukrainian president added he was "not sure it would necessarily work," and said he needed more specific details on the potential membership.

title: 5th Canadian soldier dies weeks after fire on military base
summary: Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.
story: A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.
Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.

About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton. It occurred on a grenade launcher range, officials said last month.
The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized.

"Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. "With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service."

The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.
Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained and allowed training to continue before winds suddenly shifted.
Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on Canadian soil.
"We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Carney told reporters last month.

Canada

title: U.S. facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia
summary: President Trump's senior envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said they are also preparing for the next round of trilateral talks.
story: The United States is facilitating direct engagement between Russia and Europe amid a push to secure a peace deal in the war in Ukraine, President Trump's special envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Saturday.

Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this past week as the Trump administration pushes to end the more than 4 ½-year conflict. The meetings came after the first round of U.S.-brokered talks between the two countries since February concluded on Wednesday with an announcement of plans for a new prisoner exchange and further talks, but nothing to suggest a wider peace deal.

"Our focus is now on facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks," Kushner said in a social media post on Saturday. "Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps."

Zelenskyy, in statements released Saturday, said the U.S. had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe, though he warned that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders.
"In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday.

Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
He also said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the war.

"Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."

European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent's security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future.

Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from NATO and the European Union, a strong Ukrainian military and financial support for a specified period, he said. It would also include a recovery plan, he said.
"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: Do we accept it or not?" Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian.
Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution.
"If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway."
Kushner said Saturday that a lasting peace in Ukraine requires security guarantees for Kyiv and "detailed, actionable postwar security arrangements that reduce the risk of another war."

"NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security, enhanced by stronger mechanisms for military, communication, deconfliction, and reciprocal de-escalation, with practical ways to address disputes before they become crises," he added. "This is why we are working to bring our European partners directly into these discussions. Any final agreement must be agreed to by the relevant parties, and President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine's and Europe's security and make future conflict less likely."
Zelenskyy warned that broader discussions about Europe's security could allow Putin to seek changes to NATO's military presence, including the withdrawal of American troops.
He said Putin had raised similar ideas with then-President Joe Biden in 2021, seeking a redistribution of power in Europe and the world.
"I think Putin will bring up Finland and Sweden. I'm sure he will raise the issue of Hungary and the presence of American troops in the Baltic countries," Zelenskyy said.
He said any changes to Europe's security arrangements must be decided by European NATO members only after the war ends.

"The sequence should be as follows: a ceasefire, an end to the war in Ukraine, and security guarantees for Ukraine," he said. "There can be no security guarantees in Europe, or for Europe, without Ukraine."
Mr. Trump is set to meet with Putin next week as part of a trilateral summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said.

title: Italy fines Meta $880 million over accessing users' photos
summary: The country's data protection authority said Meta accessed users' photos without their "specific" consent.
story: Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta $880 million for accessing users' photos without their "specific" consent, the country's data protection authority said on Saturday.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them," the authority said in a statement.

Saturday's latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant. In 2021, Amazon received a more than 1.1 billion euro, or about $1.2 billion, fine for breaching competition law.
That sum was subsequently reduced to 752 million euros, or about $829 million, on appeal.
Meta may also appeal the latest fine. The tech company had not responded to a request for comment by Saturday afternoon.

Meta has been fined or ordered to pay settlements over privacy issues. In September, a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies. The company said they disagreed with the jury's verdict.

title: 2 Americans die in suspected drowning incident in the Bahamas
summary: Police said the Americans were part of a group swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign cautioning against strong currents.
story: Two Americans — a woman and a man — died after swimmers were swept away by strong ocean currents on the island of Bimini in the Bahamas, officials said.

The Royal Bahamas Police said in a statement on Friday that it received a call just before 3 p.m. on Friday about a possible drowning incident at the southern point of North Bimini, near the entrance of Bimini Harbour.
Police said the victims — identified only as a 38-year-old man and a 40-year-old woman — were part of a group swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign cautioning against strong currents.
"While swimming, several individuals were reportedly swept away by the strong currents," police said. "A nearby ferry boat assisted some of the swimmers to safety."
The two Americans were unresponsive, and CPR was immediately administered, police said.
They were taken to a local clinic, where they were pronounced dead.
Police said an autopsy will be conducted, and the incident remains under investigation.

title: Trump, Putin, Xi Jinping to meet in first trilateral of its kind
summary: President Trump is looking to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals in the first formal trilateral between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia.
story: President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The Kremlin also confirmed the meeting on Saturday.

Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks and is also set to bring up the war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Mr. Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Mr. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which then-U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.

"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
