Ramirez's office did not immediately provide Fox News Digital with a comment on Monday.White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital, "This radical Democrat proposal to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security would make America less safe. The brave men and women who serve in ICE and Border Patrol put their lives on the line to secure our Homeland and remove murderers, rapists, pedophiles, terrorists, and gang members from American communities. It’s shameful that far-left Democrats continue to demonize our law enforcement officers and play politics with public safety."

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a September post on X, "Radical leftists are calling to defund the police and abolish DHS. It’s NEVER going to happen. Our 270,000 @DHSgov patriots are keeping Americans SAFE— unlike this open borders politician who refuses to prioritize Americans over illegal aliens."

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement, "America’s brave ICE agents put their lives on the line every day to enforce U.S. law and arrest criminal illegal aliens—including gang members, rapists, and murderers. Representative Ramirez should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from her district—NOT vilifying law enforcement. This type of rhetoric is contributing to a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them as they put their lives on the line. While sanctuary politicians smear ICE, law enforcement is arresting criminals and saving countless American lives."
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Inside the Denver gathering where Democrats’ upbeat, Obama-era feel meets the 2028 race
summary: Concert-style campaign posters and Obama-era energy defined the Denver gathering where Democratic leaders began jockeying for the 2028 election.
story: At the

DENVER — Live music, concert-style campaign posters and a packed schedule of Democratic leaders set the scene in Denver, where party strategists and potential 2028 contenders gathered to celebrate midterm gains and start shaping what comes next.
The industrial-style venue, with indoor and outdoor spaces, gave the two-day "What’s Next" gathering a festival feel. Democrats moved between political programming, live music and social events.
Beneath the party atmosphere, potential contenders tested their messages and sized up the field, as Democrats began jockeying over the party’s direction and who might lead it in 2028.
The event had an unmistakably Obama-era feel, with its hopeful message and celebratory campaign atmosphere.
DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE
Concert-style campaign posters at Denver’s Mission Ballroom set the scene for the "What’s Next" gathering and gave it an Obama-era campaign feel on Nov. 12, 2026. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Matt Corridoni, a Democratic strategist and communications adviser at Majority Democrats, said the comparison made sense.

"The theme of that campaign was hope, and a lot of folks who are here now either worked on that campaign or were inspired by that campaign," Corridoni said. "I think one of the themes of this event is hopefulness for the Democratic Party moving forward. It’s a comparison that doesn’t shock me."
That hopeful energy showed up in the event’s posters and playful swag, some of which Ahmad Ali, communications director for the Searchlight Institute, helped design.
DEMOCRATS RIDE MIDTERM WAVE AS 2028 HOPEFULS GATHER IN DENVER TO MAP THEIR NEXT MOVES
Baseball hats and shirts at the "What’s Next" gathering in Denver featured slogans including "new deal democrat," "tax-and-spend liberal" and "Our Get Along Shirt." (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"I think we’re seeing a Democratic Party that is younger, brighter and way more emboldened to achieve what it wants to," Ali told Fox News Digital. "So this conference, its aesthetics, whether it’s the posters you see, the fun hats, all that — it just speaks to the confidence of the era."
Ali said the party’s energy could signal a break from what he described as a period of political stagnation, with voters looking for new choices in 2028.

He pointed to former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory as moments that captured the political mood, while arguing that the Biden era did not carry the same cultural force.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Attendees gather outside Denver’s Mission Ballroom during the "What’s Next" conference, where Democrats discussed the party’s direction and the 2028 race on Nov. 12, 2026. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"We are at the end of the Trump era, but we’re also at the end of whatever the sort of period of stuckness has plagued the Democratic Party," Ali said. "And I think that is very important, not just for Democrats, but also for all voters, because now maybe they’re going to have better options come 2028."
The gathering offered a first glimpse of how Democrats hope to turn their midterm momentum into a path to 2028.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Democrats plot massive spending spree after midterm rout — and Trump could help them pull it off
summary: After their resounding Election Night victory, Democrats plot massive Medicaid restoration, ACA tax credits expansion and housing assistance funding.
story: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses reporters on Capitol Hill following key Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections. Jeffries highlights the party's legislative agenda, promising to lower costs and protect essential programs for American families.

With a resounding Election Night victory behind them, Democrats are getting to work by plotting a massive government spending expansion paired with tax adjustments to pay for it. In this quest, they may find an unlikely ally in the White House.

Though the new crop of Democrats doesn’t take office until early next year, many are already announcing plans to aggressively increase government healthcare expenditures, cut checks directly to voters, restore housing assistance funding and pressure the federal government into repealing cuts to the bureaucracy.

Republicans, increasingly abandoning their once dogmatic opposition to increased social spending, could end up backing some of the measures Democrats seek to enact in their efforts to make life more affordable. President Donald Trump, for instance, expressed interest in cutting deals with liberal lawmakers on Election Night as it became apparent that the midterms were going to be disastrous for the GOP.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance, seen by many as the president's heir apparent, have made it clear that they do not categorically oppose the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies, one of the marquee items on the Democratic agenda, but signaled that they would like to see increased verification requirements to crack down on alleged fraud. Both have also signaled an openness to raising taxes on high-earners to help the federal government balance its budget, though estimates regarding how much these new levies would raise generally fall short of the costs that would be incurred if Democrats succeed in actualizing their demands.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats are still firmly entrenched in their position that unless they get a deal on an extension to expiring Obamacare tax credits, they won't provide the votes to reopen the government. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
When approached by Fox News Digital, the White House kept the door open for compromise with the Democrats, so long as they don't go too far in their proposals.

"President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years and a stock market that has hit record-highs," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

"As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people," she continued.

Even with sizable Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the party lacks the numbers necessary to override a presidential veto, meaning that liberals will need to work with either congressional Republicans or the White House if they want to enact key portions of their agenda.

"Republicans did not lose seats because of healthcare," Michael Cannon, the Cato Institute’s director of health policy studies, told Fox News Digital when asked about whether the president should compromise with Democrats by reinstating the subsidies. "Republicans did not lose seats because they let the Obamacare subsidies for the wealthy expire, because that's what those were. When we talk about enhanced subsidies, we're talking about subsidies for people making up to $600,000 per year. That's what Democrats put in place. That's what the president rightly let expire. That's not why Republicans lost seats and, so, the president should not be afraid of standing up to the industry."
TRUMP HANDING 1 MILLION AMERICANS OBAMACARE REFUND CHECKS IN 30 STATES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., left, accompanied by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., points to a poster depicting rising medical costs if Congress allows the Affordable Care Act tax credits to expire in December as he speaks to reporters following a Democratic policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol Building on October 15, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The massive proposed spending hikes, if they are successful, would take place as the United States’ annual deficit continues to grow, reaching nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, while the government faces down a looming financial disaster as Social Security's retirement trust fund approaches depletion and Congress confronts difficult choices over taxes and benefits.
Simply paying the interest on America’s debt cost the federal government over $1 trillion during the 2026 fiscal year.

Cannon argued that, if the government spends at unsustainable levels over a long enough time period, eventually bond markets will react negatively, reducing the supply of credit and forcing the government to make steep spending cuts, as has happened in Greece and under fiscally irresponsible nations. Some on the left, however, maintain that no such shock would occur as the wealthy can simply be taxed more to reduce the need for borrowing.
Though money is tight in Washington, Democrats have not pared back their spending ambitions.
The crown jewel of the Democratic spending agenda is healthcare, specifically restoring Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies.

"During the first 100 days, House Democrats must act to reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote in a manifesto published Nov. 4.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would reduce federal Medicaid spending by about $1.2 trillion between 2026 and 2035 at the cost of cutting enrollment in the program by about 13 million during that roughly 10-year period. As of publication, approximately 65.7 million people are enrolled in Medicaid.

Republicans, especially the president, may be reluctant to work with Democrats to repeal parts of the OBBA, given the sheer amount of political capital they burned to get the bill across the finish line. The extension or expansion of ACA tax credits, however, may be more fertile ground for a bipartisan agreement.
DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE
Democrats, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Chuck Schumer and Gov. Gavin Newsom, have made some unexpected alliances during President Trump's second term. (Shutterstock/AP)

Trump, for instance, said in November 2025 that he would "rather not" extend enhanced ACA tax credits, but conceded that "some kind of extension may be necessary," signaling that he is at least willing to use the subsidies as a bargaining chip during negotiations. Vance, meanwhile, has stated that the subsidies "go to some people deservedly," but argued that they lend themselves to fraud while teasing a healthcare agreement he said would please both parties.

Extending the enhanced ACA subsidies would come with a hefty price tag. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that making the expanded tax credits permanent would add roughly $350 billion to federal deficits between 2026 and 2035, while helping approximately 3.8 million more Americans obtain health insurance in 2035.

The annual impact on the federal deficit would also climb over time, from about $23 billion in 2026 to nearly $44 billion in 2035. And because CBO's estimate only covers a 10-year period, the government would face additional costs beyond that window if the subsidies remained in place.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., accompanied by House Minority Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Cali., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J., Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Or., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., speaks following a Democratic leadership meeting at the U.S. Capitol on April 8, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Some healthcare experts argue that the federal government's spending is only part of the picture. They contend that pouring more money into insurance subsidies without addressing the underlying cost of medical care can also drive up healthcare prices, potentially leaving taxpayers and consumers paying more over time.

"If you want to know why healthcare is so expensive in the United States, why we spend more than any other country, why prices are higher, look at what Democrats are doing right now," Cannon told Fox News Digital. "Government subsidies drive up prices, they drive up healthcare spending ... the most inefficient healthcare sector in the world is using Democrats in particular, but Republicans too, I don't want to be unfair ... to get the government to keep pumping more and more money into that health sector."

Economists generally hold that subsidizing demand for a good by providing subsidies, without increasing the supply of that good, will lead to increased costs across the market. Proponents of expanded government healthcare often counter that any reductions in efficiency or increases to costs, if such things really occur, are worth enduring to ensure coverage is more equitably distributed.

Progressive Democrats led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Terri Sewell have pushed Jeffries to expand Medicare to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, set aside funds for medical debt relief and restore funding to the National Institutes of Health — proposals that could cost billions more.

Some Democratic leaders have major spending proposals extending beyond healthcare. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen by many as a top contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, released a policy document following Election Night outlining roughly 200 policy proposals that he would like to see from the newly elected Congress.

Among them are restoring government jobs at the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education, increased spending on infrastructure projects, pouring money into housing assistance programs and shoring up food assistance funding, among other priorities.
PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST

Congressional Democrats hold a rally and press conference to announce their opposition to a Republicans plan to cut Medicaid in the Cannon House Office Building on Capitol Hill on May 13, 2025 in Washington, DC. House Republicans released a spending plan this week that would cause millions of poor Americans to lose Medicaid and millions more to pay higher fees, all part of President Donald Trump's budget priorities. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Jeffries and his congressional allies, meanwhile, also highlighted restoring SNAP funding, providing more government resources to cover childcare costs and subsidizing housing expenses. Some economists have argued that, by subsidizing demand for certain goods without stimulating increased supply, the government can inadvertently raise the cost of goods for everyone.

On the Democratic caucus's left-wing flank, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders argued that Democrats must use their resounding victory to demand a $12,000 payment to each working-class family of four, free tuition at public universities, universal free childcare, making Medicare available to 55-year-olds, increasing Social Security benefits by $2,400 a year and boosting teacher pay. While unlikely to make its way through Congress, Sanders’ agenda would cost trillions.

"The Democratic Socialists want to go much further, with universal healthcare alone, which would cost between $40 trillion and $70 trillion — roughly $300,000 to $500,000 per household," Rachel Greszler, a senior research fellow at Advancing American Freedom, a think tank affiliated with former Vice President Mike Pence, told Fox News Digital. "The entire socialist agenda calls for an estimated $71 trillion to $212 trillion in new spending over the next decade — that’s between $500,000 and $1,600,000 for every household in the US."
'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, speaks to members of the media following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Paying for all of this without running up the national debt too much is also on the minds of Democrats, and represents another area where they may find common ground with the GOP.

Sen. Ron Wyden has floated taxing the unrealized gains of some billionaires; Democratic leadership has proposed increasing the corporate income tax; many Democratic senators have argued that additional taxes should be levied against those they deem to be high earners, and some have stated that taxes should be imposed on fast-growing sectors of the economy, such as data centers.

While many of these tax hikes will likely be off the table for Republicans, Trump, Vance and a handful of congressional Republicans have expressed openness to taking more money from highly productive members of society.

Vance, per reports, indicated that he would have been open to a higher tax rate for people earning more than $1 million during internal White House discussions in 2025, though the vice president has publicly expressed skepticism that taxing wealthy Americans alone could solve the country’s fiscal problems. Trump, meanwhile, has said that he would be "OK" with taxing higher earners more to assist lower- and middle-income workers — a proposal that roughly matches the Democratic policy agenda.

Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Mark Kelly have proposed exactly that through their Working Americans' Tax Cut Act, which would cap the effective tax rate for most Americans while introducing a series of surtaxes on those making over $1 million per year. The University of Pennsylvania, home to one of the best business schools in the world, estimated that the proposal would net the federal government roughly $264 billion over a decade, which is not enough to cover the extension of ACA subsidies.
The University of Pennsylvania's model did not take into account economic feedback effects, meaning that potential lost revenue from reduced investment or work was not captured in its estimate.

Republican Sens. Bernie Moreno and Josh Hawley have backed increased taxes on high earners to pay for Social Security extensions and Child Tax Credit expansion, respectively. Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, has also expressed openness to a higher rate or a new bracket for million-dollar earners.

Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren, meanwhile, recently introduced a bill that would raise the tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%, which analysts at the Tax Foundation and the University of Pennsylvania predict would raise either $242 billion or $300 billion, respectively, over 10 years. Combined with the millionaire tax proposal, it would generate enough revenue to offset extended ACA subsidies but would not come close to generating enough revenue to match the costs of expanding Medicaid.
U.S. DEBT BLOWS PAST $40 TRILLION, JEOPARDIZING QUALITY OF LIFE FOR EVERY AMERICAN
Housing affordability has emerged as a top political and economic issue as many Americans continue to grapple with high home prices and mortgage rates. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

Wealth tax proposals from the Democrats' left-wing flank, while projected to raise far more in revenue for the government, have proven to be politically toxic and have drawn the ire of economists for potentially crippling economic growth.
A near-term tax hike, however, may not be necessary if all the Democratic talk of healthcare funding is simply political posturing, something Cannon views as likely.

"This is all kabuki here. This is not real health reform that we're talking about. All that Democrats apparently have to offer is more spending, more spending at a time when they know that existing levels of government spending on healthcare are not popular with voters," he said, pointing to the fact that voters failed to approve a billionaire tax in California to fund state healthcare. "Democrats are offering only one idea, and they know that it won't fly, but they're going through the motions because they think they can get a political advantage by saying that Republicans don't care about people."
Lofty Democratic spending ambitions are not limited to the federal government.
With state legislatures and governors’ mansions across the country falling into Democratic hands, public expenditures are likely to boom.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, for instance, pledged on the campaign trail to tap $17 billion from the state's rainy day fund to send $1,500 checks to every Texas household, a proposal that would require legislative approval and has since been introduced in the state Senate.

While Republicans may be eager to slam Hinojosa for pulling cash from Texas’ reserves to send payments to voters, they will be forced to grapple with the fact that Trump promised to do the same, but on a much larger scale, if the GOP came out on top during the midterms.

title: Federal prosecutor warns Sen Warren of 'legal consequences' if records aren't preserved in Trump-linked probes
summary: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz warned Elizabeth Warren of legal consequences over her plans to investigate people close to President Donald Trump.
story: Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich reports on growing tensions between the White House and House Democrats over plans to investigate Trump administration officials and issue subpoenas. Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn explains the legal challenges both sides could face and discusses potential legal concerns involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

A federal prosecutor on Sunday warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of "significant legal consequences" if she failed to preserve records tied to potential congressional investigations involving allies of President Donald Trump.

In a letter to Warren, who is poised to become Senate Banking Committee chair in January, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz accused the senator of planning "to target private individuals close to President Trump" with investigations.

"You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates," he wrote to Warren, currently the ⁠top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee.

Reitz’s letter and accompanying social media post include various puns and references to Native Americans that appear to mock Warren over previous claims about her Native American heritage. Trump and his allies have mocked Warren for years, including by calling her "Pocahontas."
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

A federal prosecutor warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren of "significant legal consequences" if she failed to preserve records tied to investigations into allies of President Donald Trump. (Kent Nishimura / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The letter demands that Warren preserve documents and communications Reitz considers relevant to his allegations that she intends to misuse congressional investigations against people associated with Trump.

"I am writing to give you formal notice of your obligation to preserve all documents, communications, and other electronically stored information relevant to your intent to weaponize congressional investigations and deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 241 and 242. You are obligated to preserve all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities related to President Trump and the Trump Administration," his letter reads.
"Failure to do so may result in sanctions, adverse-inference instructions, or other penalties, and may carry significant legal consequences," Reitz added.
The letter gives Warren until 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 23 to confirm in writing that she received the notice and took steps to preserve the requested records.
WHITE HOUSE LAWYER'S HARDBALL WARNING TO DEMS HAS LEGAL EXPERTS ON BOTH SIDES QUESTIONING ONE KEY THREAT

The letter demands that Sen. Elizabeth Warren preserve records related to potential congressional investigations involving people close to President Donald Trump. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The letter does not establish that Warren violated federal law. Congressional investigations conducted for legitimate legislative purposes generally receive constitutional protection under the Speech or Debate Clause, although the scope of that protection depends on the circumstances.

The letter cited Warren's Nov. 8 appearance on CBS News' "Face the Nation," during which she discussed investigating corporate leaders, including Big Tech CEOs and Wall Street executives, who may have broken the law. Reitz wrote that the context "sends a strong smoke signal" that she intends to target people close to the president.
Warren is a staunch critic of Wall Street and corporate executives, including tech executive Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Other Democratic lawmakers have received similar warnings, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who received letters from Reitz, and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who received a separate letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf.

President Donald Trump and his allies have issued several warnings to Democrats over their plans to investigate the president, current and former administration officials and other people close to him. (Getty Images)

"With Senators Blumenthal and Slotkin, each already recipients of preservation demands from my office, you accused several technology companies of having 'spent lavishly to stay on the good side of President Trump,' and thereby benefiting personally and financially. You then threatened to spear them with future investigative action," Reitz told Warren.
Fox News Digital reached out to Warren's office for comment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Last week, Trump directed the Justice Department to look into what he described as Democrats’ "threatening" conduct. Attorney General Todd Blanche later refused to rule out criminal charges against lawmakers for their investigations, as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
Blanche later clarified his earlier remarks, saying there were "no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said."

title: White House calls DC policies 'insanity' after 19-year-old gunman gets probation in shooting
summary: A 19-year-old who prosecutors said fired more than 20 rounds into a D.C. neighborhood got probation, prompting the White House to slam the city's crime policies.
story: U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro discusses a 20% crime reduction in Washington, D.C., crediting the prosecution of criminals for this success. Pirro highlights cases including a Dominican national’s $1 million unemployment fraud and a former Fed advisor sentenced for giving sensitive information to Chinese spies. She advocates for lowering the age of responsibility to punish violent juvenile offenders.

EXCLUSIVE – A 19-year-old who authorities say fired more than 20 rounds into a Washington, D.C., neighborhood and wounded a boy playing basketball has been released on probation, prompting the White House to denounce the city’s sentencing policies as "insanity."

Prosecutors wanted Darius Drew behind bars for five years. Instead, a judge suspended a two-year prison sentence and ordered 18 months of supervised probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, a D.C. law U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had previously urged lawmakers to overhaul.

"The case illustrates the insanity of Washington, D.C.’s soft-on-crime policies that allow adults to receive just a slap on the wrist for dangerous crimes like firing twenty rounds of ammunition into the community," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS
President Donald Trump’s D.C. crime crackdown has led to 1,914 arrests since Aug. 7 as federal law enforcement officials sweep the city. (Getty Images)

"It is remarkable that even with these types of radical policies in place, President Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force has been able to drive down violent crime in our nation’s capital," Bis added.

Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro granted Drew sentencing treatment under the Youth Rehabilitation Act over the government’s objection, according to federal prosecutors. Drew pleaded guilty Aug. 10 to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license.
CHAOTIC TEEN BRAWL GOES VIRAL AFTER TEEN TERROR PROMPTS US ATTORNEY PIRRO'S PLAN TO PROSECUTE PARENTS

Two firearms recovered from Darius Drew’s bedroom, according to federal prosecutors. Drew received probation after firing more than 20 rounds and wounding a boy playing basketball in Washington, D.C. (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Columbia)
He was released Friday after spending nearly six months in custody following his May 22 arrest. Prosecutors opposed his release as well as the use of the youth sentencing law.
The gunfire that put him there came from two locations in a Northwest Washington neighborhood, according to the government’s evidence.
MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE
On May 11, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley before surveillance video captured him firing at a parked car, prosecutors said. The ShotSpotter gunfire detection system registered 10 shots.
Seconds later, Drew fired toward a nearby house. A boy playing basketball at a recreation center was struck in the leg.

By the time the shooting stopped, Drew had fired more than 20 rounds into the community, prosecutors said. Investigators later found two firearms, ammunition and large amounts of suspected narcotics and marijuana at his home.
REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF SHOOTING NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER HAS LENGTHY HISTORY WITH THE LAW, RECORDS SHOW
Federal agents in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 3. President Trump federalized DC's police department on Aug. 11. (Getty Images)

The probation ruling echoes a warning Pirro delivered to the D.C. Council more than a year earlier. In an Aug. 6, 2025, letter, she urged lawmakers to overhaul the Youth Rehabilitation Act, citing a separate case in which another 19-year-old received probation after shooting someone in the chest aboard a Metrobus.
SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS

The law, which the D.C. Council expanded in 2018, allows eligible offenders who committed crimes before turning 25 to receive sentences below otherwise applicable mandatory minimums and potentially have their convictions set aside, Pirro wrote. Murder and the most serious sexual abuse offenses are excluded.

In that separate case described in the 2025 letter, the 19-year-old pleaded guilty to two offenses carrying five-year mandatory minimums but received probation after four months in jail awaiting trial, according to Pirro’s letter.
SUSPECTED FLORIDA PUBLIX SLASHER WALKED FREE FROM COURT MONTHS EARLIER DESPITE VICTIM WARNINGS
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro gives remarks after her swearing-in ceremony, Wednesday, May 28, 2025, in the Oval Office. (Joyce N. Boghosian/White House)
"This sentence was a legal sentence only because he was sentenced under the YRA," she wrote.

Pirro argued the law needed changes to balance rehabilitation with accountability. Her office said 96% of defendants younger than 25 who received felony sentences in D.C. Superior Court from 2022 through 2024 were eligible for sentencing under the act.
FBI REPORTS 114% JUMP IN VIOLENT CRIME ARRESTS UNDER TRUMP COMPARED TO BIDEN’S FINAL MONTHS

The White House pointed to Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force as its response to crime in the capital, saying the operation has made more than 19,000 arrests, including those of murderers, sex offenders, drug traffickers and other violent criminals.

title: FAA ground stop timeline: Weekend chaos grounds planes and postpones games
summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said overloaded routers tied to contractor L3Harris maintenance work triggered the longest nationwide FAA ground stop in 25 years.
story: Airlines for America president Chris Sununu joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss how thousands of travelers continue to face flight delays and cancellations nationwide following a recent FAA ground stop. They discuss infrastructure challenges and how to go forward.

A communications failure brought departures across the country to a halt Friday, stranding travelers, disrupting professional sports teams and sending federal officials scrambling to restore flights and determine what went wrong.

The longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years ended after more than four hours, but the fallout stretched through the weekend as airlines worked through cancellations and investigators zeroed in on routers tied to the outage.
Here’s a timeline of the shutdown and the federal response. All times are Eastern.
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

A view from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) in California as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the States due to a telecommunications and air traffic control communication outage affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers on November 13, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Friday afternoon, Nov. 13: Communications trouble triggers nationwide ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials detected instability in radar data and communications at 3:36 p.m., affecting facilities that guide planes approaching airports and traveling between them.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. as controllers and pilots followed procedures to bring aircraft already airborne safely to the ground. About 3,500 flights were in the air.
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Duffy later emphasized that officials had not lost every radar feed or all telecommunications service. The inconsistent information was enough to trigger the shutdown as a safety precaution.
Friday, 4:16 p.m.: Duffy announces investigation into communications problem

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (Tom Brenner/AP Photo)
Duffy said the ground stop was necessary because of "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."
FAA technicians were investigating, he said.
The disruption also prompted a broader federal response as officials examined whether the failure could have involved malicious activity.
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

President Donald Trump brought federal agencies together on a call Friday, including intelligence officials, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Intelligence partners reported they were not detecting the usual signs of a cyberattack, Duffy said.

Steven Cheung, assistant to the president and White House director of communications, later said on X that the White House and administration had acted within minutes of the FAA notice, crediting Trump for the response.
UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE
"Minutes after the FAA notice posted, the White House and Administration sprang into action. Because of that speed and effectiveness, the ground stop was lifted after just a few hours," Cheung wrote.
"A Herculean effort, only made possible by President Trump's leadership."
NFL OFFICIAL DON WILLARD WILL REFEREE TWO GAMES IN ONE DAY AFTER FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS TRAVEL, LEAGUE SAYS
Friday evening: Officials address security concerns as sports teams are stranded

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack and reassured Americans with loved ones traveling.
"There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said.
TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS OVERCOME SLUGGISH OFFENSE, JET LAG TO TAKE DOWN TEXAS A&M AND KEEP CFP HOPES ALIVE

TOPSHOT - Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports.  (Kamil Krzacynski/ AFP via Getty Images)

The shutdown also left college football teams scrambling to reach Saturday’s games. Texas had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge to face LSU when the ground stop prevented departure. Tennessee’s scheduled 4 p.m. flight to College Station was also halted.
Teams including Ole Miss, Tennessee and Baylor returned to their athletic facilities as officials weighed alternate travel plans. Some teams sat aboard charter planes for up to two hours.
PRIVATE PLANES AND ROADTRIPS: AEW GOES ABOVE AND BEYOND TO GET TO PHOENIX FOR FULL GEAR DESPITE TRAVEL CHAOS
Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes / AFP via Getty Images))
The shutdown also disrupted travel for professional sports teams ahead of a busy weekend.

The Brooklyn Nets were trying to fly from New Orleans to Memphis when their flight was halted, according to The Associated Press. The Memphis Grizzlies were also in New Orleans for a Friday game against the Pelicans, with plans to depart afterward.

The Cleveland Cavaliers and Chicago Bulls also had planned postgame flights. The San Jose Sharks’ flight to Utah for a Saturday game against the Mammoth did not depart before the shutdown, while the Detroit Pistons had reached Miami earlier Friday.
Friday, 8:15 p.m.: Ground stop lifted, but recovery starts slowly
Travelers check a flight information display board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Nov. 13, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)
The FAA lifted the nationwide order at 8:15 p.m., allowing departures to resume.

Planes began leaving airports including LaGuardia, Los Angeles International and Reagan National. Some travelers at Reagan National had been waiting since around 3:30 p.m. for flights scheduled to leave around 4 p.m.
Duffy warned that reopening the airspace would not immediately get every flight moving. Departures depended on whether airlines had pilots, flight attendants and other crews available.
"It’s going to be slow," he said.
Late Friday into Saturday: College football games rescheduled

Lifting the ground stop did not immediately solve the travel problems for college teams. By 9:12 p.m. Friday, Washington, Texas, Tennessee and Oregon State were heading back to airports, but other programs faced crew availability problems.
Utah’s charter crew ran out of available hours, forcing the team to plan a Saturday morning departure for its game at Arizona. The Big 12 moved kickoff to 10:30 p.m. ET Saturday.
Just after midnight Saturday, the Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to 1 p.m. ET Sunday after the Rebels were unable to leave Friday evening.
Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny said the school objected to the change but was told it would face a forfeit if it refused to play Sunday.
Saturday, Nov. 14: Maintenance work and overloaded routers emerge as focus
Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (Ryan MurphyAP Photo)
At a Saturday briefing, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had been replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections at a remote FAA location.
The copper line was being discontinued, making the replacement necessary, he said.
During the work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming other routers and disrupting communications and radar feeds.
Investigators were examining whether installation error or faulty equipment caused the failure.
"Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said.

Bedford distinguished the routine maintenance from the administration’s broader air traffic control modernization program. Duffy also said officials would reevaluate when such work should be performed.
Saturday: Airlines regroup as FAA forecasts Sunday recovery
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.
The Transportation Department said more than 8,000 flight operations resumed Friday night after the ground stop ended, but passengers continued facing delays and cancellations Saturday.
Airlines still needed to reposition aircraft and crews, leaving travelers scrambling to rebook and check whether their flights would operate.
Officials urged passengers to check directly with their airlines for current flight information.
Sunday, Nov. 15: Router testing continues as Duffy presses for funding

Planes wait on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport, New York on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports due to communications problem.  (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Duffy said Sunday morning that air travel would improve throughout the day but probably would not return fully to normal until Monday, updating officials’ earlier prediction of a recovery by Sunday night.
Two routers from Texas and Arkansas were undergoing testing as investigators worked to determine the cause.

Duffy said work in El Dorado, Arkansas, was followed by problems involving equipment in Amarillo, Texas, where a system had been replaced about three weeks earlier. Engineers were examining the routers at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida.
"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said.
He said there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, while leaving open further investigation if new evidence emerged.

Duffy also pressed Congress for additional funding. He said the $12.5 billion already allocated covered specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, but did not fund a replacement telecommunications network.
Sunday, 2 p.m.: Travel headaches drag on
By 2 p.m. ET Sunday, 5,280 flights had been delayed and 1,709 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.
Dallas Fort Worth, Atlanta and Chicago O’Hare were among the hardest-hit airports tracked in the update, with hundreds of delays at each.
The disruptions continued Sunday afternoon as airlines worked to restore normal schedules.
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Scott Kirby, chief executive officer at United Airlines Holdings Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Sunday, Nov. 15: United CEO calls for action

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience during the disruption. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages.
Kirby said he had spoken directly with Duffy, Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees.
"This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now."
Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News' Grady Trimble, Anders Hagstrom, Stephen Sorace, Trey Wallace, and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Fake E-ZPass email threatens $100 fine over unpaid toll
summary: A fake E-ZPass email cites a real federal regulation to demand toll payments, but the law it references has nothing to do with collecting tolls.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.

You open your email and see a warning from E-ZPass. Apparently, there's a problem with your toll account, and a payment didn't go through. Maybe you recently drove through a toll plaza. Maybe your credit card expired. Either way, it's the kind of message that makes you wonder whether you owe money. And that's exactly what scammers are counting on.

We recently received a convincing fake E-ZPass email claiming an overdue toll could trigger additional penalties and even affect your vehicle's registration renewal. The message includes familiar E-ZPass branding and an official-looking violation number. There's even a big purple "Pay Now" button. But take a closer look, and several warning signs point to a phishing scam.
And here's what I find especially interesting. The scammers behind this email even borrowed language from federal regulations to make their payment demands sound legitimate.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE AAA EMAIL SCAM TARGETS DRIVERS
This fraudulent E-ZPass email claims an unpaid toll could trigger a $100 fine and vehicle registration problems, hoping recipients will click the "Pay Now" button. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How this fake E-ZPass email scam works

The email arrived with a subject line reading "Your E-ZPass Account Has an Overdue Balance." The sender identified itself as "E-ZPass Violations Dept #276797." The message displayed the E-ZPass logo and included a violation reference number. It even listed Nov. 6 as the issue date. The headline gets straight to the point: "Your toll payment could not be processed." According to the message, a recent toll crossing could not be charged because of insufficient funds, a declined credit card or an expired payment method. That explanation sounds believable because payment problems can happen with legitimate toll accounts.

Then comes the pressure. The email warns that unpaid balances could be referred to collections. It also threatens a civil penalty of up to $100 per violation and a possible hold on vehicle registration renewal. To make those claims sound official, the message cites a federal regulation. Below the warning, the recipient sees a large "Pay Now" button. There are also options to update a payment method or dispute the alleged violation. The apparent goal is to scare someone into following a link that could lead to a fraudulent payment website. From there, scammers may try to steal credit card information or other sensitive details.
Warning signs that reveal the fake E-ZPass email
At first, this email looks like a legitimate toll notice. But once you start looking at the details more closely, several red flags suggest something is wrong. Here's what caught our attention.

One of the biggest clues appears in the email details. Although the message claims to come from E-ZPass, the actual sender address ends in @cashcoma.cooljz.com. The reply-to address also uses that unrelated domain. That's a major warning sign. Scammers can make the sender's display name say almost anything. They can also copy official logos to make their messages look convincing. However, the underlying email address can reveal something very different.

In this example, the recipient field also displays noreply@ezpassviolations.com. That might look official, but an address appearing in the "To" field says nothing about who actually sent the email. Even when an address looks familiar, it's worth checking. Criminals can spoof sender information to impersonate legitimate organizations.

At the top of the message, a notice says that if the email lands in your junk or spam folder, you should move it to your inbox. It also asks you to add the sender to your safe sender list. So, an email demanding payment is also asking you to override your email provider's spam warning.

Legitimate senders sometimes ask people to check their spam folders. However, in this case, the request appears alongside suspicious sender information and a threatening payment notice. The email had already landed in the junk folder. That alone doesn't prove fraud, but it gives you another reason to investigate before clicking anything.

This may be the most revealing detail in the entire email. The message references 23 CFR Part 940, suggesting federal regulations require drivers to settle outstanding toll balances under the conditions described in the notice. There's a big problem with that claim.

23 CFR Part 940 covers intelligent transportation system architecture and standards. It addresses how certain transportation technology systems are developed and implemented. It does not establish the blanket toll payment obligation suggested by this email. The reference to federal law gives the warning an appearance of authority, even though the cited regulation doesn't support the payment demand. And let's be realistic: how many of us would stop to look up a federal regulation while worrying about an overdue bill? That's what makes this tactic so concerning.
FAKE SOCIAL SECURITY STATEMENT EMAIL HIDES A SCAM
E-ZPass transponders allow drivers to pay tolls electronically, but scammers are exploiting the system's familiar name to send fake payment notices. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

The email warns that you could face a $100 civil penalty, additional fees and even trouble renewing your vehicle's registration. That's enough to make anyone nervous, especially when the email doesn't even tell you how much you supposedly owe in tolls. And here's something else that caught my attention. There's no toll crossing location, no license plate number and no date showing when the alleged violation happened.

The email does include a violation reference number, but don't let that fool you. Scammers can easily make up a string of letters and numbers to make a message look official. Now, real toll violations can come with penalties, depending on the toll agency and its rules. But if an unexpected email suddenly threatens you with fines or registration problems, you should verify the claim directly with your toll agency before taking any action.

For years, many toll phishing scams arrived as text messages. Drivers would receive a warning about an unpaid balance, followed by a link demanding immediate payment. We previously reported on fake toll road texts targeting drivers across America. Those schemes directed victims to fraudulent payment websites designed to collect financial information. The email we reviewed uses a similar approach, but its polished appearance gives scammers another way to reach potential victims. The E-ZPass Group has warned about fraudulent emails and text messages impersonating toll agencies. It also explains that the E-ZPass Group itself does not hold customer accounts or collect toll payments. Individual member agencies handle those services.

The problem has become significant enough to show up in federal fraud data. In May, the Federal Trade Commission reported that government imposter scam reports rose 40% in 2025. The agency said bogus overdue toll notices contributed to that increase. Those messages often threaten additional fees or registration problems if drivers fail to pay quickly. It's a familiar tactic, but scammers continue to find ways to make their warnings more convincing. We reached out to the E-ZPass Group for comment on this particular email and to ask whether it has seen similar messages targeting drivers, but did not receive a response before our deadline.
How to protect yourself from fake E-ZPass emails

A suspicious toll notice can catch you off guard, especially when it threatens fines or registration problems. Before you click anything or make a payment, here are a few simple steps I recommend taking to protect yourself.

Open the official website or app for your toll provider. Avoid using the payment button inside a suspicious email. Instead, sign in through the website you normally use. Look for outstanding balances or payment problems there. If you have questions, contact your toll agency using its published customer service number. For example, New York E-ZPass customers can visit E-ZPass New York at e-zpassny.com/. Other states and toll agencies operate their own official websites. If the email claims you have a violation, ask the agency to verify it using your account information.

Avoid clicking "Pay Now" or "Update Payment Method" in an email you cannot verify. A fraudulent payment page may look almost identical to the real website. Once you enter your credit card information, scammers could use it to make unauthorized charges. For more ways to recognize suspicious links, see our CyberGuy article on how to spot and prevent phishing attacks in your inbox.

Check the complete sender and reply-to addresses. Don't rely on the displayed name or logo. If you see unfamiliar domains or addresses that don't match the organization, treat the message as suspicious. Keep in mind that even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed. That's why independently verifying an unexpected payment request remains so important.

Take time to verify any warning about fines or registration problems. Scammers often use threats because fear can make people act without thinking. An alarming message deserves additional scrutiny, especially when it references legal consequences without providing enough information to verify the alleged violation.
IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL?
Scammers are using familiar E-ZPass branding to trick drivers into paying fake toll violations and threatened penalties. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

Keep strong antivirus software installed and updated on your devices. Security software can help detect malicious websites and potentially harmful downloads. Some products also offer phishing protection that warns you when a link leads to a suspicious website. However, antivirus protection cannot guarantee that every fake payment page will be blocked. You still need to verify unexpected requests before sharing information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Report the message as phishing through your email provider. You can also file a complaint with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Include the suspicious sender address and details about the message. If possible, preserve the email until you've submitted your report. After reporting it, delete the message.

Reduce the personal information scammers can find about you online. Data brokers collect and sell information such as your name, address and phone number. Criminals can potentially use those details to make phishing messages more convincing. A data removal service can help remove your information from participating data broker websites, making it harder for scammers to find. While it won't stop every fake E-ZPass email, it can help reduce your exposure to targeted scams. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
What to do if you already clicked or paid
Accidentally clicked a link in a suspicious E-ZPass email? Don't panic. The next steps depend on what happened after you opened it. Here's how to protect yourself and limit any potential damage.

Clicked the link but didn't enter any information? Close the website immediately. Avoid clicking anything else on the page. As an extra precaution, run a security scan on your device.Entered your credit card information? Contact your card issuer right away. Explain that you may have entered your details on a fraudulent website. Ask about replacing your card and disputing any unauthorized charges. Keep an eye on your statements for suspicious activity.Shared your E-ZPass account password? Visit your toll provider's official website and change your password. Next, update any other accounts using that same password. Enable multifactor authentication wherever it's available.Downloaded a suspicious file? Don't open it. Delete the file and run a full antivirus scan. Already installed something suspicious? Disconnect your device from the internet while you investigate and remove the threat.Provided personal information? Take steps to protect your identity. Depending on what you shared, you may need to place a fraud alert or freeze your credit. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for personalized recovery guidance.Report the suspicious email. Mark the message as phishing through your email provider. You can also file a report with the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Reporting scams helps authorities track fraudulent activity and warn others.
Clicked the link but didn't enter any information? Close the website immediately. Avoid clicking anything else on the page. As an extra precaution, run a security scan on your device.

Entered your credit card information? Contact your card issuer right away. Explain that you may have entered your details on a fraudulent website. Ask about replacing your card and disputing any unauthorized charges. Keep an eye on your statements for suspicious activity.

Shared your E-ZPass account password? Visit your toll provider's official website and change your password. Next, update any other accounts using that same password. Enable multifactor authentication wherever it's available.

Downloaded a suspicious file? Don't open it. Delete the file and run a full antivirus scan. Already installed something suspicious? Disconnect your device from the internet while you investigate and remove the threat.

Provided personal information? Take steps to protect your identity. Depending on what you shared, you may need to place a fraud alert or freeze your credit. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for personalized recovery guidance.

Report the suspicious email. Mark the message as phishing through your email provider. You can also file a report with the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Reporting scams helps authorities track fraudulent activity and warn others.
Kurt's key takeaways

What really caught my attention about this scam was the reference to federal regulations. That's pretty clever on the scammers' part because most of us aren't going to look up a law when we're worried about an overdue bill. And the email looks polished enough that someone could easily overlook the strange sender address. I can see how someone might fall for it, especially if they've recently driven through a toll. My advice is to never pay an unexpected bill through a link in an email. Go directly to the toll agency and check your account. That extra step could save you a lot of trouble.
Have you ever received a toll violation notice that looked so convincing you almost paid it? Or have scammers actually managed to get your money? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Freeze, fraud alert or monitoring? What to do after a breach
summary: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring each protect different parts of your financial life after a data breach. Here's how to choose.
story: A credit freeze, fraud alert and identity monitoring service offer different protections against identity theft. Knowing how each works can help you respond to a data breach. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A data breach notice can leave you with plenty of questions. Should you freeze your credit? Is a fraud alert enough? Do you need an identity monitoring service? The right response depends on what information was exposed and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's the important distinction. A company saying your information was involved in a breach does not automatically mean someone has opened an account in your name.

An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves attention, but it does not always prove fraud occurred. However, once you confirm someone has used your information fraudulently, the situation becomes more urgent. So, which protection should you choose? Let's look at what each one actually does.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
YOU HAVE A CREDIT FREEZE; IT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH
What a credit freeze does

A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file. It makes it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name because most lenders need to review your credit information before approving an application. Credit freezes are completely free. You must place one separately with each of the three major credit bureaus:
EquifaxExperianTransUnion
Equifax
Experian
TransUnion

A freeze stays in place until you remove it, and it does not affect your credit score. If you apply for a mortgage, car loan or credit card, you may need to temporarily lift the freeze so the lender can review your report. You can do that for free.

Employment and tenant-screening checks follow different rules and generally are not blocked by a credit freeze. A freeze is a strong option if your Social Security number was exposed or you simply want to reduce the risk of someone opening new credit in your name. However, it cannot protect an existing bank account, stop a scam payment or remove a fraudulent account that was already opened.
What a fraud alert does

A fraud alert tells lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity before approving new credit. Unlike a freeze, a fraud alert does not restrict access to your credit report. Instead, it warns lenders that someone may be trying to use your information.
There are two main types:

Initial fraud alert: Free, lasts one year and can be renewed. You only need to contact one major credit bureau, which must notify the other two.Extended fraud alert: Free, lasts seven years and is available to identity theft victims who provide an FTC identity theft report or police report.
Initial fraud alert: Free, lasts one year and can be renewed. You only need to contact one major credit bureau, which must notify the other two.
Extended fraud alert: Free, lasts seven years and is available to identity theft victims who provide an FTC identity theft report or police report.

A fraud alert can be convenient if you're actively applying for a mortgage, loan or credit card and don't want to manage multiple credit freezes. Still, it offers less control than a freeze because lenders can continue accessing your credit file after completing the required identity checks. If someone has already opened an account fraudulently, placing an alert can help reduce additional risk. However, you'll still need to contact the creditor and dispute the fraudulent account.
What identity monitoring does
Identity monitoring watches for certain changes involving your personal or financial information and notifies you when suspicious activity appears.
Depending on the service, those alerts may include:

New credit accounts or hard inquiriesCollections activity or changes to credit reportsSuspicious financial account activityPersonal information found in known data breachesCertain phone account changes or identity-related activity
New credit accounts or hard inquiries
Collections activity or changes to credit reports
Suspicious financial account activity
Personal information found in known data breaches
Certain phone account changes or identity-related activity

Monitoring is useful because it can give you an earlier warning that someone may be misusing your information. But there's an important limitation. Monitoring generally alerts you after suspicious activity is detected. It does not necessarily prevent that activity from happening. And no service can monitor everything. For example, basic credit monitoring may not detect an email account takeover, medical identity theft or a payment you authorized after being tricked by a scammer.
Which tool fits your situation?
The right protection depends on what happened to your information and whether someone has already tried to use it. Here's what to do in each situation.

Start by reviewing the breach notice to understand exactly what information was involved. If passwords were exposed, change them immediately. Use unique passwords for each account and enable multifactor authentication, especially on your primary email account. If your Social Security number was compromised, consider freezing your credit with all three major bureaus right away. You can also take advantage of free credit monitoring offered by the affected company, if available. Just verify the offer through the company's official website.

An unfamiliar credit inquiry deserves a closer look, but it doesn't always mean someone has stolen your identity. Contact the company listed on the inquiry using its official website or customer service number. Ask whether an application was submitted using your information. You should also review your credit reports from all three bureaus. You can get free weekly credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If you suspect someone is trying to open credit in your name, consider placing a free credit freeze immediately while you investigate. You can also add a fraud alert.
If you confirm that someone opened an account fraudulently, act immediately.

Contact the creditor's fraud department. Explain that the account was opened without your permission and ask for written confirmation of your fraud report.Dispute the fraudulent account with the credit bureaus. Check all three reports because the account may not appear on each one.Report the identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov to file a report with the Federal Trade Commission and create a personalized recovery plan.Consider placing a credit freeze and fraud alert. An extended seven-year fraud alert may be available once you have the required identity theft documentation.

A credit freeze alone won't help if someone already has access to one of your existing accounts. Contact the financial institution or service provider immediately. If your bank account is involved, report unauthorized transactions and ask what protections can be placed on the account. If your email was compromised, change the password from a trusted device, review recovery information and sign out of unfamiliar sessions. And if your phone suddenly loses service for no obvious reason, contact your wireless carrier immediately. An unexpected loss of service can be a warning sign of a SIM-swap attack.
WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS
A free credit freeze can make it harder for criminals to open new accounts in your name, but it won't stop every type of identity theft. (Danylo Antoniuk/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
What to do during the first week after a breach
You don't need to spend the entire week worrying about what might happen. However, you should address the most serious risks right away.

On the first day, verify the breach notice through an official source. Secure any compromised accounts and change exposed or reused passwords. If your Social Security number was involved, consider freezing your credit immediately.Next, review your credit reports and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize.During the rest of the week, check your bank transactions, payment accounts and mobile phone account for unusual activity. Enable available security alerts and continue monitoring for suspicious changes.

On the first day, verify the breach notice through an official source. Secure any compromised accounts and change exposed or reused passwords. If your Social Security number was involved, consider freezing your credit immediately.
Next, review your credit reports and look for accounts or inquiries you don't recognize.

During the rest of the week, check your bank transactions, payment accounts and mobile phone account for unusual activity. Enable available security alerts and continue monitoring for suspicious changes.

Also, watch out for follow-up scams. Criminals sometimes use major data breaches as an excuse to contact people with fake monitoring offers or recovery services. They may ask for your Social Security number, passwords or payment information. Don't trust a caller simply because they know details about the breach. Instead, verify offers by going directly to the affected company's official website.
A simple decision guide
Here's the easiest way to think about these protections.

Choose a credit freeze when your priority is making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. You can temporarily lift it when needed.Choose a fraud alert when you want lenders to verify your identity more carefully but prefer to keep your credit file accessible.Choose identity monitoring when you want notifications about certain suspicious changes and additional visibility into potential misuse of your information.
Choose a credit freeze when your priority is making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. You can temporarily lift it when needed.
Choose a fraud alert when you want lenders to verify your identity more carefully but prefer to keep your credit file accessible.
Choose identity monitoring when you want notifications about certain suspicious changes and additional visibility into potential misuse of your information.

You can use more than one tool. In fact, a credit freeze and monitoring service can complement each other. Just remember that none of these options replaces contacting your bank, creditor or service provider when fraud has already occurred.
When identity monitoring can complement a credit freeze

A credit freeze makes it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts in your name, but it won't alert you to every suspicious change involving your personal information. An identity monitoring service can complement that protection by watching for certain warning signs.

Depending on the plan, you may also have access to identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate disputes, documentation and recovery after identity theft. Neither tool guarantees complete protection, but together they can help you prevent certain problems and respond more quickly when suspicious activity appears.
Not all monitoring services offer the same protections. Before choosing one, consider these features:

Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes in your credit reports, including new accounts and suspicious inquiries.Financial account monitoring: Watches for certain unusual activity involving eligible linked bank or financial accounts.Dark web monitoring: Looks for exposed personal information in certain known data breaches and dark web sources.Identity restoration assistance: Provides professional guidance to help you recover if someone steals your identity.Identity theft expense coverage: Some plans provide reimbursement for eligible recovery expenses or stolen funds, subject to plan terms, coverage limits and exclusions. Coverage varies and may not apply to every type of loss.
Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes in your credit reports, including new accounts and suspicious inquiries.
Financial account monitoring: Watches for certain unusual activity involving eligible linked bank or financial accounts.
Dark web monitoring: Looks for exposed personal information in certain known data breaches and dark web sources.
Identity restoration assistance: Provides professional guidance to help you recover if someone steals your identity.

Identity theft expense coverage: Some plans provide reimbursement for eligible recovery expenses or stolen funds, subject to plan terms, coverage limits and exclusions. Coverage varies and may not apply to every type of loss.

Keep in mind that identity monitoring cannot prevent every form of fraud or guarantee that suspicious activity will always be detected. You'll still need to contact your bank, credit card company or other affected institution directly if you discover unauthorized activity.

The bottom line: A credit freeze can help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts, while identity monitoring can help you spot certain warning signs sooner. Using both can give you broader protection and make it easier to respond when something goes wrong.

Ask one question first: am I trying to block new credit, receive an early warning or recover from confirmed fraud? A freeze focuses on blocking access, a fraud alert adds verification and monitoring provides visibility. You may use more than one, but you do not need to activate every tool simply because a breach occurred.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE
Fraud alerts require lenders to take additional steps to verify your identity, while credit freezes restrict access to your credit report. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

One thing I've noticed about data breaches is that most people don't realize how vulnerable their personal information can be until something goes wrong. And by then, the damage may already be done. That's why I think it's smart to be proactive. A free credit freeze is a great place to start, but it only protects one part of your financial life.

What I like about an identity protection service is that it adds another layer of protection by monitoring for suspicious activity that you might otherwise miss. And if someone does steal your identity, having access to restoration specialists can make a stressful situation easier to manage. No service can stop every scam, but having someone watching for warning signs and helping you respond can make a real difference. For me, it's about getting ahead of the problem rather than finding out about it after the damage is done.
